#904. Un fiable Sevilla se deshace con firmeza de un débil Osasuna

El equipo andaluz se consolida en los puestos europeos conducido por un gran Fofana

Un magnífico Sevilla derrotó con absoluta solvencia a Osasuna para asentarse en la sexta posición de la tabla. Casi nada para un equipo que ha sufrido demasiado en las últimas temporadas y que ahora es solvente y poderoso, con jugadores de gran calidad, caso de Fofana, que marcan la diferencia. Con 17 puntos, el Sevilla le saca cinco puntos al séptimo clasificado, el Alavés. Una distancia que le hace vivir muy tranquilo y que, por el momento, le permite pensar, con argumentos, en una temporada para disfrutar, con la mente puesta, por qué no, en regresar a Europa. Hasta ahora, es el mejor, con diferencia, de esa Liga en la que compiten una multitud de equipos. Después de un duro uno de nueve puntos, el Sevilla volvió a ganar, con autoridad y buen juego. Y con una entrega de la grada que anticipa tiempos felices. Osasuna no está para nada. Jagoba Arrasate tiene mucho trabajo por delante. Es un equipo muy amanerado, débil lejos de El Sadar, donde no ha ganado en toda la temporada. Sufre demasiado y tiene poco talento. El Sevilla se lo comió.

Nervión vive un aire distinto. Después de tres temporadas de sufrimiento, el Sevilla se ha convertido en un equipo fiable. Un conjunto bien dirigido por Luis García Plaza, asentado en un buen centro del campo, donde destaca Fofana, y donde el propio técnico se va gustando. Por ejemplo, jugando ante Osasuna con dos delanteros, Stassin e Isaac Romero, y con dos extremos, además, como Ejuke y Correia. Un planteamiento valiente, atrevido, que acogotó a un Osasuna todavía lejos de lo que quiere Arrasate.

Solo un par de acercamientos de los navarros en un inicio algo chisposo llevaron la inquietud a una grada entregada. Nadie entiende del Balón de Oro en un Sánchez Pizjuán que comienza a recordar al de años pasados. A un acercamiento de Boyomo a la salida de un saque de esquina siguió un partido de dominio total del Sevilla. Correia falló solo ante Aitor, este rechazó también un disparo lejano de Kike Salas y lo mejor llegó en el minuto 24. Fofana demostró con su pase que, a veces, un pase atrás es mejor que uno adelantado. La visión de juego del excelente centrocampista del Sevilla tuvo un gran colofón en el disparo de Isaac Romero. Un golazo para poner por delante a su equipo. Osasuna, demasiado premioso, incapaz de hacer un regate, sin encontrar a Budimir, cayó ante el empuje de un buen Sevilla. Castrín lanzó alto con todo a favor y Aitor le sacó un buen balón a Ejuke. El extremo disfrutó ante Bretones. Regates y velocidad para conectar con la grada.

El Sevilla no salió tan jugón en la segunda mitad. Osasuna dio un paso adelante, aunque sin demasiada convicción. Realmente, el conjunto navarro jamás encontró la fórmula para crearle peligro al Sevilla, siempre seguro atrás. Apenas un disparo de Torró que sacó Suazo generó alguna inquietud. García Plaza movió bien el banquillo. Reforzó su centro del campo con la entrada de Bueno y Vargas entró por Ejuke. El Sevilla se recompuso, hasta el punto de que empezó a encadenar ocasiones de gol. Iglesias remató al palo tras un saque de esquina y Aitor salvó los muebles para su equipo con una buena estirada a remate de Kike Salas.

Arrasate lo intentó con Raúl y Moro. Luego, con un triple cambio con Osambela, Arguibide y Barja. Todo fue inútil. Nervión entró en modo caldera, Osasuna tocaba y tocaba sin peligro, mientras que el Sevilla se hacía fuerte con su ventaja tras el gol de Isaac.

Incluso se permitió dibujar un contragolpe maravilloso en las botas de Fofana. Vargas, muy bien en defensa, le robó el balón a Barja. Fofana se cruzó todo el campo en una conducción estupenda para asistir a su compañero Correia. El extremo recortó y batió a Aitor, que no pudo hacer nada después de un toque del balón en un defensa de Osasuna. La fiesta fue ya completa en un Pizjuán que vuelve a sonreír como antaño, como en los buenos tiempos.

#906. Can Germany revive its economy before the far-right AfD gains ground?

Conflicts, rising costs and Chinese competition are testing Germany's economic model like never before. Can new growth sectors create jobs and ease voters' economic fears, thereby helping contain the far-right AfD?

Germany's export-led economic model faces unprecedented strain just as support for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party reaches a new peak.

Chinese rivals are steadily eroding the market share of major German industrial players, while persistently high energy prices, elevated labor costs and excessive red tape are adding to the structural crisis.

After two years of contraction, real GDP edged up only 0.2% last year, according to the Federal Statistical Office, Destatis. Exports to China fell 9.7% in 2025, withGerman vehicle and part shipments plunging by a third.

While there are signs the German economy is turning the corner, the government's latest forecast of 1.3% growth in 2026 is still modest compared with the pre-COVID boom years.

The AfD is currently polling ahead of all other political parties in Germany. The country's many economic challenges have been a major factor in the right-wing populists' rise.

Germany's domestic intelligence agency sees reliable indications that the AfD is right-wing extremist in its entirety.

The party has vowed to put Germany back on a growth path by ending the transition to renewable energies, lowering taxes and renegotiating European Union treaties, while also reforming welfare and sharply restricting immigration.

As Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition searches for a fresh growth strategy to fend off the rise in populist politics, the government has set out its high-tech agenda focusing on six priority sectors.

These are artificial intelligence (AI), quantum computing, microelectronics, biotechnology, clean energy (including nuclear fusion) and climate-neutral mobility.

Irene Bertschek, head of the Digital Economy research unit at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW), argues that Germany's research in these "key enabling technologies is very strong, particularly in the area of climate-neutral technologies."

Yet, the results are often commercialized abroad, Bertschek told DW, with the United States leading in AI and China closing the gap quickly.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A report published Monday by the Made for Germany initiative — a group of 147 companies and investors — builds on the government's plan, estimating that these and other new technologies could attract up to €4.1 trillion ($4.6 trillion) in investment by 2035.

Realizing that potential, however, will depend less on today's industrial giants, like Volkswagen, Siemens and BASF.

"It will not primarily be the established companies that conquer these new fields, but innovative newcomers — startups," Oliver Falck, director of the ifo Center for the Economics of Innovation and Digital Transformation, told DW.

The task, Falck said, is to create the right conditions for startups to emerge, including proximity to top universities, access to private capital and enough freedom to experiment.

He argues for state financing during the early-stage "valley of death" — the risky phase between research and commercial viability when private financing is often scarce.

There are clear signs this shift is already happening. Data from Deutsche Bank and startupdetector, a German startup database and market intelligence platform, show more than 3,000 startups were founded in Germany in the first half of 2026, up 88% from the same period last year. One-third of the new ventures have an AI focus.

Venture-capital investment soared 44% to €5.8 billion in the first half of 2026, with firms such as Neura Robotics and drone manufacturers Stark and Quantum Systems benefiting.

US investors, meanwhile, are increasingly buying up Germany's famed Mittelstand — its traditional small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) — with an eye on their specialized technology.

"The German Mittelstand is highly innovative. Now it is essential to invest in key technologies such as artificial intelligence and to tap into the potential that arises at the intersection with established technologies," Bertschek stressed.

The expert, who is also chair of the German government's Commission of Experts for Research and Innovation (EFI), thinks SMEs should make better use of their huge amounts of production data and collaborate with AI startups to help those young firms grow.

Another idea for accelerating the shift to new high-tech sectors comes from Sven Gabor Janszky, chairman of the Leipzig-based futures-research institute 2b AHEAD. He argues that Germany needs special economic zones to help catch the next wave of economic growth.

"For a few specific technologies, you lower the regulations, you recruit ambitious workers and pump money into these zones," Janszky told DW.

This, he added, would follow the examples of Silicon Valley and Chinese mega-cities Shenzhen and Shanghai's Pudong district, and echoes the conditions that helped rebuild the German economy after World War II.

In Janszky's view, these zones would help Germany position itself as a first mover in emerging fields rather than remaining tied to older industrial strengths.

"EU regulations may try to prohibit this move, but Germany will have to overcome them so we can grow the economy again," he added.

The sharp rise in Germany's defense spending will also help several of the high-tech sectors now being prioritized.

According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), the defense budget is expected to reach around €120 billion in 2026 — roughly 2.6% of GDP. The government wants this figure to hit 3.5% by 2029.

The resulting procurement will provide a major boost to the production of drones, sensors, communications systems and other dual-use technologies that have both civilian and military applications.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yet, with major rival China benefiting from much lower energy and worker costs, along with huge government subsidies, Germany will continue to face similar price disadvantages when exporting its new high-end tech. But that doesn't have to spell failure, said Falck, the ifo expert.

"Take the semiconductor industry as an example. It is probably unrealistic to aim for leadership along the entire value chain. But it is enough to lead at individual choke points," he pointed out.

"And that is exactly where Germany is strong: as a supplier of equipment for state-of-the-art chip fabs and as a supplier to the world's AI gigafactories, with power semiconductors."

In other words, with a first-mover advantage, decades of high-quality production data and a focus on specialized niches, Germany can remain a major force in advanced industrial and engineering technologies.

Union Defence Minister Rajnath Singh arrives for the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting on October 20, 2026 | Photo Credit: ANI

There can be no justification for terrorism and no double standards in tackling the menace, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said on Tuesday, called on the member states of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) to dismantle the entire ecosystem of terrorism.

He was speaking at the 25th meeting of the SCO Council of Heads of Government in Dushanbe, Tajikistan, in the presence of Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar.

Also Read: In a first since 2023, Delhi invites Pakistan Minister for inaugural SCO Civilisational Dialogue in November

“Terrorism results in the loss of innocent lives and disrupts investment and commerce. It radicalises societies and deprives youth of the opportunities they rightfully deserve. There can be no justification for terrorism, no double standards in addressing it, and no place for those who finance, support, or provide safe havens to terrorists,” Mr. Singh said.

He recalled Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s remarks at the SCO Summit in Bishkek in August and September, calling for concrete steps on security, connectivity, and opportunity. Mr. Singh said the organisation must adhere to the principles of sovereign equality, consensus, and mutual respect.

On economic cooperation, the Defence Minister called for strengthening resilient supply chains, facilitating trade and investment, and leveraging technology to address global uncertainties arising from geopolitical tensions, trade disruptions, and concerns over energy and food security. India supported the adoption of an action plan for the multilateral trade and economic cooperation programme for the period 2026-2030, he said.

New SCO mechanisms should address clearly identified needs and avoid duplication, Mr. Singh said. He welcomed the decisions to establish the Universal Centre in Tashkent and the Anti-Drug Centre in Dushanbe as permanent SCO bodies, while stressing the need for effective coordination and timely implementation.

Highlighting regional connectivity, he noted initiatives such as the International North-South Transport Corridor and Chabahar Port could connect Central Asia with wider markets. However, connectivity projects must respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all countries, he said.

The Defence Minister also highlighted India’s digital public infrastructure, start-up ecosystem, and women-led development initiatives, alongside its international efforts on clean energy and climate resilience.

The meeting reviewed economic and trade cooperation among member States and discussed transport, finance, the digital economy, and social development.

The Heads of Delegation adopted a joint communiqué, the SCO budget for 2027, and the action plan for multilateral trade and economic cooperation for 2026-2030. Mr. Singh also invited member States to participate in the first SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum, to be hosted by India later this year.

#909. "Superintelligenz" statt KI: Trumps neue Sprachregelung

Donald Trump hat die US-Behörden angeordnet, statt "Künstliche Intelligenz" künftig den Begriff "Superintelligenz" zu nutzen. Warum der US-Präsident KI für unpassend hält und was Tech-Experten dazu sagen.

Was ist nur los mit Donald Trump und seinem Bedürfnis, alles Mögliche neu zu benennen? Erst wurde der Golf von Mexiko zum Golf von Amerika - zumindest in offiziellen Dokumenten der USA, wenn auch nicht global. Dann kam der Ontariosee, nun nach Willen des US-Präsidenten der Amerikasee. Und nun soll auch die neue Technologie, die unser Zeitalter prägen wird, die künstliche Intelligenz oder KI, einen neuen Namen erhalten.

Anfang September behauptete der US-Präsident auf seiner Plattform Truth Social, der Begriff "künstliche Intelligenz" sei "ungenau" und "unzutreffend". Bessere Alternativen wären "überlegene", "extreme" oder "höchste" Intelligenz.

In einer über drei Tage in den sozialen Medien durchgeführten Umfrage gaben Trump-Fans mit 65 Prozent dem Begriff "Superintelligenz" (SI) den Vorzug über "Überlegene Intelligenz" (35 Prozent). Daraufhin verkündete Trump vergangene Woche vor der Vollversammlung der Vereinten Nationen, dass von nun an in Dokumenten der US-Bundesregierung diese neue Bezeichnung verwendet werde.

Bislang hat die Tech-Branche die Bezeichnung jedoch noch nicht übernommen und Akademiker weisen darauf hin, dass Superintelligenz ein Begriff für die Zukunft sei, wenn die Technologie den Menschen in allen Bereichen überlegen ist. Aktuelle KI-Modelle seien davon noch Jahre entfernt, betonen sie.

"KI ist in den meisten Fällen keine Superintelligenz sondern lediglich eine andere Intelligenz", sagt Pedro Domingos, emeritierter Professor für Informatik und Ingenieurwissenschaften an der University of Washington, zur DW. "KI macht andere Dinge als die Menschen, sie als Superintelligenz zu bezeichnen ist also irreführend."

Computerwissenschaftler und Mathematiker prägten den Begriff "künstliche Intelligenz" 1956 während eines Sommer-Workshops am Dartmouth College in New Hampshire, USA. "Künstlich" hieß dabei einfach "von Menschen gemacht", im Unterschied zur natürlichen menschlichen Intelligenz.

Nicht alle Experten waren mit dieser Bezeichnung einverstanden. In ihrem Buch "Denkmaschinen: Die Geschichte der künstlichen Intelligenz" zitiert Pamela McCorduck den KI-Pionier Arthur Samuel, der der Meinung war, der Begriff lasse einen an "etwas Unechtes" denken.

Doch in den vergangenen 70 Jahren hat sich der Begriff durchgesetzt. Ihn zu ändern wird die vielen Ängste im Zusammenhang mit KI - dass Jobs verloren gehen, der Mensch überflüssig wird oder wir die Kontrolle über die Maschinen verlieren - nicht mindern, sagen Kritiker.

"Die Namensänderung fördert solche Ängste: 'Oh, es handelt sich um Superintelligenz und die wird uns Menschen überflüssig machen, sich gegen uns wenden, unsere Jobs wegnehmen", warnt Domingos. "Wenn du die Gegenbewegung gegen KI maximieren willst, dann nenne sie Überlegene Intelligenz."

Die Ängste der Bevölkerung nehmen rasch zu. In einer Anfang des Monats von Public First für Politico durchgeführten Studie sprach sich etwa die Hälfte der Befragten in sechs Ländern - den USA, Kanada, Frankreich, Spanien, Deutschland und Großbritannien - dafür aus, weitere Entwicklungen im Bereich KI zu pausieren, um das Risiko zu verringern, dass die neue Technologie die Menschheit auslöschen könnte.

Einer weiteren, von SSRS für CNN durchgeführten Studie zufolge sind fast neun von zehn US-Amerikanern eher besorgt als begeistert darüber, dass die KI die menschliche Intelligenz übertreffen könnte.

Diese Bedenken haben auch den US-Kongress erreicht. Gemeinsam mit anderen hat der parteiunabhängige Senator von Vermont, Bernie Sanders, einen Gesetzesentwurf für ein "dauerhaftes Verbot der Entwicklung künstlicher Superintelligenz", die vom Menschen nicht kontrolliert werden kann, eingebracht.

Der Gesetzesentwurf fordert außerdem eine Aussetzung der Entwicklung fortschrittlicher KI-Technologien, bis entsprechende Tests und Kontrollmechanismen auf Bundesebene eingerichtet sind.

Den großen KI-Entwicklern in den USA, die ihre Modelle gerne ins Zentrum der Aufmerksamkeit rücken wollen, könnte die von Trump geforderte neue Bezeichnung natürlich gelegen kommen. Ihre Systeme sind den Menschen bereits in vielen spezialisierten Aufgaben überlegen und waren China bis vor kurzem weit voraus.

Doch sowohl Anthropic, das Unternehmen hinter dem Modell Claude, als auch OpenAI, das ChatGPT entwickelt hat, haben Pläne für einen Börsengang verschoben. Einige Marktbeobachter machen dafür die jüngsten Vorfälle verantwortlich, bei denen KI-Modelle sich in Computersysteme gehackt oder Aufgaben ausgeführt hatten, die sie nicht ausführen sollten.

Während chinesische Modelle den Qualitätsrückstand bei deutlich geringerer Rechenleistung weitgehend aufholen, könnte den US-Entwicklern eine Umbenennung, die den Eindruck bestärkt, dass sie weiterhin führend im Rennen um KI sind, durchaus gelegen kommen. Laut Zahlen von Goldman Sachs sollen die Ausgaben für KI bald die Marke von einer Billion US-Dollar (880 Milliarden Euro) übersteigen.

"Es ist ganz im Interesse der US-Entwickler, von Super-, Hyper-, überlegener oder sonstiger Intelligenz zu sprechen, weil es ihre Fähigkeiten hervorhebt. Es ist schlicht Marketing", sagt Domingos, Autor des 2015 veröffentlichten Buchs "The Master Algorithm".

Die aktuellen KI-Modelle werden immer besser und führen viele Aufgaben bereits eigenständig aus. In den Entwicklungslaboren wird jedoch viel über den nächsten Schritt, KI-Systeme, die sich selbst verbessern, diskutiert. Dies wird als rekursive Selbstverbesserung oder RSI bezeichnet.

Elon Musk hat bereits vorhergesagt, dass die Lernprozesse der KI bis Ende des Jahres oder bis 2027 automatisiert werden könnten, ohne die Notwendigkeit menschlicher Eingaben. Bei OpenAI geht man davon aus, dass es bis dahin ein Jahr länger dauern könnte. Doch selbst dann werden die KI-Systeme nicht vollständig rekursiv sein.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Anfang September argumentierte Jürgen Schmidhuber, ein deutscher Informatiker, der in der Schweiz arbeitet, in einem Blog-Eintrag: "Für eine vollständige RSI ist nicht nur sich selbst verbessernde (KI-)Software, sondern auch sich selbst verbessernde Hardware erforderlich."

Mit anderen Worten, um Superintelligenz oder RSI zu erreichen, müssten die Tech-Unternehmen Chips und humanoide Roboter produzieren und ganze Fabriken bauen, die keinen menschlichen Input benötigen.

Auch wenn die KI die Chipentwicklung beschleunigt, kann sie den Fertigungsprozess noch nicht alleine ausführen. Bis Maschinen sich ohne jede menschliche Beteiligung selbst verbessern können, vergehen vermutlich noch Jahrzehnte.

Doch neben den Wissenschaftlern, die am maschinellen Lernen arbeiten, wird auch die Politik eine große Rolle dabei spielen, ob sich die Bezeichnung "Superintelligenz" durchsetzt. Auch wenn Trump behauptete, dem chinesischen Präsidenten Xi Jinping habe der Begriff gefallen, gibt es noch keine Anzeichen dafür, dass China sich von "KI" verabschiedet.

Auf einem Tech-Gipfel mit führenden Vertretern der Branche unterzeichnete Trump am Dienstag eine Durchführungsverordnung, die US-Behörden und -Agenturen anweist, den Begriff Superintelligenz zu verwenden. Doch auch wenn einige der führenden Köpfe von Big Tech den Begriff übernommen haben, halten Experten es für unwahrscheinlich, dass er sich durchsetzen wird.

"Angesichts der politischen Ausrichtung der meisten Menschen im Bereich KI ist es wahrscheinlicher, dass sie genau im Gegenteil sagen, 'Zur Hölle mit dir. Jetzt sprechen wir erst rechtvon künstlicher Intelligenz", meint Domingos.

Adaptiert aus dem Englischen von Phoenix Hanzo.

#910. What is known about Putin's phone call with Norwegian PM, Finnish president

MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store have spoken by phone with Russian leader Vladimir Putin, the Finnish presidential office said.

Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed the report to TASS.

TASS has compiled the main details available so far.

- Stubb and Store held a phone call with Putin on October 27, according to the Finnish presidential office.

- The two leaders took part in the call on behalf of their respective countries, rather than representing Europe as a whole.

- Stubb and Store initiated the conversation with Putin to discuss the situation in Ukraine and an upcoming meeting in Abu Dhabi.

- They also discussed maintaining stability in the Baltic Sea region and the High North.

- Finnish President Alexander Stubb called the conversation frank and substantive, his office reported.

- Stubb stressed that ending the conflict in Ukraine requires continued direct dialogue with Russia.

- Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store stressed the importance of de-escalating the Ukrainian conflict during the call, the country's government press service reported.

- President Vladimir Putin held a phone call with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed to TASS.

- Peskov noted that an official statement detailing the outcome of the talks is being prepared.

#911. China’s Hengrui posts 89% rise in third-quarter net profit, beating estimates

Net profit reached 2.46 billion yuan for the quarter, also above analyst estimates

Jiangsu Hengrui Pharmaceuticals, one of China’s largest drug makers, reported a 20.55 per cent rise in third-quarter revenue to 8.95 billion yuan (US$1.34 billion), beating analyst estimates of 8.55 billion yuan amid stronger innovative drug sales.

Net profit reached 2.46 billion yuan for the three months ended September 30, jumping 88.92 per cent year on year and exceeding the Bloomberg analyst consensus estimate of 2.38 billion yuan.

Improving innovative drug sales and out-licensing revenue contributed to the growth, the company said in a Tuesday filing.

#913. Jay-Z actuará en el intermedio del LXI Super Bowl, que organiza su propia empresa

Tras la histórica actuación de Bad Bunny en 2026, el artista y empresario, propietario de Roc Nation, encabezará la 61ª final de la NFL, la liga de fútbol americano

Los rumores han quedado despejados. El próximo 14 de febrero de 2027, el rapero Jay-Z, de 56 años, será quien le ponga música al intermedio de la Super Bowl. La final número 61 de la liga nacional de fútbol americano de Estados Unidos (NFL, por sus siglas en inglés) estará protagonizada, además de por los dos equipos que logren llegar a la última instancia, por el cantante y empresario, que es además el propietario de Roc Nation, la empresa encargada de organizar el evento.

En las apuestas sobre quién cantaría en la célebre final y sucedería a Bad Bunny, estrella de este año, destacaban nombres como los de Miley Cyrus, Harry Styles, Billie Eilish y Justin Bieber. Finalmente, será Shawn Carter el encargado de subir al escenario del estadio SoFi, en la ciudad de Los Ángeles, California, en el día de San Valentín. El anuncio se hizo este lunes, 26 de octubre, durante la transmisión del partido entre los Dallas Cowboys y los Philadelphia Eagles, con un vídeo de 15 segundos con un sencillo mensaje: “GOAT’S out of the bag”, que se traduce a “El más grande de la historia se ha destapado”.

GOAT’s out of the bag. @sc #AppleMusicHalftime #SBLXI pic.twitter.com/6wnIqTKjZB

Y en un breve comunicado publicado poco después, Roc Nation ha puesto sobre la mesa el próximo misterio: quién acompañará a Jay-Z en el escenario más visto de Estados Unidos. “Por supuesto, su esposa, Beyoncé, encabezará la lista. Beyoncé fue la protagonista del espectáculo del descanso de la Super Bowl XLVII y fue invitada especial en la Super Bowl 50. Esta será la segunda vez que la Super Bowl se celebre en el SoFi Stadium. En la Super Bowl LVI actuaron Dr. Dre y Snoop Dogg. Tras acompañar a Jay-Z en su reciente concierto en Inglewood, es probable que sus nombres también se barajen como posibles candidatos”, dice el comunicado.

Hace ya seis años que Jay-Z maneja los hilos del intermedio deportivo más famoso del mundo. El neoyorquino firmó un acuerdo con la NFL, la liga de fútbol nacional estadounidense, en 2019, y lo renovó en 2024 y hasta 2029. Gracias a él, y por unos cinco millones de dólares anuales, Roc Nation es la responsable de organizar el medio tiempo del célebre espectáculo que siguen en directo millones de espectadores en todo el mundo.

Precisamente hace ahora 30 años que Shawn Corey Carter empezó su carrera y que lo hizo con Roc-A-Fella (germen de la actual Roc Nation), porque intentó publicar un álbum y ninguna compañía quería, decidiéndose así a fundar la suya propia y así lanzar su primer disco, Reasonable Doubt, todo un éxito con la crítica que el año pasado fue inducido en el Salón de la Fama de los premios Grammy. Pronto publicó un segundo álbum, In My Lifetime, Vol. 1, que le produjo su entonces amigo, el rapero y hoy condenado Sean Combs, apodado Puff Daddy o Diddy. Pero su carrera empezó a ir en ascenso dos años después, en 1988, cuando ganaba su primer Grammy y llegaba a su primer número uno en Billboard gracias a su tercer álbum, Vol. 2... Hard Knock Life. Ha ganado 25 premios Grammy, de un total de 89 nominaciones.

En sus primeros tiempos lanzaba casi un álbum al año, hasta que en 2003 empezó a espaciarlos. Su último trabajo propio es 4:44, de 2017, pero también ha producido a decenas de artistas. En 2008 cofundó Roc Nation junto a la mexicana Desirée Pérez, su directora ejecutiva, Jay Brown, Juan Pérez y Tyran Smith. Como explica la propia web de la compañía, entre sus clientes están Rihanna, Christina Aguilera, John Legen, Alicia Keys y A$AP Rocky.

La actuación de Jay-Z llega en un momento de conmemoración de su carrera. Para celebrar sus tres décadas en la industria, está realizando una gira de 30 conciertos, que precisamente ha cerrado con shows el pasado viernes y sábado en el estadio SoFi, donde se celebrará la Super Bowl dentro de cuatro meses. Además, el mes pasado, HBO lanzó una serie documental llamada Jay-Z in 8 sobre toda su trayectoria.

La Super Bowl es uno de los espectáculos más vistos del mundo entero. La del pasado febrero, en la que los Seattle Seahawks se impusieron a los New England Patriots por 29-13, llevándose su segundo trofeo, fue seguida por una media de 124,9 millones de personas. Una cifra que crece aún más durante el medio tiempo, que este año con Bad Bunny congregó a 128,2 millones de espectadores, una cifra algo inferior al récord logrado en 2025 por el rapero Kendrick Lamar, con 133,5 millones.

Lo que sí superó Benito Antonio Martínez Ocasio fue los tiempos de consumo, que durante las 24 horas posteriores al partido se dispararon, con 4.000 millones de visualizaciones ese primer día, un 137% más que el año anterior. Además, Apple Music proporcionó datos que aseguraban que la música del puertorriqueño se disparó en escuchas, y que tras el espectáculo se multiplicaron por siete. El de Bad Bunny, con intentos de boicot por parte del Gobierno de Donald Trump, fue el primer intermedio en completo en español de la historia de la Super Bowl.

Updated - October 27, 2026 04:15 pm IST - NEW DELHI

SCO National Coordinators meet in Islamabad. MEA Jt Secy, Multilateral and Economic Relations, Alok Dimri, represented India. Photo: Pakistan MoFA.

Pakistan announced that it would host the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in August 2027, as an Indian delegation led by a senior MEA official attended a preparatory meeting in Islamabad—the first such official Indian visit to Pakistan since Operation Sindoor last year.

The three-day meeting of SCO National Coordinators that began on Monday (September 29, 2026) comes days after India and Pakistan sparred with each other over the issue of terrorism and the Kashmir dispute at the UN General Assembly (UNGA). External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar and Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif traded allegations in their national addresses, while Indian and Pakistani diplomats exercised their rights of reply to the speeches on the global stage last week.

On Tuesday (September 29, 2026), India also rejected Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s reference to Kashmir in his UNGA speech.

Also Read: In a first since 2023, Delhi invites Pakistan Minister for inaugural SCO Civilisational Dialogue in November

The participation of Joint Secretary (Multilaterals and Economic Relations) Alok Dimri marked a higher level of Indian representation than at the past few meetings held under Pakistan’s Chairpersonship of the SCO this year. In mid-September, a meeting of SCO-Regional Anti-Terror Structure in Islamabad was attended by the Indian Charge d’affaires in Pakistan Satyapal Pandey, without a delegation from India.

In a statement, the Pakistan Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that Pakistan’s SCO Chairship would promote the theme of “Turning Vision into Action: Connectivity, Innovation and Shared Prosperity,” for 2026-207.

“The [National Coordinator] meeting marks an important initial engagement under Pakistan’s Chairmanship and would contribute to preparations for various high-level engagements and activities to be undertaken during the Chairmanship, including the meeting of the SCO Council of Heads of State to be hosted by Pakistan in August 2027,” the MoFA statement issued in Islamabad said.

Indian officials made it clear that the SCO coordinators’ meet was being held in a multilateral format and hence had no particular significance for India-Pakistan bilateral ties. However, the participation does leave the path open to higher-level attendance at the Ministerial-level events and the Heads of Council meet, to which Prime Minister Narendra Modi has been invited. Thus far, New Delhi has avoided the leaders’ meetings in both Delhi and Islamabad.

In 2023, PM Modi hosted the SCO Heads of Council Summit virtually, while Mr. Jaishankar hosted Pakistani Foreign Minister Bilawal Bhutto in person for the SCO Foreign Ministers’ meeting in Goa. In 2024, Mr. Jaishankar travelled to Islamabad to attend the SCO Heads of Government meeting as well. The MEA has thus far declined to comment on whether Mr. Modi would travel to Pakistan next year, but has not ruled it out either.

At a briefing on Tuesday (September 29, 2026), MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal brushed aside a question about whether India would oppose the induction of Turkiye to the 10-nation SCO, which currently comprises China, Russia, India, Pakistan, Iran, Belarus and four Central Asian States- Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan.

Turkish President Erdogan had told journalists earlier this month that Türkiye would pursue a “higher level” of engagement with the SCO than its observer status, indicating he could ask for full membership next year, particularly given close ties and the military pact with SCO host Pakistan.

“As and when any issue of membership comes it is for [SCO] members to collectively decide as to how to go forward on that,” Mr. Jaiswal said. He also criticised Mr. Erdogan for referring to Kashmir in his UNGA speech last week, when he called for a resolution of all South Asian disputes “including Kashmir”.

“India rejects the unwarranted references to India and the Indian Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir made by the President of Türkiye during his address to the UN General Assembly. This is a matter, as you would understand, pertaining to India’s territorial integrity and sovereignty, and no external party has any locus standi on this issue,” Mr. Jaiswal said on Tuesday.

#919. Bulgaria: Concerns about security in the Black Sea dominate presidential election campaign

Bulgaria's presidential election campaign has been shaped by recent drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea and the government's reduced support for Ukraine, making foreign policy a key factor in the first round.

Six months after Bulgaria's parliamentary election, the country is gearing up to choose its next president.

Although the role of president in Bulgaria is largely ceremonial, the election on October 25 — with a potential runoff on November 1 — will serve as a test for the government of former President Rumen Radev, whose party won a landslide victory in April, securing an unprecedented majority — the first in Bulgaria in almost three decades.

Although there are 27 candidates on the ballot, the race has narrowed to a duel between the incumbent president, Iliana Yotova, who served two terms as Radev's vice president and is backed by the prime minister, and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who is supported by opposition parties.

According to the Bulgarian Constitution, the Bulgarian president embodies national unity. He or she represents the country at international level (with a few exceptions), is the commander-in-chief of its armed forces, appoints members of the Supreme Judicial Council and various regulatory bodies, including caretaker governments, and has the power to veto legislation.

Hristo Panchugov, a political scientist at the New Bulgarian University in Sofia, argued that although the president's powers are formally limited, the office is particularly significant in the current context.

"For the first time in Bulgaria's modern democratic history, we have an absolutely uncontested majority that is not held together by any coalition, but rather by a single political party that faces an opposition that is completely falling apart," he told DW.

Panchugov went on to say that it would have been better if the campaign had focused more on "whether the president could serve as a counterbalance."

Opposition candidate Andrey Gyurov reiterated this point in an interview with DW: "We are seeing a concentration of power that always bears the marks of a slide toward autocracy... A president should know how to say no."

Iliana Yotova declined DW's request for an interview.

Initially, the presidential race was characterized by small rallies, a lack of televised debates and numerous personal attacks on the two leading candidates.

In recent weeks, however, following drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea, the two frontrunners' diverging positions on support for Ukraine have come to the fore.

Bulgaria's government initially declined invitations to join the Coalition of the Willing and NATO's anti-drone initiative but changed its position on the latter after the recent drone attacks.

Yotova has advocated for the establishment of a "Coalition of Peace," in which she believes Bulgaria would have a stronger diplomatic voice in the process to endRussia's war in Ukraine.

"There are many warmongers in our country; I am not one of them," she said at a campaign rally this month. "As long as I am president — and if you place your trust in me — not a single Bulgarian soldier will go to Ukraine."

Yotova has sought to reassure voters that no Bulgarian troops will be sent to Ukraine, even though this has not featured in public debate, and has been ruled out by a 2025 parliamentary declaration that reaffirmed that the Bulgarian Armed Forces would not participate in hostilities there.

Nevertheless, the recent drone attacks on commercial ships in the Black Sea have put new pressure on both the president and Rumen Radev's Progressive Bulgaria party.

"The drone strikes in the Black Sea brought the otherwise abstract geopolitical situation right into the daily lives of every Bulgarian," Boriana Dimitrova, managing partner of the Alpha Research market and social research agency, told DW.

Many in Europe, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, have laid the blame for the attacks squarely at Russia's door. The fact that Bulgaria's leaders did not clearly attribute blame for the attacks fueled frustration across the country.

After the first drone attack, President Yotova convened the country's Consultative Council on National Security. Its subsequent declaration did not name the source of the threat in the Black Sea.

A week later, after the second attack, Prime Minister Radev said, "We lack solid, clear evidence to level accusations against any specific party; however logic suggests the outcome works to the advantage of Russia." He then summoned the Russian ambassador for talks.

The stance of the government and president is having an impact on the race.

"We're seeing a slight decline in support for Iliana Yotova, which is not threatening her first-place position by any means in the first round, but there has been a decline given the ambiguity of some of the positions she has taken," said Boriana Dimitrova.

As the issue of security entered the public debate, some Bulgarians took to the streets in Sofia to protest against what they saw as the government's ambiguous foreign policy stance on this matter.

"I think the drone attacks in the Black Sea and the utterly spineless stance of the president, the prime minister, and everyone acting in unison were the last straw, and I believe that, on the eve of the presidential election, this should serve as a catalyst," Vlada Tzenova, one of the protesters, told DW.

All this is reflected in the preliminary results of the latest opinion poll conducted by Alpha Research. While expected voter turnout is up, the gap between the two frontrunners has narrowed: Yotova is still ahead, leading Gyurov by about 12 percentage points in the first round, but the margin is smaller than it was.

Nevertheless, these recent dynamics do not necessarily mean a shift in the balance of power.

Panchugov said that Gyurov's campaign has been hampered by his hesitancy to declare his candidacy, a lack of "passion" in his campaign, and the fact that he made few comments on current affairs before he joined the race.

Moreover, supporters of the candidate of the pro-Russian nationalist Vazrazhdane (Revival) party, which ranked third in the Alpha Research poll, would be most likely to support Yotova in a second round.

What could decide the outcome of the election is the fact that both GERB and DPS, two of the established parties that attracted the support of more than 660,000 voters in April, did not field a presidential candidate.

According to Alpha Research, half of GERB's supporters do not intend to vote in the first round. The party dominated Bulgaria's political landscape for 17 years but lost power in December following mass anti-corruption protests backed by opposition parties supporting Andrey Gyurov.

Most of the remaining GERB supporters are expected to back Gyurov, as the party has historically opposed Iliana Yotova's political home, the Bulgarian Socialist Party.

At the same time, both Gyurov's campaign and nationalist parties are seeing increased mobilization, with the latter drawing support from voters disappointed by the government's cautious response to the drone attacks.

"We can view these elections as the first test of confidence in the party that recently won the election," Boriana Dimitrova said. "In peaceful times, the center attracts the most attention; in turbulent times, those candidates who take a clearer stance — regardless of the direction — gain greater visibility."

#921. Bundestrainer Jürgen Klopp reagiert verständnislos auf Rassismus gegen das DFB-Team

Rassistische Kommentare begleiten die DFB-Elf seit Tagen. Rund um das Spiel gegen Serbien antwortet jeder auf seine Weise: Klopp mit klaren Worten, sein Team mit starkem Auftritt und die Fans mit viel Schwarz-Rot-Gold.

Immer wieder hallten Sprechchöre wie "Schwarz-Rot-Gold" oder "Deutschland, Deutschland" durch das Stadion in München. Die Fans schwenkten stolz ihre Fahnen, sangen und feierten ihre Nationalmannschaft. Der 2:0 (1:0)-Sieg gegen Serbien wirkte wie ein Befreiungsschlag - auf mehreren Ebenen.

Zum einen war es der erste Sieg für den neuen Bundestrainer Jürgen Klopp, dem an diesem Abend "alles" an seiner Mannschaft gefallen hatte. "Die Anfangsphase, der Mittelteil, das Ende. Es war ein perfekter Abend. Ich bin so happy und stolz auf das, was wir gezeigt haben", so der 59-Jährige.

Die Nationalmannschaft zeigte das beste Spiel unter dem neuen Bundestrainer und auch von den Rängen wurde das Team lauter und emotionaler unterstützt als bei den vergangenen Partien.

Nach der Niederlage gegen Griechenland am vergangenen Sonntag hatte es erstmals seit Klopps Verpflichtung leichte Kritik gegeben - dazu Pfiffe nach dem Spiel. Zudem häuften sich in den Sozialen Netzwerken rassistische Kommentare über die DFB-Elf.

Schon bei Veröffentlichung der Mannschaftsaufstellung vor der Partie wurde das DFB-Team als "nicht weiß genug" oder "nicht deutsch genug" für eine deutsche Nationalmannschaft bezeichnet und aufs Übelste beschimpft.

"Es gibt keinen Grund, sich über diese Menschen Gedanken zu machen. Meine Gedanken kriegen sie nicht", hatte Klopp in der Pressekonferenz vor dem Spiel gegen Serbien auf Nachfrage der Deutschen Welle (DW) erklärt. Er habe schon im normalen Leben für Dummheit wenig Zeit und in sozialen Medien auch nicht.

"Die große Crux in unserem Leben ist, dass jeder seine Meinung sagen darf", so der Bundestrainer. Solche Kommentare seien "Wahnsinn".

Auch auf politischer Ebene ist die Nationalmannschaft immer wieder Thema, vor allem einige Mitglieder der Partei "Alternative für Deutschland" (AfD) schießen regelmäßig gegen die DFB-Elf, die bereits seit Jahren Projektionsfläche für die Frage ist, wer als deutsch gelten soll.

Politiker Björn Höcke schrieb beispielsweise bei X mit Blick auf die Hautfarbe und Namen der Spieler, die während der Heim-EM 2024 auf dem Platz gestanden hatten: "Heute kann ich mich nicht mehr mit unserer Nationalmannschaft identifizieren."

Zur Mannschaftsaufstellung gegen Griechenland kommentierte der AfD-Bundestagsabgeordnete Kay Gottschalk auf X den Fotovergleich der Weltmeisterelf von 1990 mit der aktuellen Startelf, den eine rechtsextreme Influencerin dort gepostet hatte.

Er schrieb über kulturell gewachsene "Charaktereigenschaften, bestimmte Tugenden und Teamgeist". Was diese Tugenden mit der Hautfarbe der Spieler zu tun haben, erklärte er allerdings nicht.

Sein AfD-Fraktionskollege Christopher Drößler, ein Polizeibeamter der Bundespolizei, warnte davor, eine "multiethnische Gesellschaft mit der Harmonie einer Fußballmannschaft gleichzusetzen - und fordert 'Remigration im gesetzlich maximal möglichen Umfang.'"

Der österreichische Rechtsextremist Martin Sellner behauptete auf X, dass man ohne die kleine deutsche Flagge keine Ahnung hätte, welche Nationalmannschaft dort eigentlich auf dem Platz stehe.

"Diese Rassismus-Debatte ist Quatsch. Jeder gibt sein Herzblut für die Nationalmannschaft und da ist es egal, ob er schwarz ist, weiß oder welche Hautfarbe auch immer er hat", sagte DFB-Fan Jannik der DW. Jeder sei Deutscher, jeder gebe alles für Deutschland. Und auch die deutsche Fahne gehöre für ihn dazu.

"Man sollte stolz sein, die deutsche Flagge zu zeigen. Das hat nichts mit Rassismus zu tun. Es darf genauso einer, der gerade erst hierhergekommen ist, die Flagge zeigen, wie die anderen auch." Die Flagge gehöre zur deutschen Nationalmannschaft dazu.

Deutschland-Fan Pablo ergänzte: "Es ist Wahnsinn, dass man 2026 immer noch dagegen kämpfen muss. Bunter geht es kaum in Deutschland und das soll sich auch in der Nationalmannschaft widerspiegeln." Viele der angereisten Fans stehen voll und ganz hinter der Elf von Bundestrainer Klopp.

Der 59-Jährige hatte vor einigen Wochen eine Pressekonferenz für eine Grundsatzrede gegen rechts und für "positiven Patriotismus" genutzt und gesagt: "Ich würde mir oder uns gerne die Fahne zurückholen. Ich möchte, dass wir sie immer so schwingen, dass niemand denkt, was mit dir nicht in Ordnung ist. Sondern dass man einfach nur das Gefühl hat, du bist happy und verstehst, dass du Glück hattest, dass du in diesem wundervollen Land geboren, aufgewachsen und zugezogen bist."

Er wolle "Nationalstolz nicht den falschen Leuten" überlassen. "Ich kann stolz darauf sein, deutsch zu sein und trotzdem offen und vielfältig und nett, freundlich."

Klopp hat mit seinen Aussagen viele Fans in Deutschland beeindruckt. "Ich habe Gänsehaut bekommen als er das gesagt hat. Mit Blick auf die aktuelle Entwicklung in der Welt, finde ich es wichtig, dass eine Persönlichkeit wie Klopp sich so positioniert", erklärte Pablo.

Leistungen wie die seines Teams gegen Serbien begeistern die Menschen in Deutschland - und fördern den von ihm geforderten "positiven Patriotismus". Und sie lassen die rassistischen Stimmen vielleicht bisschen leiser werden - so zumindest ist die Hoffnung des Bundestrainers, der mit Blick auf sein Team noch einmal betonte:

"Die Gruppe könnte nicht großartiger sein. Die Welt dürfte sich ein Beispiel an einer Sport-Umkleidekabine nehmen. Da wird jeder aufgrund der genau richtigen Tatsachen respektiert und nicht aufgrund der falschen Meinung diskreditiert", so Klopp. In keiner Mannschaft, in keinem Sportverein sei das ein Thema.

#922. Xavi Espart estará siete semanas de baja tras salir lesionado en el clásico

Las bajas de los defensas complican la recuperación del Barcelona

Xavi Espart, el lateral del FC Barcelona que llegó a evocar a la figura de Philipp Lahm en boca de Hansi Flick, causará baja por unas siete semanas por una lesión en la “sindesmosis del tobillo derecho a causa de una acción traumática” con Aurélien Tchouameni, durante el clásico disputado el domingo pasado en el Camp Nou. Así consta en el comunicado emitido por los servicios médicos del club después de las pruebas a las que este lunes fue sometido el jugador del Barça, una de las revelaciones desde que empezó la temporada del Barcelona.

Espart ya salió con el tobillo dañado del encuentro disputado el martes en el Parque de los Príncipes contra el PSG. Las lesiones de Christensen, Koundé y Eric forzaron la alineación del joven defensa en la cita del pasado domingo contra el Madrid. Espart, sin embargo, solo aguantó media hora, momento en el que fue sustituido por un futbolista que apenas había tenido protagonismo hasta ahora como Balde. La situación de la zaga azulgrana se complica todavía más si se tiene en cuenta que Gerard Martín juega con molestias desde le partido que enfrentó al Barça con el Betis.

Aunque responde a la figura clásica de un centrocampista, posición que ocupa en la selecciones inferiores españolas, Espart ha jugado como lateral izquierdo y derecho en el Barça, autor de uno de los dos goles del equipo en el Parque de los Príncipes. El defensa forma parte de la generación del 2007 a la que también pertenecen Lamine Yamal, Marc Bernal y Pau Cubarsí. Las expectativas prevén que Flick pueda recuperar a Koundé para el partido del sábado contra el Alavés en el Camp Nou. Los próximos rivales del Barça serán el Aston Villa y el Atlético.

MEDICAL REPORTTests carried out have confirmed that Xavi Espart is suffering from an injury to the syndesmosis joint in his right ankle due to a collision with an opposing player in the game against Real Madrid. The player will be out for around seven weeks. pic.twitter.com/sd17xaw1Jd

No se espera que Eric García pueda disputar los tres próximos encuentros y por tanto se le aguarda para después del parón de selecciones en la cita con el Villarreal. Christensen, por el contario, aspira a volver en el partido contra el Atlético después de la lesión que sufrió el 19 de septiembre en Sevilla. El foco se ha puesto en las lesiones defensivas y en los resultado, una vez que el Barça ha perdido los dos últimos partidos, contra el PSG y el Madrid, después de 11 victorias seguidas desde que empezó la Liga.

#923. ¿Por qué quisiera Meta que gane Flávio Bolsonaro en Brasil?

¿Puede una plataforma digital alterar el equilibrio de una elección presidencial? En Brasil, la campaña de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva acusa a Meta, propietaria de Instagram, Facebook y WhatsApp, de perjudicar sus contenidos y dar mayor visibilidad a los vinculados a su rival, Flávio Bolsonaro. Mensajes internos publicados por 'Folha de S.Paulo' apuntan a que empleados de la compañía detectaron restricciones que afectaban a la campaña de Lula y recomendaciones algorítmicas favorables al candidato del Partido Liberal. Meta niega haber favorecido a ninguna candidatura y atribuye los incidentes a problemas técnicos. ¿Qué intereses económicos y políticos están en juego y cuánto poder tienen las grandes tecnológicas sobre las democracias?

#924. Congo’s Ebola outbreak tops 10,000 cases as authorities race to slow spread in African countries

Updated - October 27, 2026 04:05 pm IST - Bunia

A health worker checks an individual's temperature at a temporary health clinic at the Mpondwe border crossing linking Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. | Photo Credit: AP

The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in Congo has reached 10,000 confirmed cases, government data showed on Tuesday (October 27, 2026), as health authorities race to slow the spread of the disease in multiple African countries.

It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history, and nearly half of the 10,060 confirmed to have the virus have died, according to data from Congo’s Ministry of Health. That also makes it the deadliest outbreak of the disease in the country’s history.

The outbreak, declared in May 2026, is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Response teams are battling armed conflict, poor roads and violence from residents fuelled by mistrust and misinformation. Those obstacles compound the challenge of persuading people to report symptoms and accept care, in communities that have endured years of violence and repeated epidemics.

Compared to the West Africa Ebola outbreak of 2014-2016, history’s largest and deadliest, with more than 28,000 cases, including over 11,000 deaths, this outbreak has had at least three times the number of cases and deaths in the time since it was declared.

It has spread farther across Africa than any previous Ebola outbreak, reaching three regions, with cases recorded in Kenya and Nigeria as well. It has so far been recorded in five countries, including Uganda and France, both of which have no active cases at the moment.

A recurring problem in the spread across Africa is what appears to be lax surveillance, as most of the first cases were confirmed long after people started showing symptoms or after travelling.

In Congo, the disease has spread to 66 health zones across eight provinces, from three zones when it was first declared in May 2026. Responders told AP they are seeing treatment centres in some of those health zones getting overwhelmed, people still sceptical and violent towards them, and health workers regularly going on strike to protest delayed or unpaid wages.

“Some people still don’t seem to understand the seriousness of the situation, even though they are directly exposed to the risk,” said Sephora Bgosi, with the Ebola burial team in Ituri province, the epicentre. “Ebola disease is extremely dangerous and can be deadly,” Ms. Bgosi said.

About 80% of recorded cases are still coming from outside monitored contacts, showing ongoing chains of transmission that health authorities are not aware of. At least 95% of recorded cases need to be coming from known contacts for officials to say the outbreak has largely been brought under control, the Africa CDC has said.

At least half of the recorded deaths are among people who had not been admitted to treatment centres, a sign that people are still not reporting symptoms at all in many areas. In many zones, health workers are battling challenges ranging from basic needs, such as adequate vehicles, to complex ones, such as persuading families to release relatives who are sick with the disease or who have died from it and need to be buried safely.

Last week, at the Nia Nia health zone in Ituri province, some Ebola responders, including surveillance and community engagement officers, went on strike over unpaid bonuses owed since late August, a common trend across many affected localities.

More than five months since the outbreak was declared, health workers are still being attacked by angry villagers, including on Saturday (October 24, 2026), when a nurse was killed and another health worker severely injured while responding to an Ebola alert in Bafwasende, Tshopo province.

The outbreak has disrupted essential health services that are already underfunded and overstretched, and has shifted attention away from other disease outbreaks the country is battling, such as cholera. More pregnant women are dying as they avoid hospitals over fear of infection and isolation, causing maternal mortality to double in some provinces soon after the outbreak was declared. z

It has also disrupted routine health care services such as childhood vaccinations, interrupted schooling for children where millions are already out of school, caused trauma and stigma for affected families, and further strained the livelihoods of many already struggling with hardship.

#928. Germany news: AfD's Weidel calls for major EU reforms

Far-right Alternative for Germany co-leader Alice Weidel reveals the party's plan to reform the EU. Meanwhile, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was in Berlin to talk to developers and investors. DW has more.

One of Weidel's reforms is for European parliamentarians to no longer be directly elected

Nvidia's Jensen Huang had words of encouragement for Europe's growing AI economy during a conference in Berlin

Germany's Finance Ministry has erroneously introduced an approved tax hike on tobacco products months before it was scheduled to come into effect

Germany's Bundesbank has forecast growth for the fourth quarter after a dip in the third quarter

This blog is now closed. Below is a round-up of top stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, October 21, 2026.

We'll be back with the latest headlines out of the country on Thursday. Tschüss!

Alice Weidel, the co-leader of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, has presented her party's proposals for a European Union that she said was "in severe need of reform" during a visit to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, saying they rested on three core pillars.

"We would like to rebuild and reform the European Union," she said. "We would like to found the European Union on three major principles: the first one is subsidiarity, the second one is responsibility, and the third one is sovereignty."

On subsidiarity — the idea that power should reside as close to the grassroots level as possible as much as possible — she said it was important to put the "competences" on the "lowest level of decision-making," saying "we don't want the state, or the [European] Commission — that is not elected — to intrude and disturb your private life in decision-making."

"I'm an economist, and for me, the European Union is not a group of sovereign states any more," Weidel said. She said that in sovereign states' parliaments, leaders were elected, "and so the decision-making on the sovereign level should be made in the national parliaments and not here, to be very clear."

This is already the case in the vast majority of core EU public policy areas. National governments decide foreign and defense issues, finance and health policy, education policy and much more. The notable exceptions Weidel objects to are fiscal policy and the primacy of EU law, but only after sovereign member states agree to them.

She said the European Commission was not elected but had a "legislative right of initiative," saying this was a "huge disturbance of checks and balances" and of a "democratic decision-making process."

Weidel accused the EU of failing to follow its own rules, for instance on sovereign debt and whether the European Central Bank should or can guarantee it, citing issues like this as questions of responsibility.

Finally, she reiterated her desire for "sovereign states to protect their borders," saying that "if the European Union is not capable of protecting our borders, the outer borders ... then it is a decision of the sovereign states to protect our national borders."

"If Schengen is over, if Schengen doesn't work, then we need to get out of Schengen and protect our borders," she said of the open-border zone within much of the EU.

She said that if the EU fails to protect the bloc's external borders, "we should have a veto right to opt out of this chaos."

While the EU maintains a border management agency, Frontex, national authorities are responsible for the external borders of the Schengen zone and the EU.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz criticized China for "unfair practices" in trade, and said he wants EU member states to balance out their trade deficits.

That elicited a bold comparison from a journalist who said, "You sound very much like Donald Trump."

A massive stage, all in black. A colorful laser light show. Upbeat music. AI-generated videos on a gigantic screen. On stage, just one man in a black leather jacket: Jensen Huang, the 63-year-old CEO of Nvidia, which manufactures superfast computer chips needed for AI data centers and happens to be the world's most valuable company.

The relaxed Nvidia boss set out his vision of the upcoming AI revolution and, of course, the products Nvidia has developed for the "second wave" of AI. The 4,000 attendees at Berlin's Tempodrom arena were thrilled by what Jensen Huang had to say (see entry below).

Huang said Germany and Europe could be part of the next industrial revolution — not as developers of AI language models or computer chips, but as producers of robots, machines, tools, and entire factories controlled by AI applications.

"You have to transfer AI into the real world of production," he said. Europe could use its data to train AI and develop customized models for automakers, pharmaceutical companies, and many small and medium-sized businesses.

Unsurprisingly, Nvidia offers all the AI software and hardware needed to get in on the action. A new addition to the Nvidia universe is a "Giga-Factory," which is housed in modular shipping containers and can be set up in just a few days or weeks anywhere with a suitable power grid.

There was also something for consumers: a high-performance laptop with a built-in AI agent that acts as a "friend and helper," capable of taking over tasks and programming new agents. Huang went on to demonstrate four small robot ducks that had been trained by this AI agent to perform cute tricks, which were met with laughter and applause.

But it wasn't all cheers. A woman in the audience interrupted a product demo to point out that AI is also used to control Russian drones. She was escorted out by security guards, but Huang assured the audience that he would speak with her later. He was keen to add that Nvidia has also developed a security system designed to keep AI agents in check and prevent misuse.

Nvidia is now valued at €5 trillion ($5.6 trillion) on the stock market. That is roughly equivalent to the total economic output of all of Germany in 2025.

The German military, known as the Bundeswehr, has rated the threat of sabotage against it as "significant," according to a reports by the Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) and public broadcaster WDR.

A spokesperson for the Defense Ministry pointed to several recent cases, including the discovery of a drone close to an airbase in Wunstorf and acts of sabotage against Navy ships.

The military is looking to increase security to counter the threat, with the ministry spokesperson naming increased surveillance at airports and military docks by soldiers or infrared cameras.

"The incidents highlight the ability that Russia has almost certainly had for a while now, as well as very likely the increased intention, to act against Bundeswehr forces and facilities, as well as partners such as Ukraine in Germany," SZ reported based on internal military analysis.

The aim is therefore "very likely an intention to degrade the current political and society-wide German support for Ukraine."

The ministry spokesperson also pointed out that the incidents did not mark a major change, with the military facing similar challenges over the past decades.

He said "automatic defense concepts" are in place for acute terror threats, but "we are not at that point."

German trade with Russia collapsed following the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, especially due to the decision to cut all imports of Russian gas. However, some trade has continued.

According to the German Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), German imports of Russian goods were down by 96.4% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2021.

This amounted to €500 million ($561 million) in 2026, down from €15 billion. German exports to Russia were also down, but still significant, reaching €3.4 billion in the first six months of 2026. However, this was about a quarter of the exports in the same period in 2021.

Pharmaceutical products made up more than 40% of German exports to Russia, with machinery, food and animal feed also being exported in smaller quantities.

Jensen Huang, the head of chip manufacturing giant Nvidia, was speaking at a company conference for developers and investors in Berlin's Tempodrom auditorium on Wednesday.

He was seeking to encourage Europe to build out its data center infrastructure and touted Nvidia's modular tools to help speed up that process.

"Europe's AI economy is starting, and it's accelerating, and it's great to see," Huang said.

He promoted a new design for a ready-made modular computing center that comes in a box akin to a shipping container and that could make it possible to construct a data center in a matter of days. Huang said it "will change the way people build AI centers."

Nvidia has invested $10 billion (€8.9 billion) in European startups over the past year, the Nvidia boss said.

Europe has fallen behind the US and China in terms of building up data centers and is currently home to around 5% of the world's AI computing capacity in comparison to 75% in the US. This capacity is required to train AI models and its lack is seen as a major obstacle for European developers.

Most current data centers are reliant on Nvidia GPUs to run.

A spokesperson for Germany's Federal Financial Ministry on Wednesday addressed confusion surrounding the implementation of a new tobacco tax saying, "The tax increase in the law's wording was approved to go into effect on January 1, 2027, that remains the case."

The spokesperson confirmed that the mix-up over when the new law would take effect resulted from a technical error that put the law on the books immediately rather than January 1 as intended.

The issue stemmed from a mistake in the government's original writing of the law.

Customs officials have reportedly been informed and the Financial Ministry's website makes clear that the price increase will not be charged until the beginning of the new year.

"Gen Z regelt" — or Gen Z's Got It — a youth initiative, has called for mass protests in 21 cities across Germany on Saturday, October 31; including Berlin, Cologne, Hamburg and Munich.

Thousands are expected to participate in demonstrations protesting "broken schools and austerity," as well as the cost of living, social injustice, military conscription and climate change.

French protests that exploded in violence and rampant destruction of private and public property this weekend also grew out of student frustration over the national school system and soon included numerous unions, groups and individuals voicing anger over a number of issues.

Gen Z regelt's website clearly states that the initiative is "against all violence," whether directed at people or property.

Police say they are "vigilant and relaxed," adding that they intend to protect people's right to congregate and express their opinions.

Still, images of massive damage and public violence from France, Italy and Spain have raised concerns among domestic policymakers and police, who have warned against allowing the protests to be hijacked by left-wing extremists.

Andreas Roßkopf, head of the German Federal Police's GdP union, made clear that officers would deal harshly with riots and rioters, telling the Rheinische Post newspaper on Wednesday, "State, but also federal police, will offer a firm and decisive response" to any trouble.

Roßkopf also warned that radicals and extremists could insert themselves among demonstrators in order to "attack police" or "simply be destructive."

The Bundesbank, Germany's central bank, has said it is expecting to see an uptick in growth for Europe's biggest economy in the fourth quarter.

"German economic output is likely to improve again markedly in the fourth quarter," the bank said in its monthly report on Wednesday. "However, the future economic recovery depends, not least, on the development of the war in the Middle East."

The optimistic outlook follows a dip in the third quarter, which the bank chalked up largely to this summer's drought that caused such low water levels in the Rhine River, an artery in western Germany for industry, that most ships could not travel.

"The low water levels are also likely to continue to have a negative impact on foreign trade via European ports as a result of restrictions on inland water transport," the bank wrote.

The forecast will be welcomed by the Merz government as it has struggled to boost the economy after two consecutive years of recession followed by weak growth in 2025.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said he does not think Europe is on course for a trade war with China while acknowledging what he called "unfair practice" on the part of Beijing.

Speaking at a business conference in Berlin, Merz said the imbalance did not mean "the beginning of a war, of a trade war with China. We are looking for peaceful solutions, but the level for that is fair trade."

The German chancellor has been pushing for the EU to be better prepared for trade disputes with China, including calling for a means to quickly exclude non-EU countries from the EU's single market if they flood it with cheap goods.

Merz said the EU needs to be able "to protect our markets and defend ourselves against those who don't play by the rules."

"Anyone who disrupts the functioning of the markets through unfair subsidies, overcapacities, aggressive pricing, or artificially undervalued currencies must expect a response," he said.

That includes tools that "enable us to respond swiftly and vigorously to targeted attacks on our industry and supply chain, with the idea being that in the best case we will not have to use it."

Germany has a rather generous parental allowance system in comparison to many countries, with parents being able to take off 14 months, if each parent takes at least two months off, with the government paying up to €1,800 (just over $2,000) a month during that period.

However, this system has become the subject of a planned reform under the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

The plan is to reduce the maximum amount of full-time paid parental leave to 12 months. With three months each reserved for both parents and the remaining six months free to be divided up however the parents choose. It also raises the minimum payment from €300 to €330 and the maximum from €1,800 to €1,900.

The government's aim is to make cuts to help the Ministry for Family Affairs reach its savings target of €1.6 billion, while also encouraging more fathers to take parental leave. Currently, fewer than half of fathers in Germany take parental leave.

Now the Ifo Institute for Economic Research has cast doubts on the government's savings plan.

"The savings target and the goal of increasing fathers’ participation in the planned parental allowance reform are at odds with each other. The higher the number of fathers who are motivated to participate by the reform, the less the government saves," Ifo researcher Kyra Puteanus said.

The institute estimates savings of around €880 million from November 2027, when the reform comes into effect. However, if more fathers, who generally earn more and thus are able to request the highest payment, do take up the parental leave, this will quickly reduce the savings, with Ifo predicting that even if the uptake by fathers only increases by 1%, savings will fall to €597 million. An increase of 3.1% would undo any savings from the reform, according to the institute.

"Since 2010, however, the share of fathers receiving parental allowance has almost doubled. A rapid increase can therefore not be ruled out, especially if months are otherwise forfeited," Ifo researcher Franziska Nuernbergk said.

The Israel Defense Forces (IFD) said in a post on X that they have killed Tamer Mohammad Ibrahim Al-Zabaq, a member of the Hamas terror group who was involved in the October 7 attacks.

The post said that al-Zabaq had been one of the men responsible for the abduction of Shani Louk, a dual German-Israeli national.

Louk was initially thought to have been taken hostage following the Hamas-led attacks but it was later confirmed that she had been killed.

In the immediate aftermath of the terror attacks, pictures and videos shared online showed a young woman, believed to be Shani, lying face down in a pick-up truck driven by militants. It was unclear from the footage whether she was alive.

The IDF also accused Al-Zabaq of operating to "restore Hamas' military capabilities, in systematic violation of the ceasefire."

"The terrorist was eliminated in order to remove the threat he posed," the IDF said.

The claims in the X post could not be independently verified.

Israel has carried out numerous deadly strikes on Gaza since the ceasefire came into effect just over a year ago.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, addressing the Business Global Dialogue summit in Berlin on Wednesday, renewed calls for US President Donald Trump to invite South Africa (a G20 member) to the upcoming G20 summit that he will host in Miami this December.

"Whoever talks about the future of the global economy must include all important partners. Of course Africa belongs at the table," he said, adding: "The African Union is a G20 member, as is South Africa. That is why I urgently insist that South Africa be represented at the G20 summit."

Merz made a similar plea last year, when Trump angrily insisted that he would not invite South Africa to the annual summit of the 20 leading industrial and emerging economies.

Trump has accused South Africa of committing genocide on white farmers and dismissed South African pushback against his repeated claim. The anti-immigrant president also took the unusual step of offering South Africans political asylum in the US — as long as they are white.

The US President is apparently less bothered by wars of aggression, extending an invitation to President Vladimir Putin to come to Miami, despite Russia being thrown out of the G8 — now G7 — over its 2014 invasion and annexation of Ukraine's Crimea.

Beyond his plea for South Africa's inclusion, Merz said he would travel to the US with what he called a "Miami Growth Agenda" aimed at slashing bureaucracy, pushing structural reforms and making investment easier.

"Those" he said, "are the prerequisites for new economic growth and prosperity, not only in Germany, but globally."

Russian FSB agents have arrested a German national, accusing him of being a mercenary under contract with the Ukrainian army.

"The Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation has detained a German citizen who is a serving member of the Armed Forces of Ukraine," said a statement cited by Russian news agencies.

The FSB says the man, whom they described as a sniper, previously fought in Afghanistan and Syria as well as in Ukraine between 2016 and 2018.

They say he arrived in Ukraine last November and signed a three-year contract with the Ukrainian army before deserting over unpaid wages.

Last week, the FSB arrested a Swedish national whom Russian authorities also accused of fighting on Kyiv's behalf.

Russia has arrested hundreds of foreign nationals that it accuses of "espionage," "sabotage" or "treason" to long prison sentences since it began its invasion of neighboring Ukraine.

A number of foreign nationals have also been jailed over supposed "mercenary activity."
