Updated - October 27, 2026 10:06 am IST - Toronto

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney. File. | Photo Credit: AP

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Monday (October 26, 2026) that trade talks with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration have picked up slightly, but any progress is because Washington is moving closer to Canada's demands.

The comments come eight days before U.S. midterm elections, with White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett suggesting the countries are close to a deal.

“To the extent any progress has been made, it's because the US is coming closer to our position,” Mr. Carney said.

Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc's office said Canada remains in “constructive dialogue” with Washington.

Mr. Carney described a “slight, slight intensification” of discussions but said Canada's negotiating position remained unchanged.

Asked how he could be sure U.S. President Donald Trump would “sign in pen” this time, after Mr. Carney previously warned that Washington's signature was sometimes “written in pencil,” the Prime Minister replied, “I don't know that.”

Canada rejected Washington's terms in August after the countries appeared close to a deal. Mr. Carney said the offer crossed Canadian “red lines.” Mr. Trump subsequently imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion in Canadian goods, prompting retaliation and further trade restrictions.

Mr. Trump said on Friday (October 23, 2026) he would lift some 50% tariffs on Canadian goods while imposing new tariffs on dozens of other products. Two days later, he told a Michigan campaign rally that Canada was “willing to give us anything at this moment” and that a deal would be settled “pretty soon.” He told a Detroit television station an agreement could come before the midterms, although it might take months.

Mr. Trump's tariffs have become an issue in closely watched Senate races. Republican candidate Mike Rogers says in a Michigan campaign ad that Canada is “not our enemy” and “we need to end this tariff war now.” In Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins pressed the Trump administration to ease tariffs on Canadian goods used by farmers and other businesses, with Washington announcing exemptions on Friday (October 23, 2026).

Mr. Trump has repeatedly complained about the U.S. trade deficit with Canada, but energy accounts for more than the gap. The United States buys millions of barrels of Canadian oil daily, typically at a discount, and runs a trade surplus with Canada when energy is excluded.

Mr. Trump also wants automakers to move production from Canada to the United States, threatening an industry deeply integrated across the border for decades.

Mr. Trump's trade war and repeated threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state have pushed Mr. Carney to seek new markets, with a goal of doubling Canadian exports outside the United States over the next decade.

Mr. Carney hosts European Union leaders on Thursday and Friday in Montreal to pursue closer economic and security ties. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed making Canada the EU's first associate member, a status that has yet to be defined.

#1034. El regreso de María Corina Machado a Venezuela: una operación “peligrosa y arriesgada” llena de hermetismo

El entorno de la líder opositora evita los detalles “para no poner en peligro la seguridad de otras personas”

El regreso de María Corina Machado a Venezuela este domingo fue “complejo, engorroso, difícil”, explica Omar González, dirigente nacional de Vente Venezuela. Desde esa afirmación en adelante, ningún dirigente importante cercano a la líder opositora y premio Nobel de la Paz, que ahora está de vuelta en el país, quiso adelantar comentarios sobre su regreso sin exigir antes el anonimato. Hay un enorme hermetismo y mucha renuencia a confirmar detalles sobre una noticia largamente esperada, sobre la cual tanto se dudaba: una de las más relevantes de las muchas que han tenido lugar en Venezuela en lo que va de 2026.

Otra fuente cercana en lo personal y lo político a la dirigente ha afirmado que, de momento, es imposible dar detalles “porque se pone en riesgo a muchas personas”. “Hubo que tomar muchas medidas de seguridad para hacer esto posible. Fue una operación exigente, peligrosa, arriesgada, es todo lo que puedo decir”, afirma este vocero. “Aquí se había intentado entrar al país antes y no se había podido, de modo que hubo que tomar previsiones”. En cuanto al papel de Estados Unidos en la operación, toma fuerza la tesis de que hubo conocimiento, pero no necesariamente participación. “Supongo que Estados Unidos sabía lo que se iba a hacer. El propio Marco Rubio lo ha comentado, pero solamente eso”, dice la fuente.

Los pronunciamientos oficiales de la dirigencia opositora respecto al papel de los Estados Unidos son, por ahora, algo más genéricos. “Queremos expresar nuestro especial agradecimiento al presidente Donald Trump, al secretario de Estado, Marco Rubio, y al Gobierno de los Estados Unidos”, escribía en su cuenta de X Pedro Urruchurtu, responsable de las relaciones internacionales de Vente Venezuela y miembro de su dirección nacional. “Las acciones tomadas el 3 de enero abrieron un camino que hoy hace posible avanzar hacia una transición democrática”, ha dicho.

El proceso de retorno de Machado a Venezuela contó con el concurso de actores diplomáticos, y en él estuvieron involucrados varios países. Su entrada, confirman fuentes muy cercanas al proceso, fue por tierra, en la madrugada, desde la frontera con Colombia, adonde habría llegado días antes desde Panamá, donde residía.

No está clara la participación del Gobierno de Colombia en la operación. Medios colombianos hablan de poco y nada. Se supo que un plan anterior de Machado para regresar por la frontera con Colombia había sido objetado por el Ejecutivo de Abelardo de la Espriella.

“Se sabe poco de su entrada a Venezuela, en parte porque los americanos le dieron la luz verde a esto de manera súbita, de un momento a otro. Es la información que manejamos”, afirma otro dirigente nacional del partido que también ha preferido no identificarse. Sus seguidores están a la espera de que sea la propia Machado la que relate cómo fue su travesía.

Las sucesivas demoras para cumplir su promesa de regresar al país habían sembrado escepticismo en la población sobre la posibilidad cierta de un regreso. En su partido siempre se aguardó con fe militante la inminencia de su llegada. Las demoras se atribuyeron, en un primer momento, a la Administración de Donald Trump. Nunca quedó del todo confirmado, pero la Casa Blanca parecía estar detrás de las trabas que la dirigente encontró en Panamá para emprender el regreso por mar o por tierra hace poco más de un mes.

Por entonces, a Washington le interesaba, sobre todo, cerrar los acuerdos petroleros con el Gobierno interino de Delcy Rodríguez y asentar un clima político estable que garantizara la gobernabilidad. En ese esquema, la presencia de Machado en Caracas parecía incómoda e inoportuna.

#1036. Why US investors are snapping up Germany's famed Mittelstand

Increasing amounts of US capital are flowing into Germany's traditional industrial firms and family-owned businesses. As many business owners struggle to find successors, more companies are becoming acquisition targets.

What do the long-established German companies Birkenstock, Viessmann, Linde and ebm-papst have in common? All have fallen into American hands.

Traditional German family-owned businesses and small-to-medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) have become increasingly attractive to US companies and investors.

Last year, US investors were involved in 76 acquisitions and investments in German industrial and manufacturing companies, according to an analysis by financial data provider PitchBook. The transactions were valued at about $29.5 billion (€26.3 billion) in 2025, nearly double the 2022 total. As of August 19, 2026, the figure stood at $23.9 billion.

"From what we are seeing in the market, the interest from US investors in German companies is definitely still there," said Samar-Ahmad Albrecht-Mahmood of Veracity Capital Investments, which advises companies looking to invest in Germany.

German companies, particularly those in the industrial and manufacturing sector, remain attractive, "because many of them are highly specialized, have strong customer relationships and very good technical know-how," he told DW. "In many cases, these are businesses that have built up a strong position in their niche over decades."

At the same time, many German business owners are reaching an age where they are thinking about selling their business, Albrecht-Mahmood underscored, pointing out that "there is often no successor within the family."

"This brings companies onto the market that might not have been available for sale a few years ago," he said.

Notable takeovers this year include ebm-papst, the Mulfingen-based manufacturer of electric motors and fans, which was bought by US company Madison Air for $5.4 billion in August.

In June, the long-established Augsburg-based company Everllence, formerly MAN Energy Solutions, was sold to Bain Capital, with the US investment firm acquiring a 51% stake in the company.

According to Die Deutsche Wirtschaft (DDW), a German business information network focused on the Mittelstand (medium-sized and family-owned companies), no country owns more German firms than the United States. Of the total 7,861 companies identified in the database "German Companies Under Foreign Ownership," 1,750 are currently held by US investors.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), one of the world's leading auditing and consultancy organizations, also underscored the growing US investor interest in acquiring German companies. In a report, titled Destination Germany, PwC said that while the number of acquisitions and equity investments has not increased, the financial volume of the deals has jumped.

The report highlighted, in particular, the acquisition of BASF Coatings by the US investment firm Carlyle, in partnership with the Qatar Investment Authority (QIA), for around €7.7 billion.

The deal was struck on October 26, 2025, and closed on June 30 of this year.

According to a recent survey by the American Chamber of Commerce in Germany, about 62% of the US companies active in the country are expecting business conditions to improve over the next three to four years.

Meanwhile, some 52% of them are planning to expand their operations in Germany, up from 49% in 2024.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At first glance, however, the increase in US acquisitions and equity investments does not seem to align with the decline in US investment flows to Germany last year.

According to the Bundesbank, significantly less investment capital flowed from the US to Germany in 2025 than in the previous year.

While foreign direct investment in Germany has risen overall — from €57.4 billion in 2024 to a total of €86.1 billion last year — investment from the US amounted to only €11.8 billion, nearly 44% less than in 2024.

In contrast, investment from the United Kingdom rose to around €26 billion.

"I would say the trend is continuing, although perhaps not simply in terms of higher deal numbers every year," Albrecht-Mahmood said. "The general interest in good German industrial companies, especially strong Mittelstand businesses, remains high."

Relatively low valuations also play a role, the expert argued. "Compared to the US, we still see situations where German companies are valued more moderately, particularly in the SME segment. This can make acquisitions quite attractive for international buyers."

This article was originally written in German.

A dog looks on while women hold posters as they participate in a rally demanding the establishment of a humanitarian corridor to evacuate Ukrainian civilians from the town of Oleshky in the Kherson region, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv, Ukraine, on October 6, 2026. | Photo Credit: Reuters

A truce between Ukraine and Russia aimed at allowing humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky entered into force early on Tuesday (October 27, 2026), after it was announced by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump last week.

Both sides said they would observe the truce starting at 3:00 a.m. local time (0100 GMT).

AFP was not able to immediately verify whether there had been a decrease in fighting.

And Ukraine’s military said early on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) that ballistic missiles had been launched toward Kyiv.

The war-ravaged city in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region has been caught in middle of the fighting since 2022, when it was seized by Russian forces at the start of their invasion.

Former residents told AFP earlier this year that those remaining in the city were starving, lacked medicine and could not easily leave.

The Russian Ministry of Defence said on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) that the truce was in effect.

“In connection with preparations for a humanitarian operation in the area of Oleshky, Kherson Oblast, (Russian forces) have ceased fire in the Kherson sector and introduced a ‘regime of silence’,” the ministry said on its Telegram channel.

Kyiv’s human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said Ukraine was “fulfilling its commitments” to the ceasefire.

“The sides are adhering to the agreements that we reached,” he said on Telegram.

The ceasefire, which applies to a limited area, comes as the Ukraine war grinds through its fifth year.

Three-way peace talks between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv are set to resume in November after a months-long hiatus.

Neither Russia, Ukraine nor the United States have said who would monitor the truce or given details about the humanitarian operation set to accompany it.

Announcing last Friday (October 23, 2026) that she had brokered the ceasefire, Melania Trump said civilian officials from both Russia and Ukraine would visit residents in their homes and “determine the level of assistance they require”.

“Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” she said.

Newsmax, a right-wing U.S. cable network, has said it had been granted “exclusive television access” to accompany observers entering the city on Thursday (October 22, 2026).

Neither Russia nor Ukraine have said how long the truce would last.

The Russian Defence Ministry said on Friday (October 23, 2026) it would halt fire in the “Kherson sector” for the duration of the ceasefire, without giving details.

“To ensure the safety of the population and the delivery of essential humanitarian supplies... the safe passage of a humanitarian convoy to the settlement of Oleshky, Kherson Region, will be facilitated,” it quoted army chief Valery Gerasimov as saying.

Ukraine has accused Russia of blocking residents from leaving, a charge Moscow has denied.

The city, on the southern bank of the Dnipro River, was seized by Russian troops in 2022.

The population has since dropped from about 24,000 before Moscow’s invasion to around 2,000 today, including as many as 50 children, according to Ukrainian and U.S. estimates.

Russia’s human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, alleged on Monday (October 26, 2026) that most of those who wished to depart had already done so — “entirely of their own volition.”

Former residents told AFP earlier this year that remaining residents were starving, forced to hunt pigeons or subsist on whatever they had in their garden.

“They’ve forgotten what bread is. You need flour for bread, and there’s not even flour left,” said Olga, who was in touch with two families still in Oleshky.

The city was heavily damaged by the 2023 destruction of the Kakhovka dam, which unleashed major flooding along the Dnipro River.

The Ukrainian army said on Friday (October 23, 2026) it would do “everything possible to assist the residents of Oleshky and will make every effort to ensure the safety and rescue of our fellow citizens.”

The Ukrainian military has released drone footage of the town showing rows of empty apartment blocks, some charred by fire or partially destroyed by fighting.

Other videos have shown Ukrainian authorities using drones to dispatch medicine and food to remaining residents.

The Russian military does not routinely grant international media access to areas under Russian occupation, including Oleshky.

Hundreds of thousands of soldiers and civilians have been killed and millions forced to flee their homes since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, a conflict that has spiralled into Europe’s deadliest since World War II.

Russia, which denies targeting civilians, now occupies around a fifth of its neighbour: the Crimean peninsula, which it annexed in 2014, most of the eastern regions of Donetsk and Lugansk — collectively referred to as the Donbas — and large parts of the southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions.

U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine are set to resume in November, having been effectively frozen since the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February.

#1042. Los demócratas piden un fiscal especial para que revise la relación de Trump con Epstein

Los progresistas del Comité Judicial del Congreso acusan al Departamento de Justicia y al FBI de paralizar investigaciones y ocultar pruebas

Los demócratas están decididos a que el caso Epstein no caiga en el olvido. Un grupo de congresistas de ese partido ha enviado un nuevo documento al Comité Judicial de la Cámara de Representantes en el que reclaman el nombramiento de un fiscal especial, que sea independiente, para investigar los supuestos vínculos entre el financiero, pedófilo y depredador sexual, que falleció en una cárcel de Nueva York en 2019 mientras esperaba el juicio, y el presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump.

La iniciativa, presentada a poco más de una semana para las elecciones de medio mandato, busca aclarar la relación que tuvo el líder republicano con el magnate acusado de crear una red de explotación sexual para cimentar su poder. El documento presentado por los demócratas sostiene que el presidente fue “un participante activo en el abuso sexual de mujeres jóvenes por parte de Jeffrey Epstein a mediados y finales de la década de 1990”. Trump nunca ha ocultado su relación con Epstein, pero insiste en que se distanciaron en 2004, después de una discusión por un presunto comportamiento inapropiado del financiero neoyorquino con una empleada de Trump de su mansión en Mar-a-Lago, en Florida.

Los demócratas tratan de recuperar en plenas elecciones un polémico caso cuya sombra de sospecha salpica al presidente, aunque en los miles de documentos desclasificados no existan pruebas evidentes de irregularidades.

🚨BREAKING: Judiciary Democrats’ report details mounting evidence linking Trump to Epstein’s criminal activities and DOJ’s cover-up; specific accounts involving 11 women provide more evidence of potential sex crimes.https://t.co/jXKU20sJN0

El nuevo informe, titulado Tenemos ciertas cosas en común, Jeffrey, acusa al político que saltó a la fama por su participación en un concurso de telerrealidad en el que despedía gente, The Apprentice, de ser “un participante activo en los abusos de Jeffrey Epstein contra mujeres jóvenes”. No obstante, el documento apenas aporta nuevas pruebas sobre la documentación ya revelada por el Departamento de Justicia (DOJ).

El informe, de 53 páginas, contiene tres capítulos bajo los epígrafes: “El contexto: explotación sexual en la ciudad de Gotham de Donald Trump, Jeffrey Epstein y Paolo Zampolli; 8 testimonios: once mujeres que vinculan a Donald Trump con Jeffrey Epstein; y el encubrimiento: las numerosas y descaradas mentiras de Donald Trump sobre su relación con Epstein, y el incansable encubrimiento por parte del Departamento de Justicia a favor de Trump y otros posibles cómplices y coconspiradores”.

“El documento detalla pruebas que involucran a 11 mujeres, cinco de las cuales acusan directamente a Donald Trump de violación o agresión sexual en compañía o presencia cercana de Jeffrey Epstein”, asegura el comunicado publicado por el congresista demócrata por Maryland, Jamie Raskin, el miembro del partido progresista de mayor rango en el Comité Judicial.

La publicación del documento coincide con la recta final de las midterms, donde las encuestas favorecen a los demócratas. Los últimos sondeos revelan que Trump registra la menor tasa de popularidad desde que es presidente y muestran que los progresistas tienen al alcance de la mano el control de la Cámara de Representantes y tienen serias opciones de recuperar la mayoría en el Senado.

Raskin acusó al Departamento de Justicia y al FBI de “paralizar investigaciones y ocultar pruebas, alegando falta de fundamento para procesar o incluso investigar a otros coconspiradores de Epstein”. En el documento, los demócratas del Comité de Justicia aseguran que existen testimonios de “cinco mujeres que acusan a Trump de violación o agresión sexual en compañía o presencia de Epstein; otras describen aparentes intentos de Epstein o Maxwell de traficarlas con Trump”.

“Las mujeres que sobrevivieron a Epstein merecen ser escuchadas, el Congreso debe tener los expedientes completos que exige la ley, y un fiscal especial independiente debe investigar a los cómplices de Epstein y el encubrimiento del Departamento de Justicia, y garantizar que los fiscales estatales y extranjeros tengan las pruebas que necesitan para buscar justicia”, sostiene Raskin.

Israelis will go to the polls on October 27 in the first general election since the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack. The election will determine not only the fate of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu but also the country’s direction amid deep internal divisions, regional security challenges and international isolation. Mr. Netanyahu’s central campaign promise is that only his government can guarantee Israel’s security. His opponents, led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief, question his failure to prevent the October 7 attack. Mr. Eisenkot has also pledged to end the “forever wars” and repair Israel’s relations with global powers.

Who is Gadi Eisenkot, the man who challenges King Bibi? Read this profile.

Israel is known for its fractious politics. The Knesset, the country’s 120-member parliament, has never seen a single party win an outright majority of 61 seats, making coalition-building a defining feature of Israeli politics. The country holds elections every four years, provided a parliament completes its term. Mr. Netanyahu’s rightwing Likud, which won 32 seats in the 2022 parliamentary elections, has arguably been the dominant political party for years. Mr. Netanyahu, the country’s longest serving Prime Minister, has also maintained a tight grip over the party. In the 2022 elections, the Likud-led right-religious coalition, including Religious Zionism, Otzma Yehudit, Shas and United Torah Judaism won a majority and Mr. Netanyahu formed the government.

The last four years were extremely consequential for Israel. After the Hamas attack, Israel launched a disastrous war in Gaza. It is today facing allegations of committing genocide against Palestinians.Israel also widened the war in Gaza into a regional conflict, targeting Iran’s allies before striking Tehran itself, first in June 2025 and again in February 2026. Despite the succession of wars, many of Israel’s security challenges remain unresolved. Hamas remains in the parts of Gaza where Palestinians have been pushed to. Hezbollah was forced to retreat from southern Lebanon, but the Shia group remains a powerful socio-political militant outfit in Lebanon. In Syria, the government of Bashar al-Assad, an Iranian ally, collapsed. But the man who replaced Mr. Assad was Ahmad al Sharaa, a former al-Qaeda commander who is today a close ally of Turkey, another regional Israeli rival. The war against Iran has reached nowhere, with the Islamic Republic not only surviving the initial strikes but also retaliating with attacks on Israel and U.S. bases across the Persian Gulf.

To understand the security challenges Israel is facing despite its back-to-back wars, watch this episode of Global Faultlines: Is Israel winning?

Inside Israel-Palestine, settler politicians, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir (Otzma Yehudit) and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich (Religious Zionism) have supported new settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories. Settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank has escalated in recent years.

It was against this background Mr. Eisenkot built his campaign on a strong anti-Netanyahu platform. His Yashar party has made significant progress over the past year. According to most opinion polls, Likud’s tally is expected to fall from last election’s 32 while Yashar could emerge as the single largest party. In Israel, which doesn’t have a Constitution, the President usually invites the leader of the largest party to form the government. That leader typically gets 28 days to hold talks with other parties and stitch together a coalition with the support of at least 61 Members of the Knesset (MKs).

This year, although Mr. Eisenkot’s party is expected to win most seats, forming a coalition is not going to be easy for him. Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition, despite political differences, is ideologically more coherent than the centrist coalition Mr. Eisenkot wants to build. The United Torah Judaism, which left the coalition government last year, could support Mr. Netanyahu after the elections. But it’s unclear whether the Likud coalition, even with the support of the UTJ, would pass the 61-seat threshold.

On the other side, the opposition is filled with heavyweights. Besides Mr. Eisdenkot’s Yashar, the Democrats, led by former deputy military chief Yair Golan; the Yisrael Beiteinu of former Finance Minister Avigdor Lieberman and the Together alliance, led by former Prime Ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, are the key players in the opposition. Mr. Eisdenkot’s challenge is to bring all of them together–some of them such as Mr. Bennett and Mr. Lieberman, nourish their own prime ministerial ambitions.

Opinion polls suggest that even if all these parties come together, they would still fall short of a majority. Mr. Eisdenkot may have to take the support – either direct or outside support – of the Arab Raam party. As of now, he has maintained that he would not join hands with the Arab parties. If he takes direct support from Raam after the elections, it would provide a political weapon to Mr. Netanyahu even before the government is formed. If Mr. Eisenkot or any of his allies forms a minority government with the outside support of Arabs, it would be a weak government.

In many ways, this is going to be one of the most consequential elections in Israel’s history. Mr. Netanyahu’s appeal is waning, but he is not out yet. The opposition wants to build a political alternative, but they face structural challenges in a polity that has clearly shifted rightward. Meanwhile, all mainstream politicians, from Mr. Netanyahu to Mr. Eisenkot and Mr. Bennett, agree that a Palestine state should not be formed under any condition.

In the latest episode of Global Faultlines, I answer audience questions, mostly on West Asia. The crisis in the region seems to be deepening with rapid escalation of the war between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis and the growing possibility of a new round of Israeli-U.S. strikes on Iran. It’s bad news for the global energy markets. Bad news for the global economy. And bad news for India.

#1045. Brutal, revolutionary empire builder: Genghis Khan's legacy

Berlin is host to a major exhibition on the founder of the Mongol Empire and his successors. Here's how Genghis Khan disrupted the course of history.

Genghis Khan is one of history's most radical figures. A blood-thirsty invader whose conquests caused the deaths of an estimated 40 million people, he was also a visionary political thinker who established the largest contiguous land empire in history.

The founder of the Mongolian Empire died in 1227. Ahead of the 800th anniversary of his death, Berlin's James-Simon-Galerie explores his legacy and the "Mongol Century" (1250–1350) in the exhibition "Genghis Khan and the World of the Mongols."

The ruler remains "incredibly relevant" to this day, says Matthias Wemhoff, the director of the exhibition project.

"What the era of Genghis Khan — the 'Mongol century,' if you will — vividly demonstrates is how quickly established structures can collapse, how rapidly vast empires can vanish from the map and how swiftly the entire landscape can be utterly transformed," the archaeologist tells DW.

The charismatic leader's unprecedented impact on the world also evokes present-day disruptive individuals who are triggering sudden, unpredictable societal shifts, says Wemhoff: "There's always been this question: Are world politics shaped by individuals or rather by groups and sociological processes?"

In this case, the answer is clear, says the museum director, who also co-wrote a 2026 book on the nomadic leader.

"If Genghis Khan hadn't existed, the course of world history would truly have been entirely different — so much of it is inextricably linked to his person," Wemhoff says.

Genghis Khan was born as Temujin around the year 1162. His father, a Mongol chieftain called Yesugei, died when he was still a child. His family was abandoned by its tribe. To secure his familial position, Temujin killed his older half-brother, Bekter, when he was still a young teenager.

Thanks to his charismatic personality, he built alliances and found followers who helped him become the sole ruler on the Mongolian steppe. He formally adopted the title of Genghis Khan in 1206.

At its peak, the Mongol Empire covered approximately 24 million square kilometers (about 9.3 million square miles), stretching from China and Korea to parts of Eastern Europe and the Middle East, and accounting for over 16% of the Earth's total land area.

Wemhoff lists various innovations under his rule: For one, Genghis Khan transformed warfare. Commanders were promoted for skill, discipline and loyalty rather than based on aristocratic rank or tribal loyalties. Soldiers were organized into decimal units of 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000.

Despite being illiterate by modern standards, he also pushed for the introduction of the first written script for the Mongolian language, which allowed to build a state bureaucracy, track population and tax registers, record decrees, issue legal decisions and handle diplomacy.

A set of laws were established that replaced fragmented tribal customs with a unified legal system.

Trade was simplified through his adoption of a paper currency.

A policy of religious freedom was also established across the Mongol Empire, allowing all individuals to practice their chosen faith without state coercion.

Before the Mongol Empire, the Silk Road was fragmented by local conflicts and heavy taxes. Mongol rule placed the entire route under a single authority, making long-distance travel vastly safer.

The Mongol Empire is known as a period of relative political stability, economic growth and cultural exchange, an era historians call the "Pax Mongolica."

But "it all came with incredible levels of cruelty. The millions of people who fell victim to the Mongols — the mass executions, the abuse of women — this happened on a scale previously unheard of," notes Wemhoff.

The exhibition opens with a raid that happened after Genghis Khan's death, but took place just 260 kilometers (around 160 miles) away from Berlin: the 1241 Battle of Legnica, in Silesia, Poland.

It embodies the brutality and intensity of the Mongols' methods.

There came the "highly mobile, agile Mongols on small horses — lightly armored in lamellar gear, wearing helmets that left the face exposed, and wielding bows capable of firing 20 or more arrows in a single minute," points out Wemhoff.

European knights, heavily armored and mounted on large, massive warhorses, didn't stand a chance against their enemies.

"When a hail of arrows rained down on them, the horses eventually went down, and the knights ended up lying on the ground, stuck on their back, much like a June bug," he adds. "The two styles of combat were simply mismatched."

The Mongols' western campaigns shifted historic power centers in a way that still impacts world politics today.

For example, after the Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus', which was the first East Slavic state, its thriving capital Kyiv was reduced to a depopulated ruin. Moscow became a key regional power, partly because it chose to cooperate with the Mongols rather than pursue resistance.

"In our Western European collective memory, the Mongol invasion plays hardly any role. It's something of an anecdote," says Wemhoff, noting that the era of Genghis Khan and his immediate successors is barely mentioned in standard Western European school curricula.

Germans are mainly familiar with the name of the empire's founder through the 1979 Euro-disco pop band Dschingis Khan, which represented West Germany at the Eurovision Song Contest with a campy song of the same name that reduced complex history to extreme tropes.

But in eastern Europe, the Mongol invasions "changed everything fundamentally," says Wemhoff. "And so fundamentally that we still feel the consequences of it today."

The exhibition "Genghis Khan and the World of the Mongols" runs from October 21, 2026, to April 18, 2027.

Two service disruptions at Lam Tin station within 15 hours earlier this month were linked, with a failed rubber insulating component causing an overloaded cable connection, the MTR Corporation has said.

In a paper submitted to the Legislative Council’s transport panel on Tuesday, the rail operator said its preliminary investigation found that the component’s failure caused a short circuit and fire in the first incident. This in turn led to an overloaded cable connection, which overheated and caused the second disruption.

The MTR Corp also pledged to offer a special day of fare concessions once accumulated penalties for service disruptions reached HK$25 million (US$3.2 million).

#1052. El líder de una importante red de tráfico de hachís cobraba más de 5.000 euros al mes en una empresa de artes gráficas

El investigado, arrestado en Tánger el 8 de octubre, está pendiente de extradición

El escurridizo líder de una importante red de tráfico de hachís cobraba más de 5.000 euros al mes en una empresa de artes gráficas sin que se le conociera actividad laboral alguna, según una investigación por narcotráfico que ha hecho pública la Policía este martes. Su arresto, el pasado 8 de octubre en Tánger, ha puesto el cierre a dos años de investigación a un grupo criminal al que se atribuye la introducción desde Marruecos de “miles de kilos” de esta droga para distribuirlos por España y Europa. El operativo, bautizado Operación Sauron, ha terminado con 86 personas detenidas, sobre todo en Madrid, Guadalajara y Valencia, y el ingreso en prisión provisional de 18 de ellas. Los agentes han desmantelado siete puntos de almacenaje de droga e intervenido 10,8 toneladas de hachís, además de dos armas largas, 25 vehículos y casi medio millón en efectivo.

El considerado jefe del grupo criminal se escapó el pasado marzo de una urbanización de lujo de Madrid, en la que residía, durante un operativo policial. Los agentes le siguieron los pasos hasta Marruecos, donde ha sido finalmente detenido gracias a la cooperación policial. Durante sus pesquisas, no consiguieron acreditar trabajo alguno en la empresa de artes gráficas durante años, pero sí que le atribuyen tareas de logística en la red de narcotráfico que supuestamente dirigía: desde las “negociaciones con los proveedores de Marruecos” hasta la planificación de las rutas que seguirían por el mar o carretera, la compra de vehículos o casas para almacenar la droga y la coordinación de las personas que movían, cuidaban y repartían los alijos. Actualmente, se encuentra en prisión en Marruecos, pendiente de su extradición a España.

La investigación, dirigida por la Sección de Instrucción Plaza 1 de la Audiencia Nacional, arrancó a principios de 2025, cuando detectaron que los supuestos responsables del grupo utilizaban plataformas de mensajería encriptada para gestionar la entrada de la droga, el traslado a viviendas de alquiler o hasta urbanizaciones que hacían de guarderías. En esos centros de almacenaje clandestinos hacían triajes para distribuirlas en cantidades más pequeñas. El grupo delictivo también asumía el blanqueo de las ganancias falseando nóminas, como la que cobraba el propio líder, concediendo créditos fraudulentos o invirtiendo en propiedades y vehículos de lujo, según ha informado la Policía.

Las primeras intervenciones se produjeron en diciembre de 2025, cuando localizaron 2,1 toneladas de hachís en una vivienda del barrio madrileño de Las Tablas. Tres meses después se produjo la primera gran oleada de detenciones, en la que el principal responsable se escapó.

Las pesquisas de los agentes se centraron entonces en los proveedores de hachís y la infraestructura de transportistas, además de los puntos de almacenamiento. A final de junio, los agentes desmantelaron otros dos nuevos puntos de almacenamiento, a las afueras de Madrid y en Sanchinarro, con casi dos toneladas de hachís en total. Y en Valencia intervinieron otras 4,6 toneladas de hachís que, según la Policía, iban a ser trasladadas a Madrid.

En total, han sido detenidas 86 personas, 65 de ellas en Madrid, 10 en Guadalajara y cinco en Valencia. Los agentes también han hecho tres arrestos en Málaga y uno en Almería, Burgos y Girona. Se les atribuyen delitos de pertenencia a organización criminal, tráfico de drogas y blanqueo de capitales y 18 de ellos han sido enviados a prisión provisional. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will host the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting this weekend in Atlanta to strengthen efforts to advance practical cooperation on shared economic and security challenges, thereby setting the stage for the leaders’ meeting in December.

External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar is scheduled to attend the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in Atlanta on October 30-31.

“Under President Trump's leadership, the United States is returning the G20 to its core economic mission of driving growth, strengthening economic security, and delivering results for the American people,” the Department of State said in a statement.

It said Mr. Rubio will convene Foreign Ministers from the world’s leading economies to advance practical cooperation on shared economic and security challenges.

“Throughout the ministerial, the United States will work with G20 partners to address geopolitical crises contributing to global economic shocks, including threats to freedom of navigation, energy and food security, and supply chains,” the State Department said.

As a global hub of diplomacy, connectivity, and commerce, Atlanta offers the perfect backdrop for these discussions. U.S. President Donald Trump is scheduled to host the G20 Leaders’ Summit in Miami on December 14-15.

#1054. Bulgaria seeks suspects in Germany after Starlink sabotage

A Bulgarian court has issued arrest warrants for two young German nationals suspected of setting fire to Starlink antennas. The case is reminiscent of another in Poland, which Warsaw says was orchestrated by Russia.

Bulgaria on Monday issued European arrest warrants against two 19-year-old German nationals, saying it suspected their involvement in the sabotage of a series of Starlink antennas near the capital Sofia.

"The evidence gathered makes it possible to conclude that there are reasonable grounds to suspect the involvement of the two defendants," the court in Sofia rules, granting a request from prosecutors.

Ukraine's military uses Starlink's military-grade satellite internet service Starshield for battlefield communications amid Russia's invasion.

Bulgaria does not directly border Ukraine, but it is on the Black Sea, one of the flashpoints of the conflict. A similar case in Poland, which does directly border Ukraine, led to a total of four arrests last week, also in Germany.

The two teenage suspects are accused of deliberately setting fire to the antennas on the evening of October 9.

Of 18 in a mountainous region south of Sofia, three were destroyed entirely, two were partially burned and three more were damaged, according to prosecutors.

Prosecutors say the suspects entered from Serbia in a car with German license plates, claiming to be tourists, staying just a few hours around the time of the alleged crime.

Plamen Tonchev, the head of Bulgaria's domestic intelligence agency DANS, said he was working on the assumption that it was deliberate sabotage and said other such acts could not be ruled out in future.

News of the arrests follow just a week after a total of four people were arrested in Germany, accused of sabotaging a Starlink satellite communications station in central Poland in late September.

German police detained three resident men and a woman, two of them Turkish nationals, early last week.

Polish officials said they believed that Russia was behind the sabotage attempt, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk calling it an act of "hybrid warfare."

The domestic intelligence agency also claimed that Russia had cooperated with organized crime elements in Germany on the alleged operation.

Meanwhile, in the Baltic, Lithuania's prime minister on Sunday said that Russia was likely behind an attempted arson attack on a company hosting communication hardware for Starlink satellites.

Updated - October 27, 2026 09:38 am IST - LONDON

Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham speaks as he hosts a "Rough Sleeping Summit" in Downing Street in central London, on Monday, October 26, 2026. | Photo Credit: AP

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said that he stands by the principle that settlement (permanent residence) in the U.K. should be “earned” and not granted automatically. An increase in the baseline qualifying period for settlement, from 5 of 15 years had been proposed by U.K. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood as part of a draft “earned settlement” immigration overhaul last year, during the Keir Starmer administration. Individuals could qualify for shorter or longer periods depending on income, immigration violations and other factors.

Indian citizens are likely to be significantly impacted by the new rules. Indian nationals constituted the largest group from outside the EU + (EU and a few other European countries) area to migrate long-term to the U.K. for the year ending December 2025.

“We’ll set out the plan on that quite soon,” Mr. Burnham said during a TV interview on Monday (October 26, 2026) morning. He said the government was still considering the responses received in the public consultation process that took place earlier this year.  In recent weeks the Prime Minister has indicated that the government would soften the proposed stance towards social care workers. These individuals formed a significant part of the ‘Boriswave’ of migration – a surge in migrants in the early 2020s - who are now becoming eligible for settlement.

Mr. Burnham said that since the U.K. left the E.U. in 2016, things had not “played out as people said it would at the time” with the country’s economy weakening and control over immigration becoming more challenging. He said “revolving-door immigration” was being replaced by permanent immigration to the U.K.

Over the weekend, the Sunday Times had reported that Mr. Burnham had told the publication that he would be open to considering ‘free movement’ (i.e., right to live and work) between the U.K. and E.U.

In his Monday (October 26, 2026) interview, Mr. Burnham reiterated his wish to see the U.K. rejoin the E.U. in his lifetime, adding, however, that would “not move ahead of the public”.

“The British public …will be the bosses here. They will decide what will happen in relation to Brexit,” he said, as he denied that he was “testing the waters” with the public and media on how a return to the E.U. would be received.

The U.K. and EU are working towards concluding an agreement that would cover agriculture and immigration among other areas, at a summit meeting on November 20.

Mr. Burnham ruled out an early general election. The current parliament expires in 2029.

#1064. Jaime de los Santos, Alberto Nadal y el núcleo duro de Génova acompañan a Feijóo en la lista del PP por Madrid

El líder popular también incluye a un consejero y a tres alcaldesas de Ayuso

Alberto Núñez Feijóo se rodea de varios vicesecretarios, miembros de su dirección y de su equipo directo en la lista de Madrid para las próximas elecciones del 29 de noviembre. Más allá de los puestos dos, tres y cuatro, que se hicieron públicos hace unos días, y que ocupan Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo, Borja Sémper y Alma Ezcurra, el líder del PP ha incluido en la candidatura que él mismo encabeza al Congreso a varios dirigentes destacados de su núcleo duro. Así, el vicesecretario de Educación e Igualdad, Jaime de los Santos, asciende al puesto cinco (desde el 12 en las anteriores), y el de Economía, Alberto Nadal, que no fue en las últimas, será el nueve. El secretario de Internacional de la dirección, el diplomático Ildefonso Castro, también se incorpora en el puesto 11. Además, la jefa de gabinete de Feijóo, Marta Varela, concurre como número seis, y la jefa de proyección e imagen, Mar Sánchez, en el ocho. Como novedad, Feijóo ha incluido también a la nueva responsable de Estrategia de la dirección popular, María Martín, en el puesto 12.

La candidatura madrileña revela la voluntad del líder del PP de acompañarse de dirigentes del primer anillo de poder del partido, así como de otros propuestos por el PP de Isabel Díaz Ayuso, esto último como es habitual. La lista por Madrid incluye al consejero de Emergencias del Gobierno de Ayuso, Carlos Novillo, que va en el puesto siete y abandonará el Gobierno de la presidenta madrileña. También, a tres alcaldesas de la Comunidad de Madrid: la de San Sebastián de los Reyes, Lucía Soledad Fernández Alonso, en el 14; la de Alcobendas, Rocío García Alcántara, en el 16; y la de Pozuelo, Paloma Tejero, en el 18. Las candidaturas del PP para el 29-N han seguido la tónica de sumar a consejeros autonómicos y alcaldes en la mayoría de los territorios, con un objetivo de movilización electoral, pero también con la vista puesta en un eventual gobierno de la derecha. La exconsejera de Madrid Paloma Martín y el exdiputado madrileño Pedro Muñoz Abrines también repiten en la lista en puestos de salida.

El PP logró dieciséis puestos por Madrid en las elecciones de 2023, así que esos son los asegurados, aunque en el caso de que el partido llegue al Gobierno, la lista correrá muchos puestos porque se da por hecho que gran parte de los situados en las primeras posiciones acompañaría al líder del PP a La Moncloa. Feijóo ha incluido de nuevo también en posiciones de salida, en el puesto 15, al exvicealcalde de Madrid Manuel Cobo, una figura muy próxima al líder del PP, quien ejerce como asesor. El nuevo director de la fundación del PP Reformismo 21 y ex alto cargo de José María Aznar, Gabriel Elorriaga, va en el puesto 21, y el presidente de Nuevas Generaciones, Ignacio Dancausa, en el 23. El exjefe de gabinete de Aznar Carlos Aragonés, que en las últimas elecciones iba en el número nueve, se ha caído de la lista.

La candidatura al Senado volverá a ser encabezada en Madrid por el actual presidente de la Cámara alta, Pedro Rollán, a quien acompañan, como número dos, la vicealcaldesa de Madrid, María Inmaculada Sanz, y como tres, el hasta ahora diputado navarro y exdirigente de UPN Carlos García Adanero.

Two men breached a fence at the Leipzig/Halle airport while practicing for a driving test. Meanwhile, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced an industrial AI partnership with Nvidia. DW has more.

This blog is now closed. Below is a roundup of the stories from and about Germany on Monday, October 19, 2026.

Berlin's Left Party, the Greens and the Social Democrats are set to move ahead on talks to form the next coalition government in the capital city.

The SPD's state leadership approved the motion with a wide majority in an online session, and the Greens voted overwhelmingly in favor of talks at a small party convention.

The Left Party has not scheduled a conference until October 31 because members of the party may be away because of school holidays.

The Left Party is hoping to have Elif Eralp lead the state government.

The coalition talks are set to open after weeks of tense negotiations and a dispute over alleged antisemitism within the ranks of the Left Party.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang unveiled a new artificial intelligence (AI) cooperation at a glitzy investment summit in Berlin on Monday evening.

"Germany is open for business," said Merz at the Invest in Germany event, adding that the combination of German engineering and cutting-edge AI technology would help strengthen the country's economy in the long term.

"Germany is open for investment and Germany is ready to grow at a faster pace," the chancellor continued, before joking: "If I were Jensen Huang, I would put on my leather jacket, take a flight to Berlin, meet the German Chancellor, and tell him, 'I'm ready to invest.'"

The partnership with Nvidia is intended to speed up the digital transformation of German industry and secure the country's technological sovereignty.

According to the company, Nvidia invested nearly $1 billion in Germany last year and holds stakes in numerous start-ups and established companies.

But Europe's largest economy has nevertheless struggled to attract foreign investment after years of weak growth, with high energy prices and labor costs continuing to deter businesses.

German officials were hoping that Monday's summit, which was attended by more than 200 domestic and international investment executives, would showcase Germany as an attractive investment destination, highlighting its sound public finances, status as the only G7 country with a triple-A credit rating, its universities, skilled workforce and tariff-free trade within the EU single market.

Further behind-closed-door talks are set to take place on Tuesday.

Do you remember those arrests in Germany last week, connected to an arson attempt at a Starlink control center in Poland?

The government in Warsaw called it a hybrid attack and accused Russia of recruiting organized crime elements for the alleged crime.

It's much too early to say for sure, but Bulgaria has now issued a pair of European arrest warrants against German citizens in a case that seems rather reminiscent in several regards.

The two 19-year-olds are accused of driving in from Serbia claiming to be tourists, setting fire to a series of antennae south of Sofia, and leaving the country again within a matter of hours.

Hermann Höllenreiner, a Sinti German raised in Bavaria who survived the Nazis' Auschwitz concentration camp as a child, has died aged 92.

Munich's Hanser Verlag publisher and the International Auschwitz Committee said that he had passed away last Friday, October 16, in Mettenheim in Bavaria, surrounded by his family.

Höllenreiner, known as "Mano" to his large Bavarian Sinti family, spent time at the Auschwitz-Birkenau, Ravensbrück and Sachsenhausen camps as a child.

"Only later in his life did he start to tell his story and became a major witness of the era, who hauntingly reported on the horrors of Auschwitz, the perpetrators and the victims, and above all of the still-persistnent discrimination of Sinti and Roma in Europe," Christioph Heubner, executive vice president of the International Auschwitz Committee, said.

"Mano Höllenreiner's biography and tales of suffering were enough for more than one life. What he saw with his own eyes as a child in Auschwitz and what was done to him — for many decades he didn't know how to speak out about it," Heubner said, thanking Höllenreiner for his "courage and humanity" in ultimately telling his story.

Höllenriener managed to flee one of the so-called "death marches" fleeing extermination camps in as Allied armies approached.

Author Anja Tuckermann told his story in a book whose title roughly translates as: "Mano. The boy who didn't know where he was."

He was initially found on a roadside and rescued by liberated French prisoners, who took him home with them. In 1946, he was reunited with surviving relatives in Germany.

Two men have admitted to breaking through a fence at Leipzig/Halle airport while one of them was practicing for a driving test, an incident that triggered a major security operation, police said on Monday.

The two, aged 20 and 32, handed themselves in to the police on Sunday evening, following the incident. The broken fence was first discovered by airport staff late on Saturday.

Police said the 20-year-old had been at the wheel despite not having a valid license.

An investigation was opened into the learner driver for fleeing the scene after breaking through the fence.

The mass-circulation Bild newspaper reported that the car involved, of which fragments were found at the site, was an Audi.

The airport was the site of a security scare in August, when an explosives-laden drone was found there near Ukrainian cargo planes.

German officials accused Russia of having planned an attack, something Moscow denied.

Germany's Rheinmetall defense group on Monday announced that it had acquired Romania's Mangalia shipyard at auction in partnership with Swiss shipping giant MSC.

Rheinmetall said it had paid approximately €138 million ($154 million) for the facility.   Acquisition is expected to be finalized within a few weeks.   Rheinmetall and MSC plan to develop the Black Sea shipyard near Constanța into a dual-use site for civilian and military shipbuilding for both domestic and international markets.

Rheinmetall says its Naval Systems division will use the facility to build four vessels commissioned by the Romanian government, including two 96-meter (305 foot) offshore patrol vessels and two 43-meter diving support vessels.   The company also intends to modernize the shipyard's infrastructure and expand its capacity.

"In doing so," said the company, ​"Rheinmetall ⁠is creating a scalable foundation for future ⁠projects in ​southeastern Europe and strengthens its position in a strategically important market."

The Foreign Ministry has summoned Iran's ambassador after two men were convicted of preparing attacks on Jewish figures and pro-Israel targets in Germany at the behest of Tehran.

"We vehemently condemn Iran's activities. We will not allow Iran to threaten our liberal society," the ministry wrote on X.

"We do not tolerate attacks on Jewish life and those who defend it anywhere, and particularly not in Germany," it wrote.

A Hamburg court on Thursday sentenced a 54-year-old man and a 43-year old man respectively to 8 1/2 and 4 1/2 years in prison for having spied on the president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, Josef Schuster, and Volker Beck, the president of the German-Israeli Society (DIG).

In the court's opinion, their actions were carried out in preparation for terrorist attacks, including the planned murders of  Schuster and Beck.

The court said the 54-year-old, who was said to have also done the groundwork for an arson attack on a kosher food store in Berlin, received his orders directly from officers in the Quds Force.

The Quds Force is the branch of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) that is in charge of extraterritorial operations.

German industrial businesses employed some 496,000 fewer people at the end of 2025 compared to the start of 2019, according to a survey conducted by the Ifo Institute economic think tank.

Worst-hit has been the automotive industry, a key sector of the German economy, where 123,500 jobs were cut both at carmakers and suppliers, a decline of 13%.

But the metals sector also saw a marked decline in the number of jobs available, dropping 115,600 workers in the period, while the machinery sector bled 64,500 positions.

At the same time, more than 2.2 million additional jobs were created in the service sector, according to Ifo.

It said 391,000 new jobs had been established in the health sector and another 357,000 in social services, including care homes.

Joachim Ragnitz, managing director at Ifo Dresden, said the figures showed an "accelerated structural shift" in Germany.

"Ironically, the very sectors that have sustained our prosperity up to now are shrinking," he said.

"The new jobs are for the most part not being created where Germany is especially productive and innovative. That may slow down our growth potential in the future."

A German woman has died in a climbing accident in the Italian Alps, mountain rescuers said on Monday.

The 32-year-old woman, who was an experienced mountaineer, fell more than 50 meters (164 feet) to her death while on the Cengia dei Camosci, a difficult route on the 2,323-meter Grande Nabois mountain near the Slovenian border.

The rescue service said the accident was caused when a climbing hold gave way under the woman, who was accompanied by an Austrian fellow climber at the time.

Investigations are underway to clarify the exact circumstances of her death.

Carmaker Volkswagen intends to freeze the salaries of some 660,000 employees worldwide until 2030 as the company, along with the entire car industry, faces a range of challenges that have impacted its profits.

Trade union IG Metall confirmed earlier media reports of the plans, citing information given to employees by the works council.

The works council described the plans as unrealistic and said there would be considerable resistance to them.

If the company does implement them, employees could lose an estimated 10% of their purchasing power by the end of the decade.

The news comes after VW decided in September to cut 50,000 jobs worldwide in the coming years in addition to the reduction of 50,000 positions that had already been agreed.

Four plants in Germany are also at risk of being closed between 2031 and 2034.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Less than a third of leadership positions in Germany are held by women, a lower level than the EU average, statistics released on Monday showed.

According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), citing figures from the EU statistics authority Eurostat, women held just 30.3% of leadership positions in Germany, compared with 35.9% in the whole of the EU.

Only Cyprus, Italy and the Netherlands have lower rates than Germany in the bloc, while Sweden has the highest, at 44.4%, followed by Latvia, Estonia and Poland.

"The low proportion of women in leadership positions in Germany is particularly striking, as almost as many women as men are employed here," Destatis said, comparing the situation with Italy, which has almost the same level of female leadership but a much lower rate of female employment overall.

Destatis defines leadership positions as those involving the management of small companies, the management of large companies or departments within them and high administrative posts.

A two-day conference entitled "Invest in Germany Summit" is to begin on Monday evening in Berlin as the government seeks to shore up public-sector spending with private money.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz will deliver the opening speech at the conference, which will be attended by an expected 200 representatives from large German and international companies.

The CEO of the US chip manufacturer Nvidia, Jensen Huang, is to be one of the key guests at the conference.

The German government is looking to cooperate strongly with the company, whose products are central to the boom in artificial intelligence, in a bid to help Germany catch up in the sector.

The German Economic Institute (IW) has, however, warned against any too high expectations from the summit, saying that high costs for labor, energy and bureaucracy in Germany were a deterrent to investment in the country.

"It would be naive to believe that the summit will change that in the short term. Companies don't choose Germany because of a promotional event. What matters is whether they can make money here," IW director Michael Hüther told the DPA news agency.

He said it would be more effective if the government were to swiftly implement its reform agenda.

A study by Allianz Research has shown that investment in Germany fell by 6.4% between 2019 and 2025, while it grew by 6.7% in the rest of the eurozone and a whole 20.2% in the US.

The DW newsroom in Bonn bids guten Tag to all its faithful readers at the start of a new week!

Today, we will be looking at a conference in Berlin that will seek to attract private investment in Germany to help make the country fit for the future, with the field of artificial intelligence a key focus.

New statistics are also to be released on Monday on women in leadership and government positions in Germany and the EU in 2025.

And the Leipzig/Halle airport has resumed normal operations after a security incident involving a breached fence triggered a large-scale police operation.

This occurred just weeks after an explosives-laden drone that German officials believe was intended to carry out an attack on behalf of Russia was found at the airport.

Jordan said on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) it had killed more ​than 20 Islamic State militants in airstrikes on ‌southern Syria the previous evening, launched in response ​to a deadly church attack in ⁠Jordan that authorities linked to militants operating across the border.

Syria said the strikes killed seven people, including ‌three children and a woman. Jordan regretted the civilian casualties, Government Communication Minister Mohammed ‌al-Momani said in a post on X.

Jordan ‌said ⁠on Monday (October 26) its air force had ⁠struck what it described as militant hideouts in southern Syria after determining that the suspects behind last week’s church ​attack were linked to “terrorist ‌groups” based there.

Jordanian security officials said separately that security forces had arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law following a shootout linked to ‌the church attack, which killed nine people.

No group ​has claimed responsibility for the assault, although Jordan said the militants targeted ⁠in Syria were members of Islamic State.

Monday’s (October 26) strikes sparked anger in Syria. While the Jordanian military said ‌the strikes were conducted in coordination with Damascus, Syria’s government said they were carried out without prior coordination and announced an investigation.

Statements in recent days by Jordanian authorities that there had been no prior planning of the ‌church attack have added to the confusion, appearing at ​odds with Jordan’s justification for the cross-border strikes.

Syria’s foreign ministry condemned the Jordanian ⁠strikes as a violation of the country’s sovereignty.

It said, ⁠however, that Damascus was coordinating with Amman and would establish a joint security ‌committee to strengthen border security and prevent similar incidents from recurring.

#1072. The homeless man living in front of a London mega-mansion

Anders Fernstedt lives in London without any money. The Swedish native has built a most unusual home under the porch of a house worth over €200 million. How did that happen?

There's a lot of stopping and staring in Knightsbridge. This part of central London is within a stone's throw of Buckingham Palace, Hyde Park and Harrods, bringing inquisitive tourists in droves.

While it may not divert quite as many eyeballs as the seat of the British monarchy, a curious collection of plants, garden umbrellas, shopping bags and children's toys filling a building's entrance causes many a curious glance.

The peculiar arrangement on a grand portico is what Anders Fernstedt, a man from Sweden who fell on hard times, has been calling home for more than three years already.

That building hosting his makeshift setup was, just a few years ago, London's most expensive house.

The mega-mansion at 2-8A Rutland Gate sold in 2020 for a then-record £210 million (€244 million, $278 million) to Hui Ka Yan, the founder of China's Evergrande group, who was sentenced to life in prison last month.

Hui never moved in and the house was registered under his wife's name. The freezing of her assets means it can't be seized by liquidators and the house is in a state of limbo.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

So too was Fernstedt when he first stumbled across it. "I just thought, it would be a shelter for the night. I'm an avid camper, like an amateur botanist. I'm not afraid of nature," he told DW.

Fernstedt has never been inside the property, which appears to be in a state of disrepair. Instead, he gradually built his home in the portico, where grand columns guard the 45 rooms, indoor swimming pool and 116 windows. Year round he sleeps under the portico roof and a large umbrella which provides a hidden nook in which he's placed mattresses and bedding.

"I haven't had a bad night's sleep for as long as I can remember. And that goes for four seasons. It's not cold in the winter, and because I don't have walls, I get the breeze in the heat," he said.

"My conceit when I started was that sort of fake dream. Oh, I'm just a boy, my parents are in the house, everything's normal, I just asked them for permission to camp on the balcony."

Fernstedt was raised by his mother in Sweden before embarking on a range of careers at home and in the US, building a name for himself in the tech world.

In 2016, he moved to England where he worked as a journalist and fact checker at publications including The Economist, before work dried up around the time of the COVID pandemic.

A share in a tech company from his days in the US gave Anders a nest egg he relied on. But it couldn't last forever and he found himself living in a tent and then temporary accommodation, where he experienced violence and brushed up against people with severe addictions.

"Perhaps in this contemporary world, the biggest curiosity about my lifestyle is I'm completely off money," he said.

Fernstedt has built relationships with bakeries, cafes and florists in which he gets unused food, flowers for his home and use of power. He also makes use of a homeless charity in nearby Victoria for showers, clothing donations and socializing. But he's also made himself a broadly accepted part of one of London's most affluent neighborhoods.

"This is a very sophisticated neighborhood. I'd stayed for a few weeks and I knew everybody knew that I was here. And I thought, how can I sort of convey my presence without being present? And I thought, my constituency has to be the neighbors' children and grandchildren. Because if they plead my case at the kitchen table, my prospects improve," he said, by way of explaining the toys that line his abode.

"It is, in a way, a squirrel's nut collection," he added, when asked if he's worried about leaving his possessions out in the open. "I have so many nuts that I won't notice when something disappears."

There are some neighbors who do object to his presence, but Anders does his best to keep his home neat and his life quiet. Indeed, many others feel his presence prevents the house being a target for thieves or vandals. Overall though, he's found the community welcoming.

"Sometimes they introduce themselves asking what might I want or need. And my stock answer being: 'well, what you just gave me, a little bit of normal time, right? And neighborly banter'," he said. "Sometimes I'll be given food and very elegant Italian dinner jackets and clothes have arrived on a few occasions."

Not all homeless people in London have found such a stable lifestyle. Homeless charity Crisis estimates that there are over 200,000 people classified as homeless in England's capital, where "4,392 people were recorded sleeping rough in London between April and June, up from 4% on the same time last year. This is up 58% compared to 10 years ago."

According to government figures, there were 105,138 empty homes in London in 2025, or 1 in every 37 homes. Andy Burnham, who became British Prime Minister in July, has since vowed to offer "every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

With such an enormous price tag, even after six years of being abandoned, Fernstedt knows that the house he lives at could potentially become untenable at virtually any moment.

But over the last few years, it's given him something he craved when pitching up his tent or being moved from one scary temporary residence to the next.

"I'm no longer really worried that I'll cycle around the corner and everything will be gone. Because I've been here so long, I'm free of worrying now, and if we worry too much, we won't be happy."

#1073. El Gobierno retorna a Marruecos a migrantes de la entrada masiva de Ceuta tras denegarles la protección internacional

La Policía devuelve a 16 ciudadanos subsaharianos al país vecino

Los regresos no voluntarios de migrantes de Ceuta a Marruecos empiezan a ejecutarse. El Gobierno devolvió el viernes a 16 personas llegadas con la entrada masiva a la ciudad autónoma, la mayoría de origen subsahariano. Las administraciones ordenaron su retorno tras denegarles la solicitud de protección internacional, según confirman fuentes del Ministerio de Interior. Este es un escenario distinto al de los “retornos voluntarios” que se venían produciendo en suelo ceutí desde hace semanas. En su caso, a los citados 16 migrantes, “se les denegó la protección internacional” tras culminar la tramitación de sus expedientes. Tenían plazo para recurrir, “pero no lo hicieron”. Y, cumplido ese plazo, se les retornó al país vecino, según las mismas fuentes.

Este lunes, además, la Policía Nacional ha entrado en el Centro de Estancia Temporal de Inmigrantes (CETI) de Ceuta para entregar varias resoluciones de denegaciones de solicitud de asilo o de protección internacional a más personas llegadas desde Marruecos —entre las que se incluye también a migrantes de antes del cruce multitudinario—. Los localizados en el CETI todavía tienen un plazo para presentar recursos contra su expulsión. El goteo de notificaciones “va a continuar en los próximos días”, avanzan en el departamento del ministro Fernando Grande-Marlaska.

Desde principios de agosto, se había registrado el retorno de migrantes que volvían de Ceuta a Marruecos diariamente pero por su propio pie —entre unos 80 y un centenar cada jornada—. A ese grupo se sumó otra modalidad de regresos, desde principios de este mes de octubre, surgidos a raíz de los desalojos de los campamentos de las playas, del desmantelamiento de otros poblados levantados por las calles y de las operaciones policiales planificadas para localizar a migrantes en las barriadas. En todos esos escenarios, el Gobierno considera esos retornos como “voluntarios”. Interior también había expulsado a migrantes forzosamente, pero fruto de la comisión de infracciones o de delitos. En total, unos 13.000 han vuelto al país vecino desde el 10 de agosto por estas vías, siendo solo un pequeño porcentaje los obligados.

Ahora, como novedad, se añaden los retornos de los 16 ciudadanos expulsados el viernes pasado tras denegar sus solicitudes. También se añade como nuevo escenario el de las denegaciones de asilo o de protección internacional, contra las que cabe aún recurso, notificadas en el CETI y que se irán sucediendo con el paso de los días. El ministro de Política Territorial, Ángel Víctor Torres, al frente del mando único, desgranará los datos este miércoles tras la reunión del Comité de Situación en Ceuta. Hay asociaciones que denuncian que las expulsiones de los 16 migrantes del viernes son irregulares. Porque por razón de su nacionalidad, casi todos subsaharianos, es más probable que reciban el asilo, en contraposición a los magrebíes, con escasas opciones. Enfrente, el Ministerio de Interior defiende que las devoluciones sí “son ajustadas a legalidad”, ya “que los migrantes no habían presentado recurso”.

Acorde al Pacto Europeo de Migración y Asilo, el Gobierno central dispone de un plazo máximo de 12 semanas para la tramitación de los expedientes de devolución, de los que la mitad corresponde a la actuación de la Justicia. También caben apelaciones por parte de los afectados tras la resolución. Como avanzó este periódico, La Moncloa barajó la posibilidad de reducir los plazos mediante decreto, pero finalmente no se llevó a cabo la reforma legal. El Gobierno central, a través de su mando único liderado por el ministro Ángel Víctor Torres, lleva días poniendo el foco en cómo se han acelerado los retornos “voluntarios” gracias a los desalojos de los asentamientos de las playas, de los desmantelamientos de otros campamentos repartidos por las barriadas y de las batidas policiales en las calles.

Al margen de las devoluciones de este fin de semana, a finales de septiembre se dio también un caso excepcional. El día 25 de ese mes, 25 subsaharianos (de ellos, 23 sudaneses) fueron expulsados a Marruecos porque, según fuentes del Ministerio del Interior, “no habían solicitado la protección internacional”. Este fue un caso particularmente excepcional al ser personas con mayor opción potencial a que les fuera otorgado el asilo. Además, es muy infrecuente que Rabat acepte a migrantes de origen subsahariano.

Por último, en torno a un centenar de migrantes que entraron en Ceuta entre el 30 y el 31 de julio ya tienen la protección internacional que les permite permanecer legalmente en España y les reconoce el derecho a residir y trabajar en el país.

#1077. 10,000 Hong Kong homes left without water as burst pipe hits Shau Kei Wan again

‘Very annoying,’ say hit residents as second Shau Kei Wan pipe burst in three months cuts water to 10,000 homes and empties restaurants

More than 10,000 households in Hong Kong’s Eastern District have been left without fresh water after a pipe burst in Shau Kei Wan – marking the area’s second major outage in three months – forcing restaurants to close and sending residents queuing into the streets for emergency supplies.

According to the Water Supplies Department, emergency repairs are under way, with fresh water supply expected to resume before midnight.

A video circulating on social media on Tuesday shows water gushing from the ground at a worksite near a bus stop, with an excavator parked nearby.

The department said on its website that the water supply was cut at 11am, affecting Sai Wan Ho, Shau Kei Wan, Aldrich Bay and the area from A Kung Ngam Road to Island Garden.

At one point, it seemed almost impossible for Brazil’s 80-year-old President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, to turn the tide after finishing second to Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of elections on October 4. In Brazil’s history, no candidate who has finished second in the first round has gone on to win the presidential run-off. Most of the candidates who dropped out after the first round were from the right. Flávio’s Liberal Party cemented its position in both houses of Congress, while right-wing candidates won several provincial elections. But Lula, a former trade unionist and organiser, who lost a finger in an accident as a teenager, was not ready to give up. Lula and his Workers’ Party identified campaign weaknesses, shifted their attention to economic issues, promised growth and welfare, and persuaded more voters to turn out for Sunday’s run-off. Lula won 51.7% of the vote against Flávio’s 48.2%, a greater lead than his victory against Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio’s father, four years ago. Over the weeks, Lula turned the right-wing’s gains in the first round against it, highlighting the threats that a Bolsonaro victory could pose to democracy and civil rights. Flávio’s campaign pledge to free his father — he is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to overturn Lula’s 2022 victory, and impeach Supreme Court judges — only heightened the concerns of voters outside the right wing, who rallied behind a familiar face.

Lula unleashed a social media campaign to mobilise younger voters. A WhatsApp channel called ‘Lula’s Army’ with 11 million followers spread his message of continuity. He also announced plans to expand a cash payout scheme for the poor, a new debt relief package and entrepreneur-friendly measures. In the northeast, the Workers’ Party’s stronghold, he gained nearly three million votes and made considerable gains in the working-class neighbourhoods of big cities, including São Paulo. A relatively stable economic record, marked by growth and falling unemployment over the past three and a half years, also lent credibility to Lula’s appeal. His victory bucks the recent trend in South America, where Washington-aligned right-wing and conservative forces have gained ground. While Lula offers predictable stability and social and economic inclusiveness, he could also be, as the President of South America’s largest economy, a voice of resistance to Donald Trump’s imperial ambitions. At the same time, Lula will have to work with a right-wing-controlled Congress to advance his agenda. He should seek to build legislative consensus while focusing on addressing the economic challenges of Brazil, which remains one of the most unequal major world economies.
