#1080. What Earth's sixth mass extinction event means for humans

Human activity is driving plants and animals to extinction at an unprecedented rate. As countries meet in Armenia to discuss ways to reverse nature loss, DW reveals how declining biodiversity is already harming people.

From the tiniest microbes in the human gut to giant whales in the ocean, biodiversity is the sum of all life on the planet. It's another word for nature. And because nature is like a team, every player has a job.

When various species from trees to animals work together, they regulate weather, maintain soil health, purify water and support food production. These benefits are known as ecosystem services and they underpin human well-being.

"It is really an abstract concept, but we experience it absolutely every day," said Rebecca Shaw, chief scientist at conservation group WWF. "And we almost never think about it when nature is functioning."

But as biodiversity declines, Shaw and other scientists are calling on the world to really think about it. Because biodiversity is struggling as humans push ecosystems to the brink through intensive farming, burning fossil fuels and pollution from sources like plastic and chemicals.

Over the past 52 years, monitored vertebrate populations have collapsed by an average of 73%, while freshwater ecosystems are faring worse with a drop of 85%, according to WWF's recent Living Planet report.

It tallies with other studies that show a million animal and plant species face extinction unless humanity reduces its pressure on nature.

"It is a really steep decline," said Shaw. "What it's telling us is that nature is in trouble, and it's an early warning indicator that the fabric of life that we depend on for freshwater and food and for clean air is unraveling."

Some 200 countries are gathering in Yerevan, Armenia over the next two weeks for COP17, the latest UN biodiversity summit, to advance commitments to reverse nature's unraveling by 2030. But progress toward those targets remains insufficient, with funding and implementation among the biggest challenges.

Take wetlands as an example. Some 85% of these vital ecosystems disappeared between 1700 and 2000. One study from Canada's University of Waterloo found that habitats like marshes and swamps in southern Ontario provide C$4.2 billion (€2.63 billion) worth of water filtration services each year, removing nutrients like phosphorus and keeping drinking water sources clean.

The study found that as they disappear, water quality worsens, which massively increases the cost of treating it.

Another example is the decline in pollinators like bees and bats. More than 75% of global food crop types rely in part on animal pollination.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At the same time, soil and ecosystem degradation coupled with storms and heat waves linked to climate change are already damaging harvests. A recent UK government report stated that every critical ecosystem is on a "pathway to collapse," warning that nature's decline posed a grave threat to global food supply and geopolitical stability.

"The UK, like many other countries, relies on imports for much of the food and so is reliant on ecosystems around the world," said Louise McRae, a research fellow at the Zoological Society of London, who also contributed to WWF's Living Planet report. "This is why we need to care about global biodiversity."

Nature also provides the basis for many modern human medicines, with some 50% coming from natural compounds.

Penicillin, the first antibiotic, is produced by a mold and is estimated to have saved over 500 million lives. Before its discovery, a person could die from a simple cut. Around 70% of cancer drugs come from natural products or synthetic compounds "inspired by nature," according to the World Health Organization.

As biodiversity disappears, humans risk losing access to undiscovered treatments.

To return to the "nature as a team" metaphor, if a player disappears, sometimes a species with similar functions in the ecosystem can jump in as a substitute.

But not always, particularly if it's a "keystone species." They play a disproportionately large role in their environments, and their disappearance has significant knock-on effects.

The oyster is one such species. Wild oyster populations are facing massive declines, while 85% of their reefs have been lost worldwide. An adult oyster filters up to 50 gallons of water a day.

"No one would ever think they did anything but sit in a shell and be slimy," said Shaw. "But you lose oysters, you can lose water filtration and clean water, you can lose the habitat for many other species that we interact with or sometimes consume."

And, said Shaw, the humble oyster protects coastal communities from storm surges. If you lose it "you lose the coastal protection."

The loss of a single species can also lead to more disease. One study suggests a decline in red foxes in North America is linked to the spread of Lyme disease, a tick-borne illness that also affects humans.

Extinction is a natural process. But the planet has experienced five mass extinctions, when a large proportion of species globally disappeared over a short geological period. The rate at which species are disappearing today suggests Earth is experiencing a sixth event driven largely by human activity, according to scientists.

Both McRae and Shaw called the declines extremely worrying, but said they shouldn't provoke despair.

Though she acknowledges that the underlying global trend is moving in the wrong direction and cannot be ignored, McRae said "the statistics are there to just motivate us to action rather than to cause alarm."

And the Living Planet report also highlights conservation successes, showing that nature can recover.

The number of green sea turtles, for example, had fallen significantly, but has now bounced back. This is thanks to a massive worldwide effort to protect nesting beaches and changes to fishing practices that reduce accidental capture.

Sea otters are another example. Prized for their fur, in the 1800s they were hunted to near extinction on the US Pacific Coast. When they disappeared, it meant sea urchins had no predators, leaving them free to decimate kelp forests.

That matters because as well as providing habitat for other species, these giant underwater groves protect coastlines from storm surges and absorb carbon, making them important for climate protection.

Following a ban on commercial hunting, sea otters have also rebounded, helping kelp forests recover.

"You can see that ripple effect that really had an obvious and a measurable impact. But critically, it can be reversed," said McRae, adding that biodiversity loss and climate change are intertwined and exacerbate each other but have joint solutions.

"We're learning how to turn things around at very small scales," said Shaw. "Now the real challenge is to turn things around at very big scale so we can see it in the global indicators."

#1082. Del paraíso fiscal al mercado único: Andorra culmina su giro europeo en plena contestación social

El país transpirenaico firma un acuerdo de asociación con la UE, pero aparca su consulta entre la ciudadanía hasta después de las elecciones generales de 2027

Hace ya una década, Andorra decidió poner fin al secreto bancario. El país transpirenaico cerraba una larga época en la que su economía se vertebró bajo su condición de paraíso fiscal para entrar en una nueva era en la que quería potenciar su industria turística y sacar partido de un sistema tributario muy laxo para atraer empresas. La semana pasada, el Gobierno puso la guinda al pastel al cerrar un acuerdo de asociación con la Unión Europea que le da acceso al mercado interior comunitario. Sin embargo, el pacto se cierra en medio de una gran contestación social por el encarecimiento de la vivienda y con unos sondeos que señalan una victoria en las elecciones de 2027 del actual primer partido de la oposición, que está en contra de este acuerdo con la UE.

Andorra salió en diciembre de 2018 de la lista de paraísos fiscales de la Unión Europea. Lo hizo después de que el Gobierno del país acelerase un paquete de reformas que empezó a desplegar tras la quiebra de la banca BPA, la matriz de Banco de Madrid. Por aquel entonces, además, el país había empezado a negociar ya un acuerdo de asociación con Bruselas, que también quería atar su relación con San Marino y Mónaco, aunque este último acabó descolgándose. El pasado 19 de octubre, Andorra daba un salto en sus relaciones con la UE al rubricar un pacto que le da acceso al mercado único, según el Ejecutivo comunitario, “bajo normas comunes y condiciones de competencia leal”.

El actual acuerdo da un campo de juego enorme a un país que, hace diez años, ya se vio obligado por la presión de España y Francia a crear un sistema impositivo con tributos sobre el consumo, la renta y los beneficios corporativos para que ambas capitales dejaran de penalizar sus exportaciones de bienes y servicios. El Gobierno andorrano de ese momento hizo de la necesidad virtud, miró hacia Irlanda o Luxemburgo y fijó un sistema de muy baja tributación con bonificaciones fiscales muy generosas que ha acabado por atraer a youtubers e influencers, convirtiendo a Andorra en prácticamente un club formado por miembros con una factura tributaria muy baja. Con el paso adoptado la semana pasada, las empresas tendrán un mayor alcance, puesto que accederán sin límites al mercado europeo después de haber adoptado toda la legislación comunitaria. “Debemos integrar toda la normativa relativa a los ámbitos que cubre. Hoy hay muchas leyes que ya se aplican, pero no se reconoce la equivalencia jurídica. Eso dejará de ser así, abriendo a nuestras empresas la posibilidad de ser más competitivas”, sostiene el secretario de Estado para las relaciones con la UE, Landry Riba.

El Gobierno de centroderecha andorrano, presidido por Xavier Espot (Demòcrates), ha considerado que el texto debe pasar por un referéndum consultivo que será “políticamente vinculante”, según Riba. Si sale favorable, pasará por el Parlamento para luego ser sometido al consentimiento de los copríncipes del país —los dos jefes de Estado: el presidente de la República Francesa y el obispo de la Seu d’Urgell—. Pero no está nada claro que eso vaya a ocurrir. Los últimos sondeos publicados dan al no una ventaja de casi 13 puntos respecto al sí en un país de unos 90.000 habitantes. Concòrdia, un partido reformista y ecologista, se opone al pacto. “Somos un partido europeísta, que queremos hallar el encaje dentro de la UE, pero no podemos aceptar lo que incluye este acuerdo y cómo lo incluye”, sostiene Cerni Escalé, líder del partido.

Según el Gobierno, el acuerdo contempla una libre circulación de trabajadores asimétrica, total para los andorranos pero no para los extranjeros que quieran residir en el país, que mantendrá un sistema de cuotas que, según Riba, será más conservador que el actual. También queda al margen el sistema fiscal. La integración de otros sectores sensibles para el país, además, se irá haciendo de forma paulatina: las telecomunicaciones tendrán siete años para adaptarse, las finanzas hasta 15 y la industria del tabaco, hasta 30. La oposición, sin embargo, cree que el demonio está en la letra pequeña y no está de acuerdo con los apartados referentes a las cuotas, la vivienda o la gobernanza del pacto. “El desacuerdo está en varios puntos, que son definitorios de la calidad de vida, los servicios públicos, la vivienda y la capacidad de la empresa andorrana”, replica Escalé, quien afirma que, si gobiernan, procurarán que el Ejecutivo se mantenga neutro en la consulta.

La patronal andorrana sí ha dado su apoyo al acuerdo, a pesar de admitir que ni entre los empresarios existe la unanimidad. “Andorra y sus empresas se adaptan a la legislación europea, pero eso no se nos reconoce porque no existe la equivalencia jurídica. Entrar en el mercado comunitario nos debe permitir desarrollar actividades de mayor valor añadido y captar también más inversiones de ese tipo”, sostiene Iago Andreu, director de la Confederación Empresarial Andorrana. Sin embargo, la oposición ve en el acuerdo una amenaza para algunas de sus máximas preocupaciones y prioridades de cara a las elecciones, por ejemplo, el mercado de la vivienda, cuyo precio se ha duplicado en solo cinco años por la explosión demográfica de los últimos tiempos y la avidez de los inversores extranjeros.

Joaquim Llimona, abogado y profesor de Derecho Europeo en la Universidad Internacional de Cataluña, cree que el acuerdo ofrece oportunidades empresariales, el acceso a programas como el Erasmus y permite ordenar las relaciones entre la UE y Andorra. “Hay parcelas en las que se perderá soberanía, pero a cambio habrá mecanismos para participar. En el mundo actual, para conservar el poder de decisión hay que estar imbricado en la UE. Lo vio Liechtenstein, que un memorando recuerda que su relación con la UE es lo que le ha permitido sobrevivir como país”, explica. También lo ve así Riba, quien cree que con el actual escenario geopolítico Andorra por fin tendrá una mesa estable en la que sentarse con Bruselas. Los ciudadanos deberán decidir, en todo caso, dónde está el horizonte de sus relaciones con la UE, aunque todavía no hay fecha para que lo hagan.

#1089. France: Young voters blase about Glucksmann's Socialists

Raphael Glucksmann wants to lead France's Socialists to power without working with the left-populist Jean-Luc Melenchon, who is particularly popular with young voters. How can the center-left candidate win them over?

The historically working-class Parisian neighborhood of Belleville has gentrified in recent years. It was here that Raphael Glucksmann, a member of the European Parliament for France's center-left Socialists, celebrated his victory in the party's presidential primary on October 11.

Two rounds of voting had been anticipated, but the 46-year-old son of philosopher and essayist Andre Glucksmann triumphed in the first round with a convincing 66% of the vote and will be the Socialist candidate in France's 2027 presidential election.

As he left the Cantine de Belleville restaurant, Glucksmann was flour-bombed by an unidentified assailant. The following morning, he called on his rival, the left-wing French populist Jean-Luc Melenchon, to condemn attacks carried out by his supporters, though it is not clear that the attacker was indeed a supporter of Melenchon's La France Insoumise (LFI).

The incident has highlighted the issue set to dog Glucksmann's presidential candidacy over the coming weeks: How can he win over Melenchon's supporters if he refuses to work with their candidate?

"Where do you stand on Melenchon?" That was the question that dominated much of the Socialists' primary campaign. Party leader Olivier Faure spoke in favor of leaving the door open for cooperation with the LFI, but Glucksmann called for a clear break with the far left. His decisive victory is therefore also seen as a vote in favor of a clear demarcation.

The other primary candidates questioned Glucksmann's political experience. Segolene Royal, a previous presidential candidate, compared his bid for the Elysee with that of an "intern" wanting to take charge of a company. She said Glucksmann had no experience in government or even running a local authority.

Despite Glucksmann's victory in the primary, his starting position is a difficult one. A poll by Toluna Harris Interactive, published the day after his win, projects that he would win 10–11% of the vote. The same poll put Melenchon on 18%, meaning the far-left man would be much more likely to reach the runoff. But the survey was conducted before Glucksmann won the primary, and so does not take into account any potential boost the nomination may give him. Still, 10% would be an improvement on the Socialists' performance in the last presidential election in 2022, when their candidate Anne Hidalgo won just 1.75% of the national vote.

There is also the complication that the Socialists are banking on a man who is not even a party member to lead them from irrelevance. Raphael Glucksmann actually belongs to a small center-left party called Place Publique.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Glucksmann has his work cut out for him — especially with young people. In an Ipsos survey in September, which posited Glucksmann as the social-democratic candidate and Edouard Philippe as the only candidate from the political center, Melenchon scored 41% among the under-25s. Meanwhile, 20% of this age group supported the far-right nationalist Marine Le Pen. France's young electorate is politically divided, but Melenchon still dominates on the left.

The 75-year-old is currently rallying alongside the students whose protests have drawn international attention. At a rally near Clermont-Ferrand in central France, he expressed solidarity with their movement and reiterated his calls for lowering the voting age to 16 and abolishing Parcoursup, France's national admissions procedure for higher education.

In an analysis for the Fondation Jean-Jaures, a Socialist-aligned think tank, the political scientist Antoine Bristielle distinguishes between a core group of committed LFI voters and the broader left. Melenchon's most loyal supporters, he says, are often young, educated city-dwellers, and many are under financial pressure. Four in 10 households in this group live on a net monthly income of less than €2,000 ($2,200).

Bristielle estimates that just under a third of the left-wing electorate in his study care more about a left-wing victory than their allegiance to any particular party. Almost half of the people in this group are younger than 35 and would consider voting for the Socialists, the Greens or LFI. Redistribution and an active government are important to them, but most would prefer politicians who are willing to compromise.

The pattern recently observed in Germany, where young women are more likely to vote for the left and young men for the right, does not apply in France. Political scientists Anja Durovic, Nonna Mayer and Noemie Piolat found that in the 2024 European and parliamentary elections, young French women were not significantly more likely to vote for the left, or less likely to vote for the far right, than men of the same age. It remains to be seen whether this pattern will be replicated in the 2027 presidential election.

Glucksmann says he would ease the burden on earned income by reducing France's CSG social security tax while increasing taxes on inheritances worth more than €2 million. He also presents himself as a committed supporter of European integration, while Melenchon has called the EU a neoliberal institution. Glucksmann's political profile combines social policy demands with foreign policy positions that could also appeal to voters from the camp of the current president, Emmanuel Macron.

France's Ukraine policy is one such issue. Glucksmann favors decisive support for Kyiv. Manon Aubry, a member of the European Parliament for Melenchon's LFI, says her party supports military assistance only under certain conditions, namely: The provision of aid to Ukraine must first be subject to democratic debate; it must not enable attacks deep inside Russian territory; and it must not weaken France's own defense capabilities. In 2024, LFI MPs voted against the French–Ukrainian security agreement.

The tension between the parties of the left was once again apparent in the aftermath of the flour attack in Belleville. The LFI MP Sebastien Delogu posted a declaration of support on X for the taxi driver who was going to have to clean his car.

Glucksmann must win over a lot of voters from Melenchon's camp if he is to have a chance of winning the presidency. This is likely to prove a much more difficult task than simply distancing himself from Melenchon.

This article was originally written in German.

#1093. Microsoft busca recortar una cuarta parte de su plantilla a nivel mundial

La empresa ofrecerá 60.000 salidas voluntarias con bonificación como parte de sus planes para ahorrar costes

Microsoft se dispone a recortar hasta una cuarta parte de su plantilla a nivel mundial. El gigante del software, que presentará resultados el próximo 28 de octubre, planea ofrecer un programa de salidas voluntarias bonificadas a 60.000 trabajadores de la compañía, el equivalente al 27% de su plantilla total. El recorte de personal llega en plena carrera de inversiones para no quedar atrás en la inteligencia artificial.

Según detalló Microsoft en sus resultados correspondientes al año fiscal 2026, finalizado el pasado mes de junio, a cierre de ese mes contaba con 223.000 personas trabajando a tiempo completo en todo el mundo, 121.000 de ellas en Estados Unidos y 102.000 repartidas en diferentes países. En concreto, el plan de ajuste afectaría a un 27% de su plantilla si se acogieran todos los trabajadores al plan de bajas incentivadas de la compañía.

Las acciones de la compañía repuntan algo más de 1,1% tras conocerse la noticia de los recortes laborales.

La compañía tecnológica dirigida por Satya Nadella ha disparado su inversión en centros de datos y ha dirigido ingentes recursos a desarrollar Copilot, su agente de IA, para mantenerse en la carrera por el desarrollo de la tecnología. Microsoft proporcionando servicios en la nube a Anthropic, OpenAI y otros laboratorios de inteligencia artificial. empresas. Esa apremiante necesidad de recursos ha llevado a la empresa a examinar su estructura de costes en busca de financiación para no descolgarse de la creciente necesidad computacional de la IA. Hace apenas seis meses, el pasado abril, puso en marcha el primer programa de jubilación voluntaria dirigido al 7% de sus empleados en Estados Unidos. En julio, presentó un plan para despedir a 4.800 trabajadores.

“Esta oferta brinda a los empleados elegibles que estén considerando un futuro fuera de la empresa una nueva opción para realizar esa transición ahora con apoyo”, dijo la directora de Recursos Humanos, Amy Coleman, en una nota a los trabajadores recogida por Bloomberg. Los trabajadores recibirán beneficios similares a los de una indemnización por despido estándar, agregó la portavoz.

El plan de bajas voluntarias afecta a empleados de las divisiones de Estados Unidos, Canadá, India y el Reino Unido que trabajen en las filiales de Xbox, CoreAI, Windows +, Copilot y finanzas, según fuentes conocedoras del plan. La compañía deja fuera del programa al personal especializado en centros de datos, ventas, marketing, ciberseguridad y computación cuántica.

La compañía asegura que el plan de bajas no se basa en la edad, la antigüedad ni el rendimiento, a diferencia de otros planes presentados en el pasado. Microsoft también indica que podría considerar una futura oferta de salida voluntaria “cuando exista una necesidad empresarial o de personal”, según una nota interna registrada en la web de Recursos Humanos del gigante tecnológico..

La plantilla de Microsoft se ha mantenido más o menos estable desde 2022, cuando, tras los recortes posteriores a la pandemia, la compañía fundada por Bill Gates comenzó a realizar contrataciones para invertir en inteligencia artificial y centros de datos.

El gigante tecnológico, la cuarta mayor compañía del mundo con una valoración de cerca de cuatro billones de dólares, presentará resultados trimestrales el próximo miércoles. El grupo, con sede en Redmond (Washington) registró un beneficio neto de 133.749 millones de dólares, al cierre de su ejercicio fiscal 2026, un 31% más que un año antes gracias al negocio de la nube englobado en su plataforma Azure.

La empresa logró una facturación total de 331.839 millones de dólares (289.790 millones de euros) en los 12 meses terminados el 30 de junio, un 18% más.

La compañía tiene depositadas muchas esperanzas en el negocio en la nube. Espera que los ingresos de Azure crezcan algo más de un 40%. Los inversores esperan, además, que el grupo destine más de 50.000 millones en recursos para alimentar la carrera de la IA, con la construcción de nuevos centros de datos y almacenamiento para su negocio en la nube.

Published - October 27, 2026 07:09 am IST - Seattle

A voter enters the King County Elections headquarters in Renton, Washington, on October 23, 2026. Photo: Getty Images via AFP.

The Trump administration on Monday (October 26, 2026) asked Washington state to set aside any ballots received from more than 400 people it suspects registered to vote without U.S. citizenship.

In a letter to the Washington Secretary of State's Office, the Justice Department said it had identified 1,500 votes cast by over 400 people in prior elections. It asked the state to set aside any ballots the people might cast in next month's midterm until state officials can confirm they are legally eligible to vote. The state has more than 5 million registered voters.

“We are asking the state to set aside those ballots until we can confirm they are legal voters,” Acting U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd said in a news conference.

Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs was reviewing the administration's demand. His office noted that it had received about 60 subpoenas from the Justice Department since last month seeking information about voters.

“We take our responsibility to protect voter information seriously and will only respond to requests that follow due process,” Hobbs said in an emailed statement. “We see what's happening in California and don't want Washingtonians to be harassed.”

The effort is the latest by the administration to identify noncitizen voters, even though noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare. President Donald Trump has repeatedly sought to undermine public confidence in elections. The request in Washington is similar to Justice Department attempt to require California to sequester mail ballots from up to 20,000 people the federal government suspects may not be citizens.

California has challenged that, and during rare Sunday arguments, a panel of federal appellate judges questioned the timing, constitutionality and authority of the Justice Department's demand. The Elections Clause of the U.S. Constitution gives state legislatures the power to set the time, place and manner of congressional elections.

Los Angeles County Assistant Registrar-Recorder Monica Flores said in a court filing that her staff went through a sample of 200 records from the Trump administration's list. They found the sample included canceled or inactive registrations, people with no voting history and voters who appeared to have been born in the United States.

The Justice Department told Washington it anticipates sending the state an additional list of people it suspects are not citizens prior to Election Day. It also noted that some of the people it suspects registered without citizenship may have since become naturalized.

Investigations into prior allegations of noncitizen voters have revealed far fewer instances than the Trump administration has claimed. In Nevada, Trump's administration alleged there were 1,500 potential noncitizen voters on the rolls, but subsequent investigation found zero.

In Maricopa County, which includes Phoenix, the county Recorder, who is a Trump supporter, announced that there were 207 possible noncitizens on the county's rolls. The Republican County Attorney determined there were actually eight.

In a regulatory filing, Anthropic said it will list its stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol ANT. File | Photo Credit: Reuters

Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind Claude, has filed to go public in the United States, disclosing rapid revenue growth, expanding enterprise spending and the high cost of developing and running advanced AI models.

The company filed a registration statement with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on October 26. It intends to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol “ANT”. The number of shares to be offered and the price range have not yet been determined.

The public filing follows Anthropic’s confidential submission of a draft registration statement to the SEC on June 1, 2026. The proposed IPO remains subject to regulatory review.

The company reported more than 11,900 customers generating at least $100,000 in revenue over the preceding 12 months as of September 30, up from more than 950 a year earlier. More than 1,900 customers generated at least $1 million, while approximately 250 generated at least $10 million.

For the six months ended June 30, 2026, Anthropic reported revenue of $16.3 billion, up from $1.16 billion in the corresponding period a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $80.7 billion from $13 billion, largely because of accounting expenses arising from changes in the estimated value of certain financing instruments as the company’s valuation rose.

Anthropic reported an operating loss of $693 million in the first half of 2026, compared with $2.14 billion a year earlier. However, using its own adjusted measure, which excludes certain expenses, the company reported operating income of $1.6 billion, with a margin of about 10%.

It reported $8.95 billion in computing and infrastructure expenses in the first half of 2026, reflecting the costs of developing and running advanced AI models. As of June 30, the company held $131.7 billion in cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments, according to the filing.

ALSO WATCH Anthropic loses over $80 billion in first half of 2026

The prospectus flags risks including dependence on computing infrastructure providers, competition and the cost of developing increasingly capable AI models. Major cloud providers supply Anthropic with computing capacity and help distribute its products, while also developing competing AI services.

The filing also outlines a governance structure intended to protect Anthropic’s long-term public-benefit mission. An entity formed by its seven co-founders will hold a special share carrying 50.1% of general voting power, while the company’s Long-Term Benefit Trust will have the right to appoint a majority of the board. This would limit the ability of ordinary shareholders to influence corporate governance, even after the company lists publicly.

Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be offered or the proposed price range. The timing and terms of the IPO will depend on the regulatory process and market conditions.

#1102. Is Germany's eight-hour workday under threat?

Would you work 12 hours straight? The CDU/CSU and SPD are locked in a dispute over reforms to the Working Hours Act. Workplace flexibility, collective bargaining agreements and worker protection rules are at stake.

The town of Leuna, in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, is one of the country's largest chemical industry hub, where more than 100 companies have established operations. Among them is the Finnish biotechnology group UPM, which has recently built a biorefinery for wood-based chemicals in Leuna. It's now hiring.

One of the job listings is for a chemical technician to oversee the rollout of new facilities. But to qualify, candidates must be willing to work 12-hour shifts. Is that legal? According to German law, standard working hours are limited to eight hours per day. It is permissible to extend this to ten hours, provided that workers receive compensatory time off for the overtime, and there must be at least 11 hours of rest between two shifts.

Business associations and the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties have long called for these rules to be made more flexible.

Rainer Dulger, president of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations (BDA), points to the European Working Time Directive, which allows for a maximum weekly working time of 48 hours. "The allowance is being taken advantage of almost everywhere else — except here," Dulger told the dpa news agency in August.

Companies say they often find the existing rules too rigid, particularly in industries with seasonal fluctuations — such as tourism — or in project-based work, or during irregular peaks in workload, such as in the restaurant industry. They could deploy their staff more efficiently, says Dulger: "The Working Hours Act dates back to the era of fax machines and rotary-dial phones. It knows nothing of laptops or daycare hours."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In their 2025 coalition agreement, the CDU/CSU and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) agreed to reform the Working Hours Act. "In keeping with the European Working Time Directive, we want to allow for a maximum weekly rather than daily working time — also and especially to promote a better work-life balance," the agreement said.

The SPD would have preferred to leave the law unchanged, but had to accept the conservative parties' plans. The Social Democrats pointed out that longer working hours are already permitted in exceptional cases, such as in emergency services, the health care sector and security services. Workers in power plants, refineries and the chemical industry are also allowed to work up to 12 hours at a time.

Even Chancellor Friedrich Merz himself seemed unaware of this exception until quite recently. After visiting the UPM refinery in Leuna in September, he recounted to business leaders at the German Employers' Day in Berlin that he was "completely surprised" to learn that the facilities operate on a continuous 12-hour shift schedule, thanks to the approval of the works council.

Merz recounted the shift supervisor describing the work schedule as "really great" — with three-day work weeks. "He said we have plenty of time for our families — it's a great way to organize things." Merz went on to conclude that this demonstrates the benefits of relaxing the Working Hours Act.

"Working more than eight hours is not exploitation. Rather, it can be a good opportunity to organize working hours more flexibly — both for businesses and for the people working there," the chancellor said. "We should do it."

But there is resistance from within the SPD and from trade unions opposed to amending the Working Hours Act. The trade union Verdi argues that significantly longer workdays would have negative consequences for employees' health and would disadvantage people with family and caregiving responsibilities. In certain industries, employees could also be put under pressure to accept longer shifts.

An initial reform draft was drawn up in June 2026 by the Labor and Social Affairs Ministry, headed at the time by Bärbel Bas, an SPD politician who has since resigned for personal reasons.

The draft includes some conditions, including a collective bargaining agreement between employers and unions if any schedule changes were made, as well as health and safety regulations, and working hours to be tracked electronically.

Annika Klose, spokesperson for labor and social policy for the SPD parliamentary group, explained the thinking behind the idea. Flexibility, she said, is "not a one-way street." The coalition agreement explicitly aims to promote a better balance between family and work. "So that it's sometimes possible to take your child to football practice in the afternoon and then continue working afterward — but not that my boss tells me against my will: 'You're working the shift from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. tomorrow.'"

The CDU/CSU immediately rejected the draft. Businesses were also up in arms. "This draft must be withdrawn and completely revised," demanded Dulger in a statement, saying it was "steeped in mistrust." The German Confederation of Skilled Crafts (ZDH) spoke of a "breach of the commitments agreed to in the coalition agreement." The reform has been on hold ever since.

At the Employers' Day event, Merz held out the prospect of progress. "This is indeed long overdue. I believe we can accomplish this relatively quickly and create flexibility in the labor market."

It remains to be seen, however, whether the new SPD Labor Minister, Alexander Schweitzer, shares this view. In early October, his party released a paper on reforming working hours that read like a declaration of war against the CDU. "Self-determination, Not Deregulation" is the title of the seven-page document that was signed by the SPD working group on labor, the youth organization Jusos, the "60plus" working group and the women's wing of the SPD.

In the paper, the Social Democrats not only reiterate the points that already appeared in Bas' draft back in June. They also demand that, in the future, employers and employees should decide on working hours "jointly and by mutual agreement." They argued that it is not "in the spirit of a modern reform of working time law" if only employers can determine when employees finish work.

From a political perspective, the dispute over reforming work hours has long become more than just a debate over legal provisions. It is a fundamental dispute over how much flexibility workers should be expected to tolerate in the future and to what extent the state should protect them. And it is yet another stumbling block for the already beleaguered government in Berlin.

#1103. Elma Saiz asegura que el Gobierno aprobará otra deducción para que el salario mínimo no tribute en el IRPF

La portavoz y ministra de Seguridad Social insiste en que el Ejecutivo quiere aprobar la subida del SMI antes de las elecciones

La portavoz del Gobierno y ministra de Inclusión, Seguridad Social y Migraciones, Elma Saiz, ha asegurado este lunes que el Ejecutivo tiene previsto, después de aprobar la nueva subida del salario mínimo interprofesional (SMI), aprobar también la deducción fiscal necesaria “para que esta renta no tribute en el IRPF”. Para que el SMI quede exento en la práctica, el Gobierno debería incluir esa medida dentro de una norma legal que deberá aprobarse en la diputación permanente del Congreso de los Diputados.

Saiz ha garantizado en un primer momento en una entrevista en la Cadena SER que la subida del salario mínimo —fijado actualmente en 1.221 euros al mes en 14 pagas— se producirá antes de las elecciones. A continuación ha precisado que, al menos, “eso es en lo que está trabajando el Gobierno”, ya que, según ha recordado, primero tiene que culminar sus trabajos el grupo de expertos que aconsejará al Ejecutivo cuál debe de ser ese incremento. El Gobierno baraja una cifra en torno al 5%, frente al 7% que exigen los sindicatos.

De esta forma, Hacienda, según explica un portavoz del ministerio, decidirá cómo evitar que el incremento del SMI se traduzca en un mayor pago de IRPF una vez se haya aprobado el nuevo suelo salarial. El precedente más reciente apunta a que el departamento de Arcadi España volverá a recurrir a una deducción en la declaración de la renta, en lugar de modificar los umbrales del impuesto o la reducción por rendimientos del trabajo. Esta última fórmula es la que Hacienda utilizó durante años para adaptar la tributación a las sucesivas subidas del salario mínimo. Sin embargo, en la última actualización optó por mantener los límites y compensar a los trabajadores que cobran el SMI mediante una deducción.

Hasta 2024, cada incremento del SMI iba acompañado de una actualización de los umbrales del IRPF para evitar que los trabajadores que cobraban el salario mínimo empezaran a tributar por el aumento de sus ingresos. Cuando el sueldo mínimo se elevó a 15.876 euros brutos anuales ese año, Hacienda situó en esa misma cuantía el límite de ingresos a partir del cual los contribuyentes con más de un pagador estaban obligados a presentar la declaración. Fue la última vez que se modificaron estos límites, pese a que el SMI ha seguido aumentando hasta los actuales 17.094 euros brutos anuales.

Desde entonces, Hacienda ha optado por una vía diferente para evitar que los perceptores del salario mínimo vean reducida su nómina neta por el pago del impuesto. En lugar de elevar los umbrales de ingresos exentos, el Gobierno ha ideado una deducción en la declaración de la renta que permite compensar el IRPF que les correspondería abonar. De esta forma, los trabajadores pueden quedar exentos de pagar en la práctica, aunque el mecanismo para conseguirlo sea distinto. La contrapartida es que deben presentar la declaración para recuperar, un año después, las retenciones soportadas mes a mes durante el ejercicio previo.

Respecto a la tributación de esta renta Saiz también ha arremetido en varias ocasiones durante su entrevista contra el candidato del PP a la presidencia del Gobierno, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, a quien ha acusado de no saber que el salario mínimo está exento de tributación, después de que la pasada semana semana el líder popular asegurara, también en la Cadena SER, que el salario mínimo sí tributaba en el IRPF. Aseguró que, con las últimas subidas del SMI “ya hubo una gran discusión en el Parlamento que nosotros votamos que estuviera exento, pero el Gobierno quería que estuviese incluido”.

La subida del salario mínimo para 2027, condición imprescindible para que puedan aplicarse los cambios fiscales previstos para sus 2,6 millones de beneficiarios, debe aprobarse antes de final de año para que entre en vigor el 1 de enero. Todo apunta a que el Gobierno lo hará mediante un decreto en alguno de los Consejos de Ministros previos a las elecciones, previsiblemente antes del último previsto para el 24 de noviembre. Para ello, Trabajo espera antes el informe del grupo de expertos, encargado por Yolanda Díaz para esta misma semana y que prevén entregar este viernes o el próximo martes, como muy tarde. Previsiblemente propondrán dos posibles incrementos: uno si el Gobierno actualiza y aprueba una nueva deducción, como ha dicho hoy Saiz, y otro si el SMI pasa a tributar efectivamente en el IRPF.

La ley obliga a tener en cuenta factores como la inflación, la productividad, la participación de los salarios en la renta nacional y la situación económica, aunque los expertos también valoran objetivos como situar el SMI en el 60% del salario medio neto, en línea con la Carta Social Europea, y reducir la pobreza laboral. Habitualmente recomiendan aplicar el mayor incremento entre el necesario para alcanzar ese umbral o el requerido para preservar el poder adquisitivo.

Este año, la urgencia con la que se ha solicitado el informe y el hecho de que mantener el poder de compra vaya a exigir una subida superior a la necesaria para conservar el SMI en torno al 60% del salario medio apuntan a que la recomendación se alineará prácticamente con la inflación provisional de octubre (en el entorno del 5% que prepara el Gobierno antes mencionado) e incluso podría incorporar una cláusula para recoger una posible revisión al alza del dato definitivo de noviembre.

Aunque persisten discrepancias entre expertos y ministerios sobre la metodología para calcular si el SMI alcanza realmente el 60% del salario medio, este debate tendrá menos relevancia al vincularse la propuesta a la inflación. De hecho, el ministro de Economía, Carlos Cuerpo, sostiene que ese objetivo ya se ha alcanzado tras la subida acumulada del 66% desde 2018 y defiende aprobar el aumento antes de las elecciones para reducir la incertidumbre de los trabajadores afectados.

Updated - October 26, 2026 10:58 pm IST - Moscow

Russian presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov. File | Photo Credit: PTI

Russia said Monday (October 26, 2026) that it would not slow down its offensive on Ukraine despite upcoming U.S.-brokered talks on ending the conflict but that it could agree local "humanitarian" ceasefires.

The Kremlin said that it was open to short-term "humanitarian" ceasefires along the front line, ahead of a truce in the ravaged Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.

A ceasefire is to start in the southern Ukrainian city early Tuesday (October 27), brokered by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump after months of reports that residents faced dire food, water and medicine shortages.

Asked whether Russia would consider more local truces, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters: "For humanitarian purposes, absolutely."

But Moscow vowed not to let up in the overall pace of the war, even as the sides prepare to restart stalled talks under U.S. mediation next month.

"The decision to resume trilateral talks does not imply any restrictions on combat operations," Mr. Peskov said.

"Our armed forces continue to carry out massive strikes on Ukraine's military-industrial complex," he added.

Russia has intensified drone and missile attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks, hitting energy sites around major cities in what Kyiv says is a bid to plunge the country into cold and darkness throughout the winter.

Strikes last year left millions without heating or electricity with temperatures as low as -20C.

The two sides are to meet next month with U.S. envoys to discuss ways to end Europe's worst conflict since World War II.

Several previous rounds have failed to move the sides closer to a deal. Russia demands more territory in eastern Ukraine and sweeping military and political restrictions on Kyiv.

Ukraine and its allies say the demands are tantamount to a capitulation that would leave the country exposed to a future Russian attack.

#1110. How reliant is Ukraine on the US-controlled Starlink internet service?

Kyiv keeps issuing warnings that the satellite internet system Starlink is being restricted in Ukraine. How dependent is the country on the system, and what would happen if it went down?

Few technological systems have played such an important role in the war in Ukraine as Starlink, central to the communications, reconnaissance and drone operations of the Ukrainian armed forces. There are currently widespread concerns that Elon Musk's satellite internet service in Ukraine may be restricted or even switched off. In recent days, Kyiv has repeatedly reported disruptions and restrictions affecting its use.

Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukraine has made extensive use of the satellite internet service, which is operated by the US company SpaceX. With it, military personell can continue to communicate and exchange data, even when infrastructure has been destroyed or cellphone networks are down.

According to the Center for Security Studies (CSS) at ETH Zurich, around 50,000 Starlink terminals were in use in Ukraine in 2025. These are the system's specialised receiving and transmitting devices, which enable communications on the battlefield. They are also used to relay orders between command levels and receive drone footage.

The importance of the Starlink network can in part be explained by events at the beginning of the war. According to a CSS analysis, the KA-SAT satellite system previously favored by Ukraine was targeted in a cyberattack just hours before Russia's invasion. Starlink quickly became a vital alternative.

When discussing current affairs, the terms "Starlink" and "Starshield" are often used interchangeably.

However, Starlink is SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service, whereas Starshield is specifically designed for governmental and military use. While based on the same technological infrastructure, it is designed for security and defense applications.

This distinction matters, because the latest reports of restrictions seem to primarily concern systems used for military purposes. Elon Musk recently stated that Starshield systems are controlled by the US government, whereas Starlink is a commercial service operated by SpaceX.

Alongside communications, Starlink is mainly used for drone operations. The system provides an internet connection for ground, naval and aerial drones.

This connection means video footage can be transmitted almost in real time, while drones can be controlled over long distances. Ukraine uses these systems for reconnaissance and attacks deep behind enemy lines.

According to ETH Zurich, images and GPS coordinates of Russian positions are also transmitted via these communication channels. The data is sent to artillery units and used to coordinate operations.

According to Ukrainian media reports, on Tuesday night, SpaceX temporarily introduced a speed restriction for Starlink terminals in Ukraine, limiting terminals in motion to a speed of about 160 kilometers per hour (100 mph).

Such a restriction has direct consequences for fast-moving Ukrainian drones, some of which travel at speeds of up to 300 kilometers per hour (186 mph). If the connection to the drone is lost, live video footage can no longer be transmitted, and the systems can no longer be controlled in real time. The drones effectively have to continue their mission while flying blind.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Restricting or even shutting down a Starlink network would therefore not only make communication more difficult. It would also affect Ukrainian drone operations, and other military activities.

However, Starlink and its military counterpart, Starshield, are only one essential component of Ukraine's defense system. Ukraine also receives reconnaissance data from western partners, including information about Russian air attacks, missile launches, troop movements and anti-aircraft positions, as well as potential routes to avoid them.

This information helps with air defense and offensive operations. Without this intelligence, it would be significantly harder for Ukraine to carry out long-range drone operations against targets in Russian territory.

The two elements are particularly effective when combined. Reconnaissance data provides information about potential targets and routes, while Starlink ensures that this data can be quickly relayed to units.

This is why reports that the US is limiting access to its reconnaissance data are as worrying as the possibility that Starlink might be throttled. Other NATO countries, such as the United Kingdom and France, can also provide reconnaissance data, but not to the extent as the United States.

Europe has several alternatives to Starlink, including Eutelsat/OneWeb. However, their ability to match Starlink's performance in wartime conditions has not yet been tested on a large scale.

The recurrent concern about possible restrictions makes clear that satellite communications have become a central component of Ukrainian defense. And while relying on a single provider simplifies operations, it also shows how dependent modern armed forces have become on private technology companies. Experts say this marks a fundamental change in warfare.

Meanwhile, Ukraine's successful use of Starlink has helped the system to achieve global recognition.

This article has been translated from German.

#1112. El Supremo indemniza a la mujer de un paciente sometido a una vasectomía porque nadie le informó de que podía quedarse embarazada

El tribunal fija una compensación de 35.000 para el hombre y otra igual para su esposa porque el fracaso de la intervención “afecta por igual a ambos”

La pareja de un hombre que se haya sometido a una vasectomía tiene derecho a ser indemnizada si los médicos no le informan adecuadamente de que la intervención puede fallar. Así lo ha establecido el Tribunal Supremo, que ha reconocido el derecho de una mujer a cobrar una compensación porque se quedó embaraza después de que su marido sometiera a esa intervención como método anticonceptivo. La Sala de lo Contencioso-Administrativo considera que, en parejas estables, la vasectomía es “una decisión adoptada en el ámbito de la planificación familiar” y su fracaso “afecta por igual a ambos miembros de la pareja”, por lo que fija para la mujer una indemnización del mismo importe, 35.000 euros, que para su marido.

El asunto sobre el que ha debatido el Supremo tiene su origen en una vasectomía realizada en mayo de 2018 en el Hospital Severo Ochoa de Madrid. En algún momento después de la intervención, se produjo una recanalización espontánea de los conductos que habían sido cortados para impedir que los espermatozoides llegaran al semen, una circunstancia poco frecuente (menos del 1% de los casos) que supone el fracaso de la intervención. La mujer se quedó embarazada poco después y la pareja reclamó una indemnización para él y otra para ella, pero tanto la Consejería de Sanidad de Madrid, como un juzgado de la capital y el Tribunal Superior de Justicia de Madrid aceptaron indemnizar al hombre porque admitieron que existió un déficit en la información que recibió el paciente, pero rechazaron compensar a la mujer.

La pareja llevó el caso al Supremo, que no solo ha incrementado la cuantía en que los anteriores tribunales habían cifrado la compensación para él (primero 6.000 y luego 12.000 euros), sino que han considerado que ella también ha sufrido las consecuencias del fallo en la intervención y debe ser compensada porque nadie le informó de que la vasectomía podía fracasar. Para llegar a esa conclusión, los jueces distinguen entre el derecho a la información asistencial y el consentimiento informado, un derecho fundamental que se circunscribe exclusivamente al paciente; y las consecuencias derivadas de su vulneración que, señala el Supremo, también las sufrió la mujer.

La sección quinta de la Sala de lo Contencioso razona que la pareja no recibió información suficiente sobre la vasectomía, lo que condicionó su forma de actuar y les privó del derecho a tomar decisiones en el ámbito de la planificación familiar “con libertad y con conocimiento de los riesgos de un posible embarazo”. “Es evidente que resulta afectada la autodeterminación reproductiva no sólo del paciente, sino también de la mujer, y su derecho a decidir sobre una futura maternidad, con adopción, en su caso, de otros métodos o medios anticonceptivos para evitar un nuevo embarazo”, señala la sentencia, que recalca que el servicio público de salud, al no informar al paciente de los riesgos de la intervención, “ha causado también un daño a su pareja”.

La sentencia fija doctrina para supuestos similares: en los casos en los que sea demostrable que se ha omitido información relevante sobre el riesgo de fracaso de una vasectomía, la pareja estable del paciente puede reclamar responsabilidad patrimonial por los perjuicios propios derivados de esa omisión. Esta interpretación, advierte el tribunal, no nace de que la mujer tenga derecho al consentimiento informado, que es exclusivo para el paciente, sino de la existencia de un daño “autónomo” sufrido “por quien resulta afectado por las consecuencias de la falta de información”.

Published - October 27, 2026 07:00 am IST

The floating solar panels at Periyakulam (Ukkadam Big Tank) in Coimbatore. | Photo Credit: M. Periasamy

The global trend towards electrification has been recognised by the climate process, and the policy challenge is that the shift will involve less commonality and greater differentiation.

This suggests shifting the discussion from the global impact of coal-based emissions to the role of electricity in national well-being. The shift will be away from reliance on global models to a review of national actions. Global emissions of carbon dioxide deal with the symptoms, not the root cause of the problem: national energy use.

The G7 should not be allowed to set the agenda, as the Paris Agreement did 10 years ago. Shifting the global policy focus from production to consumption patterns will require a reframing of the climate process. Real collaboration will only come with a new conceptual framework that treats the global crisis as a collection of national inactions.

Academics in the West, acting as “epistemic communities”, set up the framework of climate policy and law. This framework comprises interlinked ‘global values’ that are universal, ‘global goods’ that are determined by global science, complex ‘global models’ based on global projections and ‘global rules’ arrived at through multilateral conference diplomacy in global organisations.

Official experts described complex issues as the best available knowledge to be universally accepted. They achieved this by using institutions of the United Nations as mechanisms to produce technical reports and frame policies, lending them legitimacy under the banner of international cooperation. International law was then used to enforce within countries the decisions driven by global ‘consensus’.

In the case of climate change, the gap between the evolving science of global ecological limits and the growing energy needs of urbanising countries seeking comparable levels of well-being was resolved through arm-twisting in an unequal world. There was no commitment to transfer financial resources as ‘means of implementation’.

Western diplomats converted a political claim in a vaguely worded treaty into workshops and meetings, where the Global South gained nothing but empty resolutions. Technology transfer has been treated as a ‘scientific’ issue rather than an ‘implementation’ issue. This framing ensured continuing dialogue without any outcome.

The lesson from 35 years of diplomatic negotiations as well as alternate models of growth to those of the West is the need to reframe climate policy.

First, in a major reversal the United States is echoing reservations of the Global South. The Executive Order “Putting America First in International Environmental Agreements”, January 20, 2025, underlines that the United States shall “henceforth prioritise economic efficiency, the promotion of American prosperity, consumer choice, and fiscal restraint in all foreign engagements that concern energy policy”.

Second, as energy use in the Global South grows to achieve comparable levels of well-being, ‘carbonising’ will precede ‘decarbonising’. This is only partly recognised in the UN’s new call for stabilisation, rather than reduction, of emissions. Third, the amount of energy needed for human well-being has never been discussed. China has emerged as the world’s second-largest economy and a major global manufacturing power, achieving levels of well-being comparable to those in the West with much lower energy use.

Fourth, China’s nationally driven path to achieving stabilisation has been missed in UN Reports even though it provides an alternate to the approach of the West. U.S. emissions increased by 133 megatons in 2025. China’s significant steps suggest that the technology aspect of the energy transition should look forward to electrification using renewable sources, rather than focus backwards on eliminating fossil fuels.

Fifth, China’s and India’s insight lies is limiting consumption as a percentage of GDP, replacing the internal combustion engine, and meeting new energy demand through solar, wind and hydropower. China’s more rapid progress shows that because solar and wind power have become “cheaper” than coal and gas, they will not drive the energy transition by themselves. Renewable energy is decentralised, intermittent and has zero-marginal-cost energy, requiring a strategic decision by the state on how to transform the energy system.

China installed more wind turbines and solar panels in 2025 than all other nations combined, adding about ten times as much capacity as the U.S. As this trend is expected to continue, 50% of electricity generation could come from non-fossil- fuel sources by 2030. About 5.62 million new energy vehicles were registered in China during the first half of 2025.

Climate policy should now by driven by practice, as a societal problem and not through global models, natural science and environmental law. First, emerging countries are using much less energy to achieve well-being in cities than the West did earlier, redefining lifestyles and ecological limits. Electrification is making the internal combustion engine redundant. Yet this technological trend in energy use is not captured in global emissions models used by the UN.

Second, in material use, the West’s much smaller share of the global population, around one-fifth, is balanced by the sustainable development of the Rest. The demographic trend is now towards ageing. These societal trends are ignored in global models, and taken together with West’s continuing disproportionate use of energy, suggest there is no global crisis, but rather a few national crises.

Third, given the increasing intensity and frequency of extreme events which affect the Global South, where insurance coverage is limited, continuing with token provision of climate finance by developed countries in negotiations needs to be reviewed. More practical measures include global early warning and regional technical cooperation in disaster relief.

The real question for India is how to build support for a new agenda centred on climate justice. The coming discussions on electrification offer an opportunity to shift UN policy development from finger-pointing towards achieving comparable levels of well-being., leveraging India’s status as the third largest economy with emissions half the global average.

(Mukul Sanwal is a Former UN Diplomat and Policy Adviser UNFCCC.)

#1119. La Agencia del Medicamento alerta del riesgo “mortal” que las lociones crecepelo suponen para los gatos y otras mascotas

Los animales de compañía sufren graves intoxicaciones al entrar en contacto directo con el minoxidil que usan sus dueños o indirecto a través de almohadas y sábanas

La Agencia Española de Medicamentos y Productos Sanitarios (AEMPS), dependiente del Ministerio de Sanidad, ha alertado este lunes del “riesgo que supone que los animales de compañía entren en contacto con medicamentos tópicos de uso humano que contengan minoxidil”. Este principio activo es el más usado frente a la alopecia androgénica —causada por factores genéticos y hormonales— en lociones, espumas y otras presentaciones que se aplican sobre la piel de las zonas en las que se quiere evitar la pérdida de pelo.

“Estos medicamentos pueden producir cuadros graves de toxicidad cardiovascular y desenlaces mortales, especialmente en los gatos”, sostiene el comunicado suscrito por la agencia. La exposición de los animales al fármaco puede deberse a la ingesta directa, pero “también de forma indirecta a través del contacto con personas que utilizan formulaciones tópicas a través de la piel contaminada (por ejemplo, las manos), o por contacto con objetos que hayan estado expuestos al medicamento, como las almohadas o el resto de ropa de cama”, informa la alerta.

El minoxidil es un vasodilatador que, aplicado de forma tópica, estimula el crecimiento del cabello. “Su exposición en mascotas de forma directa o indirecta puede provocar efectos cardiovasculares como hipotensión, taquicardia refleja, edema pulmonar, derrame pleural e insuficiencia cardiaca congestiva, debilidad, letargo, hipotensión, ataxia y temblores”, expone la AEMPS.

La Agencia hace hincapié en que este riesgo es desconocido por los dueños de las mascotas, por lo que “una mayor sensibilización facilitará el reconocimiento precoz de los casos y mejorará su notificación” ya que “algunas manifestaciones clínicas suelen ser inespecíficas y muchos casos pueden no ser reconocidos o no relacionarse fácilmente con la exposición a minoxidil de uso humano en el entorno doméstico”.

La nota publicada por la agencia explica que la evidencia disponible sobre estos efectos procede de publicaciones científicas, entre ellas análisis retrospectivos de centros de toxicología, casos clínicos y una revisión reciente de la literatura científica sobre la toxicidad del minoxidil en animales de compañía que muestran “de forma consistente este riesgo, especialmente en gatos, que parecen ser particularmente susceptibles a la toxicidad por minoxidil y varios informes describen efectos cardiovasculares graves y desenlaces mortales”.

La evidencia se basa en los datos proporcionados, entre otros, por el Centro de Control de Intoxicaciones de Animales de Estados Unidos (ASPCA, en sus siglas en inglés). De 211 exposiciones notificadas, este organismo identificó signos clínicos tanto en perros como en gatos tras exposiciones muy pequeñas (por ejemplo, unas pocas gotas o lamidos). En los casos notificados, se produjo la muerte en 8 de los 62 gatos (12,9%) que desarrollaron signos clínicos. La exposición indirecta a través de personas tratadas con minoxidil fue la circunstancia identificada con mayor frecuencia en gatos.

“Además, una revisión de la base de datos europea ha identificado al menos 8 casos relacionados con la exposición a minoxidil (3 en Bélgica, 1 en Estados Unidos y 4 en España). Los casos afectaron a 3 gatos y 5 perros”, sigue la nota de la AEMPS.

Hace dos años, el Centro de Farmacovigilancia de Navarra identificó 11 casos de lactantes cuyos padres utilizaban minoxidil por vía tópica que habían desarrollado hipertricosis, un cuadro clínico que se manifiesta por el crecimiento de pelo en todo el cuerpo y que también es conocido como síndrome del hombre lobo. Este hallazgo llevó a la Agencia Europea del Medicamento (EMA) a revisar la ficha técnica de estos fármacos para incluir un aviso sobre este riesgo.

#1121. How big is Russia's threat against Germany?

Experts believe that, so far, Germany has been ill-prepared — both militarily and mentally — for Russian provocations. They also warn against the idea that ending support for Ukraine would make Germany safer.

Warnings keep mounting about Russia's threat to Germany. On October 12, Sinan Selen, president of Germany's domestic intelligence agency, the BfV, said that Russia's covert attacks and destabilization efforts against Germany and other European countries are "not a temporary development but a long-term hybrid attack."

Even if the war in Ukraine were to end, said Selen, the Russian threat would not disappear. "For Russia, this is about completely redrawing the map of Europe and redefining its own role within Europe and in global politics."

He added that Russia's aggression would continue to be felt not only in Ukraine, but also in the Baltic states, in Poland and in Germany.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has described the threat situation as one in which "our country is not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare." Russia's goal, he said, is not to defeat Germany militarily "but to subdue us politically and socially."

Security experts, however, are not so sure that Russia is only interested in exercising political and social influence. Last year, political scientist Carlo Masala told the political talk show Maischberger that "Russia is preparing for a major war." And he didn't mean just a cyberwar. Inspector General Carsten Breuer, the Bundeswehr's highest-ranking officer, agreed.

For now, though, Russia remains tied up in its war against Ukraine. According to NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, there is no immediate military threat to NATO territory. But according to military experts, European intelligence agencies, and the German Defense Ministry, Russia will have the personnel and equipment to wage a conventional war against NATO by 2029. The Russian defense industry is running at full speed, and Moscow plans to expand its armed forces to 1.5 million soldiers.

At the moment, Russia has other objectives, believes Stefan Meister, an expert on Eastern Europe at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP): "I don't think Russia has any interest in a direct military conflict with NATO right now. It wants to test NATO and also display its capabilities," he tells DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

An example of Russia's hybrid war might be the failed attack with an explosive-laden drone against a Ukrainian transport aircraft at Leipzig-Halle Airport in August. Soon after, the German government stated that it was certain Russia was behind the attack.

Security expert Nico Lange told DW at the time that Germany was very lucky the explosives did not detonate: "Honestly, it was pure coincidence and not the result of German defensive measures."

As for why Germany was targeted specifically, Lange said: "I believe that Germany has always been a primary target of Russian influence and hybrid warfare. Russia believes that Germany is the key to European decision-making. Germany is now leading the way in supporting Ukraine."

Moscow swiftly responded to the German government's accusation with an angry denial. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said it was "the beginning of a real war," though there was no immediate further escalation.

Nevertheless, there is always the risk that things could spiral out of control following a Russian provocation and subsequent response, according to Stefan Meister: "Accidentally shooting down an aircraft that they were trying to intimidate would trigger a counter-reaction. But I don't believe that Russia is currently aiming for a direct war but rather for provocations, polarization, and sowing uncertainty among the population."

Not everyone shares the assessment that Russia poses a threat to Germany — some believe that the threat can be averted.

Despite the war in Ukraine, politicians from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the populist left-wing Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) want to improve relations with Russia, resume Russian energy supplies and end support for Ukraine.

AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said in early September, "People are fed up with this escalation against Russia, with the billions being squandered there on a system that is actually funded by German taxpayers' money."

The message appears to have resonated among the population, especially in eastern Germany. The AfD saw strong gains in all three state elections in September. In Saxony-Anhalt, it became the strongest party by far and may even run the government there soon, which would be the first time that a far-right party has held power in Germany since the end of WWII.

The CDU's security policy expert Roderich Kiesewetter disputed the claim made by the AfD and BSW that ending aid to Ukraine would mean greater security and more money for German schools and infrastructure: "Spending on education, social policy, and infrastructure is only possible if we live in freedom and democracy — and, above all, in peace and security. Anyone who believes that we'll have more money for social programs if we stop supporting Ukraine and let Russia have its way is either gravely mistaken or is making themselves a tool of Russian propaganda."

The perceived security threat has led the German military, the Bundeswehr, to fast-track significant modernization through substantial investment. But it is struggling to find enough recruits for its planned expansion. Many young Germans have taken to the streets to protest against plans to reintroduce conscription. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius faced criticism from inside his own party, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), for saying that Germany must become "capable of waging war." Many found the statement to be too militaristic.

Is Germany prepared for a military threat? "Not at all. Germany is not well prepared militarily or in the civilian sector, and the population isn't mentally prepared for it either," said Meister. "Just look at the demonstrations against conscription and the military that continue to take place, even though Germany needs a draft. For decades, we've grown up in this culture of pacifism, in a comfort zone. I believe there is very limited societal resilience, but above all, we are not at all mentally prepared for war."

Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) are under increasing political pressure — especially from the far right — to scale back support for Ukraine. But Merz never tires of emphasizing that Ukraine will continue to receive support under his chancellorship, calling it a matter of Germany's security. He recently visited Kyiv once again and, together with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, surveyed the destruction caused by Russia.

But this also means that the threat from Russia will continue and even intensify, says Stefan Meister: "I believe we will see a massive increase in attacks such as the one in Leipzig, of provocations involving drones. We will see attacks on infrastructures and possibly also on specific individuals within the military-industrial complex. I believe this is the real, concrete danger facing Germany in the coming months."

#1128. Un caso sospechoso de ébola llega a Suiza desde Nigeria

El hombre ha sido ingresado en el Hospital Universitario de Zúrich

Un hombre con sospecha de infección por ébola ha sido ingresado en el Hospital Universitario de Zúrich, según informó un portavoz del centro. El paciente había llegado a Suiza procedente de Nigeria. Previamente, el Gobierno nigeriano había indicado que una mujer con ébola había salido el lunes por la mañana en un vuelo de evacuación médica hacia Suiza y que su marido, diplomático de profesión, viajaba en el mismo avión. Algunas webs de seguimiento de vuelos señalaron que el aparato aterrizó en Suiza el lunes por la tarde.

El portavoz del hospital no identificó al hombre, pero precisó que también se había trasladado a una mujer a Ginebra para recibir tratamiento. Lo lógico sería pensar en el diplomático, pero las autoridades de la ciudad declinaron hacer comentarios y señalaron que el Gobierno suizo emitiría en breve un comunicado con los detalles.

Según el periódico helvético Blick, la mujer del diplomático es una ciudadana suiza de 42 años. Su estado ha mejorado, pero aún podría ser contagiosa, según las autoridades nigerianas. Nigeria notificó su caso el pasado 21 de octubre. Era el primer caso de ébola del país en más de una década. La mujer tiene nacionalidad suiza, pero vivía en Abuya, la capital de Nigeria. A principios de octubre había viajado a Uganda, donde hay un foco de la enfermedad activo. Comenzó a sentirse mal el 7 de octubre.

“El ébola afecta actualmente a tres regiones de África. La situación exige medidas urgentes y liderazgo político al más alto nivel”, declaró entonces Jean Kaseya, director general de los Centros para el Control y la Prevención de Enfermedades de África (Africa CDC). El organismo convocó una reunión virtual de alto nivel de los ministros de Sanidad africanos que tendrá lugar el miércoles 28 de octubre, “ante la creciente amenaza que representa el actual brote de ébola para la seguridad sanitaria del continente”. La epidemia ha dejado al menos 9.600 casos registrados y 4.646 muertes relacionadas en República Democrática del Congo, epicentro de la crisis, nueve casos en Kenia y 20 en Uganda. La cepa Bundibugyo, para la que aún no hay vacuna, la guerra en el este de la República Democrática del Congo y el desmantelamiento de parte de la ayuda internacional han desbordado a las autoridades africanas, incapaces de frenar una nueva epidemia, que de momento no llega a los números de las de 2014 y 2016.
