#1129. China's influence in the gaming industry is growing

Home to more than 700 million gamers, China is the world's largest gaming market — but it's also one of the most tightly regulated. The effects reach far beyond China, impacting players around the world.

In a dark underground hideout, dim light spills from a handful of oil lamps. A comrade fiddles with a rifle. A red flag hangs on one of the roughly hewn stone walls, bearing a hammer and sickle on a white star — the symbol of the ChineseWorkers' and Peasants' Red Army. Weapons are scattered on the ground. One is picked up, and soon the action moves into the snowy forest, where gunfire erupts among the trees.

Such a scene could fit in a new installment of "Call of Duty," the popular first-person shooter game that transports players to battlefields past, present, and future. But it is actually from "The Defiant." The game is currently being developed by the Chinese studio Hoothanes Technology in Hangzhou. It tells the story of Chinese forces fending off the Japanese army in the 1930s and 1940s.

Developer Connor Xu tells DW the weapons featured in the game are unique. They were used only in Asia and are therefore unfamiliar to many Western players, he says. The same goes for the story, which Xu says has never before been told in a video game.

"The Defiant" is also designed to appeal to an international audience. In just a few years, China has emerged as a major player in the global gaming industry despite strict regulations, censorship and a former ban on video game consoles.

More than 700 million people in China regularly play video games. According to market research company Newzoo, most consider gaming an important part of their lives. Many use games to stay in touch with friends.

"Games make life more interesting," developer Xu says. "I can try different roles, different stories, different characters, because we only have one life to live, but we can play a role in another story. That's really attractive, I think, to Chinese users."

People in China primarily play games on PCs and smartphones, while consoles are much less common. There are historical reasons for that: While gamers in Europe and North America debated whether PlayStation or Xbox was the better console in the early 2000s, the devices were not officially sold in China between 2000 and 2014. Chinese authorities said the restrictions were intended to protect children and teenagers from becoming addicted to gaming.

Minors in China are currently allowed to play online games for no more than three hours a week. There are no such limits for adults, but gaming is subject to strict controls. Anyone who wants to play must register using their real name and a personal identification number. That effectively allows the state to track who plays what and when, as well as whom they communicate with.

There is also a gray area that the Chinese government appears to tolerate. Some players log in using VPNs, giving them access to games that are not officially available in China. Some younger players use their parents' accounts to get around the limits on gaming time.

Despite its strict controls on underage gamers, China has become increasingly receptive to video games in general, having recognized the industry's enormous economic potential. Early on, games released for Chinese players often appeared to be copies of Western titles. At the same time, Chinese tech companies such as Tencent and NetEase invested in numerous Western gaming companies.

One distinctive feature of the Chinese market is its licensing system. "Unlike a lot of the other big video games markets in the world, China has a tightly regulated and licensed official video games market," George E. Osborn tells DW. The journalist advises NGOs and governments on video games and spoke at the Gamescom congress. In his book "Power Play," he describes how authoritarian states use video games to pursue political objectives.

The rule for all games in China is simple: No license, no sales. "That system essentially forces developers who want to release their video games to go through multiple layers of approval from China's Ministry of Propaganda, Ministry of Culture," Osborn says.

Games are prohibited from containing material that threatens China's unity, sovereignty or territorial integrity, among other restrictions. Pornographic content and gambling are also banned. Games may not incite crimes that threaten national security or spread information authorities believe could disrupt public order.

"The whole point around this criteria is that it's deliberately designed to be pretty vague," Osborn says. Whether a game violates the rules is a matter of interpretation. Sometimes games are altered even after release. In the 2025 action role-playing game "Wuchang: Fallen Feathers," for example, enemies based on famous Chinese figures from the Ming Dynasty suddenly could no longer be killed. Instead, they would collapse from exhaustion.

The Chinese action role-playing game "Black Myth: Wukong" became an unexpected international hit in 2024. By then, it was clear Chinese developers could do more than cater to the domestic market — they could create successful games for a global audience as well. The game was inspired by the 16th-century Chinese literary classic "Journey to the West."

Osborn sees nothing wrong with bringing Chinese culture to audiences around the world. The question, he says, is how much the state actually intervenes in the games themselves. "I think in general, video game players are actually quite deeply skeptical of these kinds of things. They are generally very good at spotting when someone might be selling to them or someone might be propagandizing. And so I think if it's too obvious, it won't work," he says.

Because of the licensing system, Western developers also have to comply with government requirements if they want to sell their games in China. And they do want to, Osborn says, because the market is too big to ignore. "But I think when you start thinking about the potential impact this has on creative standards around the world, I think it's really important that developers ask themselves the question of what will we or won't we compromise on here?"

He fears the real danger lies in self-censorship. That could lead developers, for example, to leave queer characters out of their games. That would represent a major step backward, he says, because games help many people explore their identities.

China is not the only country where games are modified to comply with national regulations. In Germany, for example, symbols that violate the country's constitution, such as the swastika, may not be shown in games unless the game in question explicitly contributes to the country's culture of remembrance. Depictions of extreme violence also have to be removed from German versions.

Glorifying violence is prohibited in China, too, yet Xu's team is still allowed to develop a war game. How does this add up? Xu explains it this way: "I think in this game, the most important thing is not violence. The most important thing is to tell history."

Xu says the team is committed to delivering a historically accurate product. Whether it succeeds will be for historians to judge.

#1138. ¿Presento mi candidatura a la dirección de un centro?

La percepción de los propios conocimientos y capacidades de los aspirantes para ejercer la dirección importa sobremanera, ya que la cualificación para el ejercicio directivo no deriva solo de las prácticas docentes

La evolución del acceso a la dirección de los centros, en el sistema educativo, ha evolucionado, tras la promulgación constitucional, de procesos de elección, por los miembros de los Consejos Escolares de los propios centros —desde 1985 hasta 2002—, a los de selección, realizada por una específica Comisión de Selección con representantes del centro y de la comunidad educativa —a partir del año 2002 y hasta la actualidad—.

En el primer caso, la elección era el resultado de una votación. Y en el segundo, de la resolución de un concurso de méritos para el desempeño directivo, con un requisito y a la vez mérito de especial relevancia: aportar un proyecto de dirección. Así las cosas, no es desajustado señalar que la presentación de una candidatura a la dirección de un centro resulta de un proceso de toma de decisiones en el que deben considerarse tres aspectos principales: el conocimiento con que se cuenta del centro que se pretende dirigir, la percepción de las propias competencias y capacidades para hacerlo, y las situaciones que influyen significativamente, incluso determinan el procedimiento de selección.

Aunque se dé preferencia a las candidaturas del propio centro, en el concurso de méritos para el acceso a la dirección pueden concurrir docentes de otros centros, por lo que el conocimiento de las características y realidades del centro a cuya dirección se opta es relevante. Se trata, así, de conocer antecedentes significativos, identidades y singularidades, conflictos relevantes, desarrollo profesional de los docentes, naturaleza de la planificación institucional, relaciones entre sectores de la comunidad educativa, incluso la distribución del poder ­ —es una obra de referencia, en tal sentido, el libro La micropolítica de la escuela, del sociólogo de la educación británico y analista de políticas educativas Stephen J. Ball, con primera edición de 1987—.

La percepción de los propios conocimientos y capacidades de los candidatos y candidatas para ejercer la dirección importa sobremanera, ya que la cualificación para el ejercicio directivo no deriva solo de las prácticas docentes. Por tanto, las capacidades y destrezas para asumir la dirección, los modelos de dirección y los estilos de liderazgo, el acceso a la formación específica, el propio desarrollo profesional, e incluso la tolerancia y la resiliencia forman parte del elenco de aspectos en los que también conviene reparar.

Y queda el análisis de las situaciones en que se pretende acceder a la dirección, ya que, como se adelantó, pueden condicionar o determinar tal acceso. Una es la situación de continuidad, cuando el director o directora concluye su periodo de mandato (cuatro años) y las renovaciones que establecen las Administraciones educativas tras la evaluación positiva del desempeño. Otra la de relevo, cuando la candidatura a la dirección se presenta por un miembro del equipo directivo cuyo director o directora no continua. Y también son factibles la concurrencia de varias candidaturas en el mismo centro o el carácter externo de la candidatura o candidaturas presentadas, al tratarse de docentes de otros centros.

En cualquier caso, el contenido del proyecto de dirección, que deben presentar las candidatos y candidatas ante la Comisión de Selección —aunque se verifiquen disfunciones a las que habrá que prestar atención en otro análisis—, es un aspecto principal para la valoración que han de realizar los integrantes de esa Comisión. Se trate de la continuidad del director o directora, que actualizará la orientación de su ejercicio en el proyecto; del relevo, con aportaciones particulares del aspirante; de la concurrencia de candidatos, para subrayar las diferencias; o del ajuste del proyecto por las candidaturas externas.

Como puede advertirse, tomar la decisión de presentar la candidatura a la dirección de un centro es bastante más que responder, directa y ligeramente, a la voluntad de hacerlo.

Antonio Montero Alcaide es inspector de Educación y rofesor de la Facultad de Ciencias de la Educación en la Universidad de Sevilla.

#1140. The Bundestag has debated the genocide Germany carried out in Namibia a century ago. But will it spur progress on addressing colonial crimes?

Opposition parties have forced a debate in the Bundestag on the early-20th-century genocide Germany carried out in Namibia. Will this finally spur progress in addressing colonial crimes?

Gaob Daniel Timotheus Frederick was sitting in the front row of the visitors' gallery in the Bundestag this week. Wearing a suit and hat, he had traveled all the way from Namibia to see this parliamentary debate unfold. For almost 120 years, his family had been waiting for the return of human remains of their ancestor, Cornelius Frederick (sometimes spelled Fredericks), who had led the Nama resistance against German colonial rule and died on Shark Island in Germany's first concentration camp.

In the name of his great-grandfather and as a member of the Nama Traditional Leaders Association (NTLA), Frederick was there to demand an "unconditioned apology" from Germany.

Sitting next to him, in uniform and white gloves, with a carved lion on the handle of his walking stick, was the head of the Ovaherero Traditional Authority, Paramount Chief Mutjinde Katjiua. Speaking before the Bundestag debate, the chief said: "We call upon the Bundestag to recognize unequivocally the genocides committed against the Ovaherero and Nama peoples."

Many people wonder why the German parliament hasn't already done this — and why the government has not yet issued an official apology. There is a draft joint declaration with Namibia in which the German government acknowledges that "from today's perspective, [it] would be called genocide." But there is no German-Namibian reconciliation agreement. The evidence is overwhelming: From 1904 to 1908, the German Empire waged a war of extermination against the Indigenous people of southwestern Africa, including the Ovaherero (also known as the Herero), the Nama, the Damara and the San. At least 100,000 people were killed, and just as many displaced. Many were subjected to forced labor and forced prostitution. The land seizures and expropriation carried out at the time continue to affect their descendants today.

Jürgen Zimmerer, a professor of history at the University of Hamburg whose research focuses on Africa, told DW that the Bundestag and government lack the will to confront this era in German history. "There are Bundestag resolutions on the Armenian genocide, one on the Holodomor [in Ukraine], and one on the genocide against the Yazidis [by the "Islamic State" in Iraq]. But there is no recognition of the genocide against the Herero and Nama by the German Bundestag." If there were any political will to do so, Zimmerer said, it could happen very quickly.

The socialist Left Party initiated the Bundestag debate by drafting a resolution calling for full recognition and compensation in collaboration with representatives of the descendants. The goal: "restorative justice." Paramount Chief Katjiua has rejected the existing agreement between the Namibian and German governments. "Development aid cannot substitute for comprehensive reparations," he said.

Since 2021, the governments have been negotiating a joint declaration that pledges €1.1 billion ($1.24 billion) in reconstruction aid to Namibia over 30 years. Once the agreement is signed, Germany's president is set to issue a formal apology.

But the Foreign Ministry warned: "Legal claims to compensation cannot be derived from the recognition of genocide. With these negotiations — which are unique worldwide — Namibia and Germany have broken new ground and are pioneers in confronting their colonial past."

Political scientist Andreas Mehler, the director of the Anton Bergstraesser Institute at the University of Freiburg, said the government's plan sounded like "checkbook diplomacy."

Zimmerer also said there was a financial calculation: "If we were to recognize an obligation to provide reparations to the families of those killed — given the millions of victims of World War II, the victims of the Germans — it would ruin us."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Four lines in the 144 pages of the coalition agreement of the current German government — between the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU)/Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — summarize the extent of the government's commitment to reconciliation with Namibia.

"We will intensify our efforts to come to terms with colonialism," the text reads. "This includes transnational research into artifacts and the restitution of cultural property in dialogue with the countries of origin. Particular attention will be paid to establishing a dignified memorial site and the repatriation of human remains."

Compared with the efforts to address colonialism led by the SPD-led government from 2021 to 2025, "the issue has lost visibility," said Alexander Stroh-Steckelberg, a professor of political scientist at the University of Bayreuth who specializes in Africa.

Zimmerer has an even more critical take: "I wouldn't even call it a stalemate anymore. I believe this government is rolling back the progress that has been made in terms of raising awareness of colonial injustices."

Much remains to be done, as far the descendants of the Ovaherero are concerned: The remains of tens of thousands of people are believed to still be in Germany. Gaob D. Timotheus Frederick and other descendants of the victims have been fighting to heal these wounds for generations.

In March, Germany established a coordination council, headed by the Foreign Ministry, which stated that the government did not wish to "dictate to the countries and societies of origin which cultural artifacts and human remains they should reclaim, what priorities they should set or how restitutions should be handled."

Serap Güler, a state minister in the Foreign Ministry and the chair of the coordination council, defends the government's actions so far. Recounting her own official trips — she has already been to Togo, and next week she plans to travel to Rwanda and Burundi — she said: "Everywhere I go, I receive recognition for our sincere and trusting approach to the past — as well as for our determined commitment to a future of freedom, security and prosperity."

Zimmerer said Germany "has earned a reputation as a country that takes a critical view of its own history and learns from its mistakes" — which gives it "enormous cultural capital" on the world stage. But he is concerned that this capital is currently being squandered.

The government's memorial policy does not appear to address colonialism. Zimmerer even detects an attempt to "marginalize German colonial crimes" in the recent proposal by Minister of State for Culture Wolfram Weimer to create a dignified memorial site in Bremen. He notes that victim groups have not been included in Weimer's proposal and said the colonial capitals of the German Empire — Berlin and Hamburg — must also become sites of remembrance.

Ninety-five percent of the colonial troops set sail from Hamburg's Baakenhafen, including Commander Lothar von Trotha, who issued the orders to exterminate the Ovaherero and Nama. According to Zimmerer, the fact that a new opera house — rather than a memorial site — is being built at Baakenhafen constitutes a staggering case of "art-washing of history." Mehler also hopes that a productive debate on memorial sites will still take place and that, overall, "many more places will come to terms with colonial history."

Meanwhile, Gaob D. Timotheus Frederick continues to call for a collective effort to come to terms with the past: "Let us give opportunity to the affected communities that are being represented by us to have a seat on the table to discuss with them the rest of the way."

This article was originally written in German.

Updated - October 26, 2026 09:02 pm IST - SAO PAULO

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate for presidential re-election, greets supporters outside his residence on the day of the presidential runoff election, in Sao Paulo, Brazil on October 25, 2026. | Photo Credit: Reuters

In an election victory whose results will reverberate across Latin America, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured a historic fourth presidential term, defeating Flávio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party (PL) in Brazil’s runoff on Sunday (October 26, 2026). Mr. Lula secured 64 million votes, the highest total ever recorded in a Brazilian presidential election, defeating Mr. Bolsonaro by more than four million votes.

Declaring a “defeat for lies and denialism”, Mr. Lula pledged to govern for all Brazilians and protect the country’s sovereignty.

“Brazil is nobody’s backyard,” Mr. Lula declared at a midnight rally, sending a message to U.S. President Donald Trump as he said Brazil has defeated the far-right lies, foreign interference and election meddling by social media firms.

In an emotional speech, Mr. Lula thanked women and older voters for their support and praised the mobilisation of young people on the streets and on social media.

“People went out to vote because we managed to convince them that their votes were extremely important to safeguarding democracy in the country,” he said. He also said he had learned many lessons from the election and promised to change his approach to governing, ensure greater public participation in government decisions and give digital communication a more prominent role during his fourth term.

“The future begins today, and its name is youth. I salute the women who made all the difference. I salute the older people who made sacrifices and made their way to the polling stations to vote,” Mr. Lula said.

Also Read: Left leaders hail Lula’s fourth win in Brazil, say it offers hope to workers’ movements

Mr. Lula secured an unprecedented comeback in the election. He trailed in the first round, receiving 45.16% of valid votes against 47.03% for Mr. Bolsonaro.

As the prospect of a Bolsonaro presidency caused a major concern among the young, especially about public education, healthcare and transport, millions of people joined weekly rallies across the country, pledging support for Mr. Lula and demanding protection of public services.

On Sunday (October 25, 2026), Mr. Lula told his young supporters that their voices have been heard.

“We will make increasing investment in the Unified Health System, develop a national artificial intelligence system, continue to expand public universities and support the digital and creative economies,” said Mr. Lula amid loud cheers and applause.

The turnaround after the first round of election on October 4 was not only historic but also dramatic.

Mr. Lula’s official campaign team almost took a back seat as millions of people came out on the streets and joined the social media campaign. With most opinion polls predicting a neck-and-neck race and some even giving an edge to Mr. Bolsonaro till a few days back, the Workers’ Party shifted its messaging from a comparison of the candidates’ personal records to a forward-looking agenda centred on concrete promises.

Even as Mr. Lula made his promises to the electorate, his campaign faced a big challenge: Big Tech firms openly supported Mr. Bolsonaro’s campaign while suppressing advertising by Mr. Lula’s team.

In his speech on Sunday (October 25), Mr. Lula said he had to overcome “interference” by digital platforms and pledged to regulate big tech companies in Brazil.

“This election was one in which we had to overcome interference coming from outside and through digital platforms. We will have to regulate them,” Mr. Lula said.

On October 16, after an expose in the Brazilian media, Meta admitted that its artificial intelligence tool had blocked the generation of advertising material supporting Mr. Lula while allowing the same technology to be used by Bolsonaro campaign.

With this historic mobilisation of people and victory, Mr. Lula also seems to have defeated Mr. Trump, who had repeatedly made clear that his preferred candidate in the race was Mr. Bolsonaro.

Even on Sunday night (October 25), Mr. Trump questioned Mr. Lula’s victory, comparing it to the 2020 U.S. election, which he lost to Joe Biden and alleged that Brazil had followed the “Joe Biden playbook.”

Mr. Lula’s victory has dealt a setback to the growing number of Trump-backed right-wing leaders across Latin America. His win is “a defeat for the United States’ defence strategy in Latin America, based on the Shield of the Americas,” said Celso Amorim, special foreign policy advisor to the Brazilian president.

On Sunday night (October 25), the veteran diplomat hailed the result as “a great victory, made even greater by the circumstances.” “The Brazilian people rose up,” said Mr. Amorim, who served as Foreign Minister and Defence Minister under Mr. Lula.

He also ruled out any possibility of Brazil joining the Shield of the Americas, an alliance launched by U.S. President Donald Trump in March this year, ostensibly to combat drug trafficking across the region.

Mr. Lula’s victory also drew congratulations from political leaders across Latin America, many of whom underscored the importance of democracy and continued regional cooperation with Brasília. Leaders from Mexico, Chile, Paraguay, Bolivia, Panama and other countries welcomed the result in posts on X.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum celebrated Brazil’s democratic process and popular participation, declaring: “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil have won. Congratulations, President Lula!”

Even as Brazil’s historic election creates waves across the world, Mr. Bolsonaro has refused to accept the election result, announcing that he would seek its annulment. He accused the Federal Supreme Court of “changing the rules midway” after a judge ordered voting across the country to be extended until 7 p.m. when Mr. Lula complained about many right-wing mayors curtailing bus services in poor areas in many cities.

“It is impossible to recognise the election result in the context in which these things happened,” said a glum-looking Mr. Bolsonaro.

But on Monday (October 26), Brazilian media quoted three justices of the Supreme Court and the Brazilian Election Commission (TSE) as saying the decision to extend voting hours by two hours on Sunday (October 26) is “unlikely to provide grounds for annulling the election or invalidating votes”. The TSE has also announced plans to counter “any attempts to overturn the election results”.

On Sunday (October 25) , Brazil rose up to protect its democracy.

After Mr. Lula finished his speech on Sunday night (October 25), the crowd broke into a rendition of Brazil’s national independence song, sending a message to the far-right, Trump and Meta.

#1147. La Policía alerta de un nuevo ciberacoso: los “curis” que ridiculizan a alumnos y profesores en redes

Algunas comunidades autónomas, como Aragón, ya remiten instrucciones para actuar si se detectan publicaciones que difunden contenidos vejatorios hacia la comunidad educativa

Los memes han evolucionado. Los adolescentes, desde primero de la ESO hasta el segundo de bachillerato, han inventado un formato completamente nuevo que ya ha llegado a las aulas de los distintos institutos de España y que se ha vuelto un fenómeno viral: los curis. Son cuentas creadas con el nombre de los respectivos colegios, principalmente en TikTok, que recrean escenas de la vida cotidiana escolar. Si bien la mayoría de las situaciones parecen ser inofensivas, la Policía Nacional ya alerta de posibles conductas delictivas detrás de las publicaciones anónimas, como el ciberacoso o el bullying.

Un vídeo publicado en las redes sociales oficiales de las fuerzas de seguridad señala que ya se han registrado casos que humillan o ridiculizan a los miembros de la comunidad educativa. “El acoso en redes puede ser delito, una cuenta anónima no te hace intocable. Las cuentas curis pueden hacer humor sobre lo que está pasando en clase, el problema empieza cuando conviertes a un compañero o a un profesor en el blanco de las burlas. Aunque uses un dibujo y no pongas su nombre, tus compañeros pueden reconocer perfectamente a quién estás señalando”, ha indicado uno de los agentes. También la Guardia Civil, en colaboración con el INCIBE, ha pedido que no se difundan esos contenidos: “Si encuentras una cuenta de este tipo, no difundas su contenido. Repórtalo, cuéntaselo a un adulto de confianza”.

Desde la Policía Nacional han explicado que, en función de su gravedad y de las circunstancias de cada caso, estas conductas pueden constituir delitos contra la integridad moral o injurias graves, así como responsabilidades civiles. “El uso de dibujos o la presentación de una publicación como una broma no impiden que se valore su contenido y el daño causado, aunque se realice desde un perfil anónimo”, señala la nota de prensa que ha sido dada a conocer en la mañana de este viernes.

Las burlas sobre el aspecto físico, la difusión de rumores o los montajes vejatorios pueden exponer a la persona afectada ante su entorno escolar, por lo que los agentes han instado a reportar y denunciar los contenidos de este tipo. “Si te llega una publicación que humilla, no la compartas, repórtala y apoya a quien la esté sufriendo. Si te está pasando a ti, guarda capturas, el usuario y también los enlaces, habla con un adulto de confianza, o en tu centro educativo, y denúncialo ante la Policía Nacional”, ha insistido nuevamente el oficial.

Algunas comunidades autónomas ya han tomado medidas para “prevenir y abordar estas situaciones de forma homogénea en todos los centros”. Es el caso del Departamento de Educación, Ciencia y Universidades del Gobierno de Aragón, que ha remitido a todos los centros educativos de la comunidad unas instrucciones comunes para actuar si detectan cuentas, perfiles o publicaciones en redes sociales que difundan contenidos vejatorios o lesivos hacia la comunidad educativa, según ha reportado el periódico local Hoy Aragón.

En La Rioja, los curis ya han provocado denuncias, como la interpuesta por la dirección del IES Rey Don Sancho de Nájera. La broma ha dado paso a un contenido “ofensivo y difamatorio”, ha explicado en Radio Rioja Cadena SER el director del centro, Antonio Hernández Lobo.

En Andalucía también se han reportado casos en varios institutos, según han dado a conocer desde la Asociación Andaluza de Directores (Asadipre). Sylvia Frey, de la delegación de Málaga, ha indicado que la situación genera preocupación, sobre todo en torno a la generación de estos contenidos por parte de niños de primaria. “Preocupa el hecho de que tengan la gratuidad de poder publicar cosas pensando que son anónimas. Con la investigación se acaban encontrando quiénes son los autores. Las familias tienen que ser conocedoras de que son las últimas responsables de todo lo que ocurre. Puede llegar a tener consecuencias penales”, ha expresado a través de una conversación telefónica.

La representante de los directores andaluces ha recordado que, una vez que identifiquen a los autores, estos serán sancionados. “Tenemos un reglamento de organización interna. Es una falta grave contra la convivencia en el centro y tiene sus medidas y sus sanciones”, ha zanjado.

Trucks carrying flour supplied by an Egyptian committee arrive at a bakery in Deir al-Balah, in the central Gaza Strip, on Saturday, on October 24, 2026. | Photo Credit: AP

A ceasefire agreement in Gaza has not stopped what a group of independent experts commissioned by the UN say is genocide carried out by Israel in the territory, the team said in a new report on Monday (October 26, 2026). They also accused Israeli forces of crimes against humanity, including torture and rape, in the West Bank.

Israel, which denies both the genocide and the sexual assault claims, did not immediately respond to the report's publication.

The Associated Press could not independently corroborate multiple graphic accounts described in the report of sexual assaults by prison guards and soldiers on Palestinian detainees since October 2023. In one, female guards strip-searched a pregnant Palestinian woman. .In another, guards beat and hurled sexist slurs while denying a detainee access to the toilet and sanitary pads. She bled onto her clothes and interrogation chair.

The findings by the Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which seeks to document in minute detail the allegations and evidence of crimes to bolster accountability for perpetrators, could be used by prosecutors at the International Criminal Court or in other jurisdictions to try to bring justice to victims and their relatives.

The report on Monday (October 26) said Israel was “continuing to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza.”

The report also accused Israel and members of its security forces of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the West Bank and Gaza, including extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence and persecution against civilians. File | Photo Credit: AP

Much of the harm has come, the report says, from Israel's expansion deeper into Gaza during that period. Since October 2025, when the ceasefire was signed, Israeli forces have gone from controlling 53% of Gaza to at least 60%, the commission said.

In that time, Israeli fire across the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians – including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls.

The report also accused Israel and members of its security forces of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the West Bank and Gaza, including extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence and persecution against civilians.

The commission said that it had recently documented six cases where Israeli guards were sexually violent toward male detainees from Gaza in the Sde Teiman military prison. In one case, it says guards raped a Palestinian detainee.

The commission says it drew its conclusions after investigating seven cases between November 2023 and June 2026, where Israeli forces caused bodily harm to Palestinians, often children, who did not appear to be posing a threat.

#1151. Who was Eva Mamlok? Berlin square renamed after Jewish anti-fascist resistance fighter

She started taking action against Hitler as a teenager and never stopped until her death in a concentration camp. Berlin's Blücherplatz is now being renamed after her.

In the history of German resistance to Nazism, some names have become symbols: Sophie Scholl, Claus von Stauffenberg, Dietrich Bonhoeffer and Georg Elser. Yet many others have remained largely forgotten.

Among them is Eva Mamlok, a young Jewish woman from Berlin whose acts of defiance began in her teenage years and continued until her murder in a Nazi concentration camp.

Now more people will get to know her story as Berlin renames Blücherplatz, a square in the district of Kreuzberg, Eva-Mamlok-Platz on October 16.

"Eva Mamlok was a very remarkable person. As a young Jewish woman from Berlin, her spirit of resistance was particularly striking," said cultural researcher Alexandra Weltz-Rombach, who has worked extensively with the historians' network "Gruppe Eva Mamlok."

Mamlok was born on May 6, 1918, into a Jewish family in Berlin. They ran a wholesale wine business, and the family belonged to the vibrant Jewish middle class that formed an important part of Berlin's social and economic life during the Weimar Republic.

But Eva came of age just as Germany was descending into dictatorship. When Hitler became chancellor in 1933, she was only 14 years old. She was also a member of the Socialist Workers' Youth (SAJ). Following the suppression of the left-wing political youth organization later that year, she became active in the underground resistance.

According to testimony from Inge Berner (1922-2012), the sole survivor of Mamlok's later resistance group, Eva climbed onto the roof of a department store on Blücherplatz as a teenager and painted the slogan "Down with Hitler."

"She was caught doing that, though she wasn't arrested at that particular moment — that didn't happen until a year later," noted Weltz-Rombach.

Mamlok first appeared in official records in November 1934, after she was arrested for taking part in commemorations for socialist leaders Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht at Berlin's Friedrichsfelde Cemetery.

Authorities determined that the 16-year-old held "hostile views toward the state" and placed her in "protective custody until further notice" — a euphemism the regime used to justify imprisonment without trial. She was sent to the women's concentration camp at Moringen in Lower Saxony, where she remained until May 1935.

After her release, she continued her anti-Nazi activities despite the increasing danger, facing persecution both as a political dissident and as a Jew.

In these underground circles, she met Pieter Siemsen (1914–2004), and they remained a couple until he emigrated to Argentina in 1937. The only known surviving photograph of Eva comes from his personal archive.

She had a daughter, Tana, in 1939. The father's identity is unknown, however. The child was placed in a Jewish orphanage in Berlin and deported in 1942 to the Auschwitz-Birkenau extermination camp, where she was murdered.

Meanwhile, because she was Jewish, Mamlok was forced to perform compulsory labor at the Berlin firm F. Butzke Schrauben-Industrie in 1940. There she met other women who shared her opposition to Nazism.

Together they formed what later became known as the "Eva Mamlok Group," an informal resistance network of Jewish and non-Jewish women. They distributed anti-Nazi leaflets and wrote slogans critical of Hitler.

They also shared banned books. "They were books that are today part of Germany's educational canon," from Thomas Mann to Lion Feuchtwanger, said Weltz-Rombach. That the Berlin Central and Regional Library (ZLB), Germany's largest public library, stands on the new Eva-Mamlok-Platz is a fitting symbol of this act of resistance and the importance of books, she added.

Mamlok and others in her group were arrested for distributing this forbidden literature. On January 13, 1942, she was deported from Berlin to the Riga Ghetto in occupied Latvia.

According to Inge Berner's testimony, Mamlok remained active in the resistance there too. For example, she arranged for a contact still in Berlin to send her a cake with a miniature camera hidden inside it to document persecution in the ghetto.

In October 1944, she was sent to the Stutthof Nazi concentration camp, where she died in December of that year.

Blücherplatz was named after the Prussian field marshal Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, whose most renowned achievement was leading his army against Napoleon at the Battle of Leipzig in 1813 and the Battle of Waterloo in 1815.

Several places, including streets and parks, have been named after him in Germany.

"There is no shortage of Blücher memorial sites," said Weltz-Rombach. "And perhaps it's also time to put an end to this old Franco-German enmity — which is, of course, inherent in the name Blücher, given its Prussian tradition — and to establish, in its place, a different form of remembrance."

The square also happens to be the site of the Carnival of Cultures, a multicultural street festival and parade held every year to celebrate Berlin's global diversity.

Having first heard about Mamlok when a Stolperstein commemorating her was laid in 2011, Weltz-Rombach has been researching her biography for the past few years. The Berlin-based filmmaker, producer and curator has also been sharing the resistance fighter's story through various projects, including an exhibition in 2024 and a podcast series with young Berliners.

Since Mamlok was only a teenager herself when she became politically active, the workshop participants can easily relate to her fate.

These teenagers learn about Mamlok's experiences at the actual locations where she was active, helping them imagine what it would be like to be arrested and imprisoned for six months without trial for doing things that normally wouldn't be considered crimes — such as simply expressing an opinion publicly or laying flowers at a commemorative event, explained Weltz-Rombach.

"Above all, she is, of course, a role model — an example of how one would like to act oneself, and how courageous one would like to be."

"[Women's] resistance was often of a more everyday nature, rather than planting bombs," said Weltz-Rombach. Their stories offer examples of "forms of resistance that have only recently received more attention." Other examples include a 2024 exhibition and the launch of a database dedicated to female resistance fighters.

Even though many of the eyewitnesses are now dead, Weltz-Rombach believes there are still many more of these stories that deserve to be brought into the spotlight: "There are definitely many names we do not know, that are waiting to be further researched."

A French flag flies as protesters stand on the Marianne statue of the Place de la République during a demonstration against the cost of living and rising fuel prices in Paris as part of nationwide protests called by the "Yellow Vests" movement, joined by French high school and university students, teachers and parents demanding better school conditions and government action, as well as labour unions, workers, farmers and retirees, in France, on October 17, 2026. | Photo Credit: Reuters

France is in turmoil. More than half a million people hit the streets on October 17, as protests swept across the country. As the administration greeted the protesters with a large deployment of riot police, peaceful demonstrations were engulfed by violence in many places. Arsonists set fire to the Lyon tourist office and burnt down the Limoges City Hall, a historic municipal building. Protesters stormed the townhall in Marseille and attacked the prefect’s residence in Bordeaux. In Paris’s Place de la Republique, protesting youth who clashed with the police torched vehicles and looted shops. Luxury retailers such as Louis Vuitton, Hermes, Dior and Galeries Lafayette suffered millions of dollars in losses as their stores were ransacked. Police arrested or detained more than 6,000 people, including hundreds of minors.

With the police outnumbered and unable to protect public and private property, several cities resorted to full or partial curfews. Government officials have blamed the unrest on “seditionists from far-left fringe groups”. They have accused La France Insoumise, or LFI (France Unbowed), the leftwing political party launched by veteran politician Jean-Luc Melenchon (75), of inciting the protests with the aim of extracting political mileage ahead of the presidential elections in April 2027.

#1158. Las universidades de Madrid irán a la huelga el 4 y 5 de noviembre por la “estafa” del acuerdo de financiación de Ayuso

Los convocantes del paro, independiente del educativo, denuncian que la inversión en los campus se sitúa en el 0,4% del PIB, frente al 0,75% nacional y al 0,92% europeo

La Coordinadora en defensa de la Universidad Pública ―que aúna a la mayoría de sindicatos y muchas asociaciones de estudiantes― ha convocado este jueves una nueva huelga en contra de los recortes del Gobierno de Isabel Díaz Ayuso en los seis campus de Madrid. Los trabajadores (docentes investigadores y de administración y servicios) y los estudiantes están llamados a parar el 4 y el 5 de noviembre contra “la infrafinanciación de la Universidad Pública, que propicia la privatización y la mercantilización de nuestra formación universitaria, y la reivindicación de los derechos políticos de trabajadoras y estudiantes”.

En la capital hay ya 14 universidades privadas ―sin contar con las sedes de centros extranjeros o españoles― abiertas frente a seis públicas y la opción de que lleguen a ser 17, porque el Ejecutivo regional tiene encima de la mesa otros tres proyectos que cuentan con un informe negativo de los técnicos del Ministerio de Ciencia, Innovación y Universidades.

El apagón del 28 de abril de 2025, que dejó a oscuras España, provocó que la primera huelga convocada pasase desapercibida. Tuvo entonces un gran seguimiento en la Universidad Complutense, la más asfixiada, y poco en la Autónoma, Alcalá, Politécnica, Carlos III y Rey Juan Carlos. Pero la tensión de los rectores con la Comunidad de Madrid fue escalando y la siguiente convocatoria, los días 26 y 27 de noviembre, sí que tuvo un éxito incontestable en los campus, salvo en la Politécnica y Alcalá (recibe fondos de Castilla-La Mancha).

Al final del curso pasado, la Coordinadora en Defensa de la Universidad Pública comenzó a trabajar en esta huelga de noviembre que casualmente coincide ahora con la precampaña por el adelanto electoral. No es una consecuencia de la huelga educativa, también concebida hace meses, ni la convocada por la vivienda.

El paro es casi idéntico al del año pasado, cuando miles de estudiantes y profesores recorrieron el centro de la capital, tras vaciar las aulas, para exigir el aumento del presupuesto. El impacto mediático fue tal que en la Puerta del Sol decidieron tomar medidas para frenar el descontento universitario en las calles a año y medio de las elecciones autonómicas. Cambiaron al consejero -provocando un cataclismo de dimisiones-, escucharon a los rectores que se sentían ninguneados y cerraron en marzo de 2026 un acuerdo que calificaron como “histórico” y un “hito” el nuevo plan de financiación.

El pacto selló una inversión en los campus públicos de 14.800 millones de euros desde este año hasta 2031. Pero las cifras están hinchadas, pues se incluye la partida que pagan las familias y parte del aumento está condicionado a que las universidades cumplan objetivos.

“El presupuesto destinado a nuestra Universidad sigue siendo insuficiente, manteniéndose en el 0,4 % del PIB, muy por debajo del 1% que establece la LOSU [Ley Orgánica del Sistema Universitario] y, por tanto, por debajo de la media nacional, de 0,75%, como de la europea, 0,92%”, se afirma en el comunicado leído en una rueda de prensa celebrada este jueves en la Universidad Autónoma. “Dicho acuerdo, que vendieron como ‘histórico’, es una estafa y desde entonces consideramos que tanto el Gobierno del Partido Popular como la CRUMA [los rectores madrileños] son responsables de la crisis de la Universidad Pública”, prosigue.

La Consejería de Educación, por su parte, no entiende la huelga. “Los convocantes alegan una supuesta falta de financiación que, simplemente, no se sostiene. El acuerdo sobre el modelo de financiación plurianual firmado con los rectores, que han sido elegidos como representantes de las universidades públicas, pone en manos de estos seis centros 14.800 millones de euros hasta 2031 para que puedan seguir creciendo y liderando la consolidación de Madrid como el mayor hub universitario del sur de Europa”, señala a preguntas de este diario.

Hasta ahora, Madrid, pese a ser la comunidad más rica, ha sido la que menos financiación aporta por alumno universitario de toda España, según un informe publicado anualmente por la Fundación Conocimiento y Desarrollo, que mide la contribución de los campus a la sociedad. Habrá que esperar una nueva edición del análisis para ver dónde se posiciona Madrid tras la inyección económica, pero no subirá mucho porque el aumento de fondos es pequeño para repartir entre 220.000 universitarios matriculados en la red pública de Madrid.

Para calentar la huelga, el 28 de octubre habrá una concentración ante la Consejería de Educación para “reivindicar una universidad de calidad y libre de represión”. Y en la semana de los paros se celebrarán jornadas de la Uni en la calle, donde docentes impartirán algunos de los contenidos de sus clases fuera del aula. Esta forma de protesta se inauguró en 2012 para hacer frente a la subida de tasas y bajada de becas impulsada por el ministro José Ignacio Wert en plena crisis económica. El escenario, sin embargo, ahora es otro.

#1159. EU promotes sovereign, trusted AI as it struggles to catch US and China

At an international AI summit in Dublin, EU leaders promoted trusted and independent artificial intelligence. Critics question whether the bloc can close the gap with the US and China while maintaining strict regulation.

If supremacy in artificial intelligence was an Olympic discipline, there would only be two serious contenders for gold on current trajectories: the US and China. The European Union, as has been the case in many areas of cutting-edge technology in recent times, is barely in the AI conversation.

Former European Central Bank President Mario Draghi, whose 2024 report highlighted the EU's desperate need to be more innovative to become more competitive, said recently that AI is "perhaps the most promising" route the EU has to raise growth today. However, he decried the fact that the European Union controls little of the value chain.

"Being cut off from AI, once the economy runs on it, would be more like being cut off from the US financial system," he wrote in an opinion piece for the Financial Times. "The effects would be catastrophic."

Draghi's spirit was on full display in Dublin on Wednesday at an international AI summit the Irish government convened as part of its six-month stint hosting the rotating EU presidency.

The summit's motto, "Harnessing AI to Revolutionize Europe's Competitiveness," might as well have been dreamed up by the Italian former prime minister.

Harnessing AI has become a lot more complicated. A slew of controversies around AI agents going rogue, from the Hugging Face attack in June when 1,200 agents hacked an online platform, to an Anthropic-designed agent sending a fake tip to US police over an unsolved murder, have caused alarm.

Many from within the tech industry, including Microsoft founder Bill Gates and the leading AI frontier labs themselves, have called for a development pausein order for safety measures to catch up.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yet positivity was largely the name of the game at the summit, with tech and AI industry leaders joining Irish and EU politicians to declare AI's transformative economic and societal potential — while also emphasizing the need for strong regulation and safety standards.

Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin made it clear that Ireland was all in on AI. He echoed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's recent assertion that the technology represented a "tipping point." He also repeatedly highlighted what he sees as the bloc's commitment to safety.

"We are determined to capture the dividend by mitigating the risks," Martin told the event. "In Europe, we have charted our path ... balancing innovation and opportunity with a trustworthy, human-centered approach to AI."

Meanwhile, Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, security and democracy, revealed at the event that the EU had begun its first enforcement actions under its new AI Act, requesting information around security and safety from advanced AI model providers.

However, other topics that concern AI's many critics, from those fearing the massive environmental impact of data centers to others warning about possible AI-related job losses, were largely absent from the discussions.

Outside the venue, a group of protesters led by People Before Profit, a left-wing Irish political party, criticized the summit for not focusing on these issues.

"There is a deliberate blurring of the line here with the type of AI that is being promoted," Alexandra Day, one of the protest organizers, told DW.

"It is really being pushed on workers with very little consent. There's no right for workers to opt out of using AI now that it's coming into the workplace."

A sense of urgency was palpable from the speakers inside the summit. Executives from some of the world's biggest AI and tech firms talked up Europe's potential. Yet the EU evidently has plenty of ground to catch up on in terms of AI development.

Despite ramping up its data center capacity, it still lags far behind the US and China. It hosts 5% of the world's AI computing capacity compared to around 75% for the US.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The EU is conspicuously absent from lists of the leading AI frontier labs, with only French company Mistral coming close to rivaling the top labs. Its production of leading-edge chips is also nowhere near that of the top US or Taiwanese producers.

As part of its plan to make ground on the US and China, the Irish government, in its role as EU presidency host, presented a policy document at the event.

The so-called "Dublin Declaration" outlines political commitments to strengthen Europe's AI capabilities, including infrastructure investment and financial backing for European AI companies.

In keeping with Draghi's calls for Europe to develop its own AI sovereignty, particularly in supply chains and infrastructure, the declaration suggests that European firms reliant on non-EU cloud and computing services may face additional compliance pressures.

However, not everyone is convinced by the EU's capacity to either ramp up AI capacity or develop effective regulation.

Eddie Wilson, CEO of European airline Ryanair, said he doubted Brussels could regulate AI well without stifling innovation.

"The last thing you want is people regulating this industry who don't know anything about it," he told DW. "That's generally what happens in Brussels."

Ryanair recently made a major deal with Google to use its cloud data system and its AI platform Gemini Enterprise. It's precisely the kind of collaboration with US AI supply chains that the EU says it wants companies to move away from.

"I worry for Europe because these tech companies need to move at speed," said Wilson. He believes the environment in the US is more amenable to innovation.

"If they're not going to do it here, they're going to do it elsewhere. They're going to do it in China and they're going to do it in the US."

#1163. Princess Anne begins her official visit to Hong Kong in 1971 – from the SCMP archive

On this day 55 years ago, Princess Anne received a warm welcome to British Hong Kong, sailing Victoria Harbour to kick off her royal tour

This article was first published on October 27, 1971.

Princess Anne, radiant in a stylish knee-length beige suit and a matching wide-brimmed hat, flew in yesterday (October 26, 1971) to a warm welcome from the people of Hong Kong.

She begins her official visits today (October 27, 1971) – a public holiday – when thousands of people will be able to see her during her calls at places like the Tung Wah Hospital, the Po Leung Kuk and the ancient Man Mo Temple.

The Princess, who has heard a lot about this “Pearl of the Orient” from her father, will do a little sightseeing, and perhaps a little shopping too in Sheung Wan, a district which boasts a history almost as long as that of the Colony itself.

#1166. Aislamiento o ventilación: el debate energético de los arquitectos se dirime en un piso piloto de Alicante

La normativa que rige las construcciones en España divide a los especialistas ante el aumento de las temperaturas y la necesidad de reducir el consumo eléctrico

El objetivo es el confort y la sostenibilidad. Lograr que la temperatura de las viviendas oscile entre los 19 y los 27 grados, intervalo térmico en el que no haría falta el uso de aparatos de refrigeración o calefacción. Pero los arquitectos se debaten entre dos modelos diametralmente diferentes.

La línea oficial, la del Consejo Superior de los Colegios de Arquitectos de España (CSCAE), apuesta por edificios “muy bien aislados para reducir el consumo” energético, según Laureano Matas, su vicepresidente. Desde el ámbito mediterráneo, y en general, desde la costa, donde la humedad es una variable ineludible, proponen en cambio la ventilación y el sombreado de las casas, con una mayor intervención del usuario. En ambos casos han encontrado un obstáculo: el apartado de eficiencia energética del código técnico, la normativa que rige cualquier construcción.

Una especie de piso piloto repleto de sensores es el centro de operaciones del Departamento de Construcciones Arquitectónicas de la Universidad de Alicante (UA). “Podemos demostrar que una casa del siglo XVIII se comportaba mejor que las actuales”, asegura Carlos Pérez Carramiñana, profesor, uno de los integrantes del grupo que dirige Ángel Benigno González. Todas sus investigaciones tienen la mirada puesta en allanar los complicados cálculos que los arquitectos deben aplicar para que el código permita propuestas diferentes al aislamiento. “Meter los datos en el edificio virtual que se proyecta exige un esfuerzo tecnológico importante”, concede Matas.

Cuatro variables lo cambiarían todo, a juicio del grupo de la UA. La protección solar mediante balcones y otros elementos de sombra, como toldos o las lamas de las persianas mallorquinas. La ventilación, no computable por el programa informático que les impone el código técnico, subrayan, que obliga a más aislamientos y aires acondicionados. La ganancia solar, que aprovecha el sol del invierno con ventanales más grandes. Y la inercia térmica, el uso de materiales capaces de retener el frío o el calor y que “con la industrialización de la vivienda”, se han cambiado por materiales con los que las viviendas “se calientan o enfrían muy rápido”, indica Carramiñana. “Ajustando estas medidas hemos rebajado las horas de ocupación de vivienda que se salen de la temperatura de confort de un 20% a solo un 4%”, afirma.

La legislación está “pensada para casas cerradas, sin porche ni patios, cubos aislados y herméticos todo el año”, “lo cual es un sacrilegio en el sur de Europa, porque nosotros tenemos que ventilar”, añade María Isabel Pérez Millán, profesora e integrante del grupo. “Si en España solo te dedicas a aislar, con planchas externas, en un clima en el que el sol entra por las ventanas, solo producirás un efecto invernadero”, avisa. Con ventanas completamente herméticas, “la humedad de climas con esta variable muy alta no sale”. Las paredes se resienten y puede aparecer el moho. Carramiñana cita al INE e informes de diferentes ministerios para advertir de que “entre el 40 y el 60% de la población española”, según la franja que se elija, “vive a menos de 50 kilómetros del mar”.

En departamentos públicos de vivienda ya aprovechan el pequeño resquicio que deja el código técnico para introducir novedades si demuestran que son válidas. El Instituto Metropolitano de Promoción de Suelo y Gestión Patrimonial (IMPSOL) del área metropolitana de Barcelona promueve “edificios con voluntad de permanencia, materiales de bajas emisiones y autosuficientes”, manifiesta su director, Josep Maria Borrell. “Ya sabemos que no necesitamos calefacción, apenas unos días al año. Y en verano, el 100% de nuestra ventilación es cruzada o generada por ventiladores, nada de aires acondicionados”, sentencia.

Un atrio circular común en una promoción en Sant Just Desvern. Persianas alicantinas con varios usos en un edificio de Castelldefels. Un sistema de enrejado de seguridad que permite la ventilación en un inmueble de Montgat. Ventanales de varios tamaños y un aparcamiento que sirve de respiradero en El Masnou. Son algunas de las innovaciones adjudicadas por el IMPSOL y que exigen la implicación de los nuevos propietarios. “No damos opción; en un momento, con poca oferta y mucha demanda, premiamos a quien esté dispuesto a vivir de forma sostenible”. “El código técnico es una normativa que no nos encaja, porque mantiene una estrategia que con el cambio climático hará que nos achicharremos en 2050”, declara Borrell.

“En las Baleares se genera mucha corriente térmica por la diferencia entre la temperatura del mar y la de la tierra; corren muchas brisas”, explica José Francisco Reynés, director general de Vivienda y Arquitectura de la Consejería de Vivienda, Territorio y Movilidad de las islas. En sus proyectos, tratan de aprovecharlas. “Son variables difíciles de introducir en el programa, aunque permite soluciones innovadoras”, reconoce. Pero “viendo la evolución de la temperatura en el centro y norte de Europa, a quienes lo han redactado les hará replantearse la edificación, sobre todo de cara al verano”, avisa. “Ya le ven las orejas al lobo, daban por residual el uso de aires acondicionados y ahora igual se lo plantean”.

En el CSCAE no comparten este punto de vista, indica Matas. Explica que el código técnico es el reglamento en el que se deben apoyar todas las construcciones de España en materia de seguridad y habitabilidad. Nació en 2006 a partir de una normativa de la Unión Europea; está regulado por la Ley de Ordenación de la Edificación, de 1999, “ha sido sometido a varias revisiones y las seguirá habiendo”, porque la presentación de alegaciones es constante. El próximo 15 de septiembre, el CSCAE se reunirá de nuevo con representantes del Ministerio de Vivienda.

“Es cierto que ha cundido la idea de que la ventilación está prohibida” y que “de manera indirecta, parece propiciar viviendas estancas”, admite. Que promueve unos “niveles de aislamiento” procedentes de los países del norte continental, “donde no se abren las ventanas”, similares a los de las passive houses, una corriente también nacida en ámbitos fríos y que incide en la hermeticidad y la renovación de aire por medios mecánicos. Sin embargo, esta propuesta también choca con el código técnico, que “no considera” e incluso “penaliza” la envolvente, que Matas define como “la piel del edificio”, y que “debería entenderse como un elemento fundamental”.

No obstante, señala que “tenemos herramientas para demostrar que no tenemos que llegar a la estanqueidad” de Alemania o Noruega, por ejemplo, sostiene. Y reconoce que “por salubridad, necesitamos renovaciones puntuales del aire” para las que se “proponen sistemas mecánicos o híbridos para recuperar el calor o el frío”, según la época del año. El código debería “trasladar a las diferentes regiones sus necesidades climáticas”, “tiene que ser más cercano a la realidad y más amable”, zanja.

#1168. Formula One in Rwanda: Sportswashing claims vs. hopes for African legacy

Formula One will return to Africa for the first time since 1993. There is concern Rwanda are using it as another sportswashing opportunity, but there is also hope the event's legacy can impact wider African society.

Rwanda's sports portfolio has grown after confirming it will host Formula One races from the early 2030s. The track is to be built in Bugesera near Kigali International Airport, which Qatar Airways, an F1 sponsor, owns 60% of.

"To be an African and to see it happening in real time, for me in my lifetime because Kyalami [the track in South Africa where F1 was last hosted in Africa] was before I was born, I'm more than happy to have it on the continent," South African presenter and content creator Nqobile Khwezi told Sky Sports.

"To be able to give that taste back to the rest of the world and the audience of Formula One would be an absolute delight."

F1 have also highlighted the benefits for the host nation.

"Through this race we have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to our more than 100 million fans across Africa and firmly believe that sport can be a positive force for good," an F1 spokesperson told The Athletic.

DW contacted Rwanda's Ministry of Sports for comment, but did not receive a promised reply.

For the country's President, Paul Kagame, another move into sport is hardly a surprise given his ventures into European football and the NBA in recent years. Rwanda even sponsored Bayern Munich, but fan and media backlash over the deal caused the Bundesliga club to drop the commercial element with the country's tourist arm, Visit Rwanda, last year.

With many critics accusing Kagame and Rwanda of sportswashing, the arrival of F1, a sport valued at approximately $34 billion (€30 billion), according to sports business website Sportico, brings fresh questions.

"This deal may have positive economic and social impacts across Africa, but we should be realistic about circumstances on the ground in Rwanda," Lewis Mudge, Central Africa director at Human Rights Watch, told DW.

"Human Rights Watch wrote to Formula One in February 2025 to ask how it is addressing the human rights impacts of its activities, including regarding Rwanda and other countries’ bid to host a F1 Grand Prix. We did not receive a response," said Mudge, adding that F1 should only approve racing in the country after addressing the human rights impacts of hosting a race there.

"Rwanda, like other countries, has also used high-profile sports deals and races in the past to distract from its abysmal human rights record. Rwanda is currently the power behind the abusive M23 rebel group in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and its military forces have been implicated in unlawful displacement and deaths of civilians in violation of international humanitarian law."

For Mohamed Keita, returning the sport to Africa is overdue, but the choice of country is telling.

"The fact that F1 excluded the world's second largest continent from its race series for three decades is indefensible in its own right and is actually a stain on a sport which claims to be global," Keita, Senior Policy Officer, Africa, at the Human Rights Foundation told DW.

"The choice of Rwanda, however, is deeply controversial," Keita continued. "Rwanda is a brutal dictatorship. Its regime is under partial US sanctions for its military occupations of territories of eastern DRC. Rwanda is arming and financing a militia involved in rapes, massacres, forced recruitment and violent plunder of natural resources."

Formula One has history on the continent. In 1958, there was a race in Morocco and more recently, in South Africa, where the last F1 race in Africa took place at the Kyalami racetrack in Johannesburg in 1993. Many previous races in the country were overshadowed by the policy of apartheid.

Despite Rwanda securing the deal first, South Africa believes it will host before them. When Rwanda announced their hosting, South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa sent his congratulations in a social media post, adding: "This contract is a recognition of the capabilities of the Rwandan nation and of our continent more broadly."

South Africa's Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie also congratulated Rwanda, but pivotally added that South Africa "will get F1, even before 2030."

There is no denying that hosting a race in South Africa would cost significantly less time and money, given the existing infrastructure.

In either country, comes a legacy opportunity. Sports such as Formula One, where the majority of decision-makers, drivers, team principles and engineers are white men, are a living example of the unlevel playing field. The hope of racing in Africa is that it will go some way to changing that.

"I think that's the kind of aspirational drive of hosting a Formula 1 race. It's leveraging STEM [science, technology, engineering, and mathematics] education, technology, aspiring young girls or women, leveling the playing fields, if it's for all those other reasons and we can make it work then I say yes to Formula 1 in Africa," Dr. Kamilla Swart-Arries, an expert in South Africa's events industry and the legacy of sports events, told DW in 2024.

"I hope F1 will consider further investment in developing African talent in motorsport," said Keita. "There's a lot of good that F1 can do if it genuinely wants to grow the sport in Africa, but Rwanda does not make sense at this moment unless you're doing it purely for the benefit of one dictator and the beauty of the hilly terrain."

"The proposition here is to take the world's most expensive sport to Rwanda, which is one of the world's poorest countries. Rwanda is consistently listed among the UN's list of the 25 least developed countries in the world," said Keita.

The return of the fastest show in sports is a huge moment for both Rwanda and Africa. It raises questions about President Kagame's use of sport, but it also offers an opportunity to shape the event's legacy. Unlike the race Rwanda wants to host, this is not about being the fastest but about making the most of the chance.

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate for presidential re-election, celebrates after winning the presidential runoff election in Brazil | Photo Credit: Reuters

Leaders from Left parties on Monday (October 26, 2026) congratulated Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on his historic fourth presidential win, with CPI(M) General Secretary M.A. Baby saying it offers hope to people's movements fighting for workers' rights.

Mr. Lula da Silva, a vocal critic of U.S. President Donald Trump, was re-elected on Sunday (October 25, 2026) in a result that offers relief to critics of expanding U.S. influence in Latin America. With 100% of the votes counted, Brazil's electoral court announced that the soon-to-be 81-year-old Mr. Lula had secured an unassailable lead of nearly 4.4 million votes over his opponent Flávio Bolsonaro.

Also Read: Lula wins a record fourth presidential term as Brazil defeats far-right, defies Trump and Meta

In a post on X, Mr. Baby congratulated Mr. Lula and the people of Brazil on the "historic fourth presidential term".

"Salute to the Workers' Party, PCdoB and other progressive and democratic forces who valiantly fought to make this victory possible," the CPI(M) leader said.

ALSO WATCH Brazil presidential election 2026: Lula da Silva wins historic fourth term

Referring to the ongoing protests in India against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral rolls, which has led to the removal of over 13 crore voters from the list, Mr. Baby said Mr. Lula's victory would "reinvigorate" the youth in India.

"Your remarkable campaign showed the world that the politics of hatred and division can be defeated when the people stand united. This victory offers hope to people's movements everywhere fighting for workers' rights, social justice and public welfare," he said.

"The youth who took to the streets to defend democracy will reinvigorate our own youth who are fighting the same battle here," he added.

Mr. Baby said the people had sent a clear message: "Brazil is no one's backyard!"

CPI (ML) Liberation General Secretary Dipankar Bhattacharya also congratulated the people of Brazil for defeating the "U.S.-backed far-right".

"Congratulations, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, on being reelected President of Brazil. Well done, Brazil, for defeating the US-backed far-right!," he said in a post on X.

Mr. Bhattacharya also referred to Serbia, where long-serving strongman leader Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat on Sunday (October 25, 2026) in an election that pitted him and his right-wing party against a diverse student-led opposition movement that spent two years protesting his government.

"Two elections, two inspiring outcomes! In Brazil, Lula has won a fourth term defeating Bolsonaro. In Serbia, the student movement has now ended the increasingly authoritarian reign of Aleksandar Vučić," Mr. Bhattacharya said.

Mr. Vučić, who had been endorsed by Russian President Vladimir Putin and accused the student movement of being a foreign-backed attempt to unseat him, had wielded near-absolute power in the Balkan country for 14 years.

He was seeking to become Serbia's Prime Minister after serving nearly two full terms as President. He resigned from the presidency last month to lead the campaign.

#1189. La nuova trattoria a Milano del pizzaiolo che fa le pizze, ma non qui

Noto a Milano come pizzaiolo, Pasquale Pometto ha aperto da qualche settimana una trattoria, Don Mario, tra via Torino e le 5Vie. Più precisamente, a Casa dei Grifi, al 5 di via Valpetrosa, una traversa di via Torino. Un palazzo risalente al Quattrocento, con un bellissimo cortile colonnato rinascimentale, che ospita due locali ormai storici di Milano, Govinda e il Football Pub, oltre naturalmente a Damario.

Govinda è un ristorante vegetarian-vegano che segue i principi dell’alimentazione ayurvedica (è un Hare Krishna Restaurant), aperto più di 40 anni fa. Al suo fianco, pochi metri prima di Don Mario, il Football English Pub, un vero e proprio pub inglese, aperto a Milano dal 1996.

Ma via Valpetrosa e Don Mario si trovano al centro di un’area di Milano che si estende lungo i due lati di via Torino, ricca di locali e in particolare di pizzerie. A poche decine di metri da qui, ad esempio, troviamo Confine. Ma lo stesso isolato di Don Mario ospita la pizzeria Piz e, sul retro, Pomet, due dei locali di Pasquale Pometto a Milano.

Anche se Pasquale Pometto a Milano fa il pizzaiolo, il menù di Don Mario non prevede pizze. Pochi piatti, una cucina tradizionale, il tiro magari ancora da aggiustare, ma promettente. Non tanto per originalità, o per fedeltà a una presunta tradizione, quanto per normalità e onestà.

Un cuoco d’esperienza, che a volte si lascia prendere la mano dalla salagione. Un servizio disinvolto, accogliente, amichevole, a partire da Giancarlo, socio in sala, anche lui una lunga esperienza. Se proprio vogliamo, a un certo punto un cameriere si aggirava per la sala un po’ a vuoto. Niente di che.

Il menù mette in primo piano l’ossobuco con risotto alla milanese (26 €). Giusto per ribadire che la trattoria Don Mario sta a Milano. Ben cucinato, un filo salato, forse avrei preferito l’ossobuco appena più morbido. Come ‘benvenuto della cucina’, un medaglione di riso al salto, macchiato di pomodoro e fiordilatte.

Provato anche un piatto di tortellini in brodo tradizionali (13 €), non male. I tortellini li fa un pastificio in periferia.

Il Parmigiano arriva in tavola in una classica scodella con cucchiaino.

Un must: la trippa, tipico piatto da trattoria a Milano, a cui Don Mario non poteva certo sottrarsi. Non era però alla milanese, con i fagioli bianchi: ma, come recita il menù, trattasi di “trippa tradizionale italiana” (14 €). Ma l’assenza dei fagioli l’ha resa appena un po’ blanda.

Niente dolce – ero tentato dal tiramisù, ma viene servito in un piccolo contenitore a forma di water, abbastanza respingente. Ma forse sono io che faccio un po’ troppo il fighetto: gli altri avventori, turisti per lo più, lo apprezzavano molto. Consiglio comunque di proporne una doppia versione, la seconda in contenitori più normali, per noi clienti snob della trattoria Don Mario – dopotutto, siamo in una zona elegante, le 5Vie, a due passi dal Duomo.

Invece del dolce, un piattino di formaggi (omaggio). Ecco, non prendo mai formaggi a fine pasto. Male.

Pochi piatti in carta. Gli antipasti (caprese, acciughe del Cantabrico, tagliere, crudo e mozzarella) vanno da 12 a 18 euro. I primi (trofie, carbonara, lasagne) da 13 a 14 euro (16 € i tagliolini alla colatura di alici). 10 euro per il minestrone, 12/13 euro pasta e fagioli, taglierini e ceci.

Oltre all’ossobuco con risotto a 26 euro, la trattoria Don Mario propone al pubblico di Milano un tortino di parmigiana a 18 euro. Ma anche un poco comune spezzatino (alla Don Mario, 15 €). Ci sono anche alcune insalatone a 13/14 euro.

Per antipasto-primo-secondo si spendono in media sui 45 euro.

Allora. Ho scoperto che la trattoria Don Mario era uno dei locali di Pasquale Pometto solo dopo la mia cena. Stavo uscendo, quando ho incrociato un tipo che entrando dice a Giancarlo (socio e maître del locale) qualcosa tipo stai attento a parlare con questo qua, lo conosco, è Emanuele Bonati. Dice anche qualcosa d’altro, io gli chiedo ci conosciamo?, lui dice io ti conosco, chiedo chi sei?, risponde uno che va in giro.

Solo dopo Giancarlo mi dice che era Pometto, il proprietario – ci siamo solo incrociati sui social, ovviamente non l’ho riconosciuto. E pure sono stato, e ho scritto, nei suoi locali: AM, anni fa, e poi Piz e ’Napiz, e Pomet, che allora faceva panini di pizza. Sia Piz che ’Napiz figuravano ai primissimi posti fra le migliori pizzerie di Milano – e ’Napiz è tuttora prima.

Don Mario si trova in pieno centro a Milano, in una via pedonale semiclandestina. L’ho scoperto quasi per caso, passeggiando, in una delle zone più belle e antiche della città, ricca di tracce della Milano romana e medievale. Per di più, nascosta dietro la curva che conduce verso piazza San Sepolcro: bisogna proprio cercarla.

Uno direbbe: ci sarà poca gente, magari milanesi che abitano o lavorano in zona. E invece ho scoperto che la trattoria Don Mario a Milano è quasi una meta internazionale. Ci sono stato due volte, la sera, e c’erano comunque più stranieri che italiani. A mezzogiorno, la trattoria è pressoché sempre esaurita.

Come se non bastasse, le pareti sono ricoperte da graffiti, firme, nomi di clienti e città – moltissimi stranieri. Un po’ come le cartoline che una volta i clienti mandavano alla loro trattoria, o bar, del cuore. Oggi che le cartoline sono quasi scomparse, e che sarebbe difficile esporre eventuali email di saluti, ecco i graffiti. Don Mario si adatta al desiderio di convivialità e di familiarità che pervade anche Milano, e rifornisce di penne e pastelli i suoi clienti. Che gradiscono molto, con aria divertita.

All’esterno, Don Mario è piuttosto anonima, con due vetrine appena ravvivate da volantini che magnificano la specialità della casa e di Milano – il risotto alla milanese. Il design degli interni è estremamente semplice: corridoio d’ingresso, la cucina sul fondo, una cinquantina di posti disposti lungo le pareti, qualche tavolino al centro. A rallegrare la vista è il consueto bric-à-brac che raccoglie poster, quadretti, neon, fotografie, specchietti. Un effetto a metà fra il nostalgico e l’autentico, lontano dai dettami del design contemporaneo. Il tutto fa di Don Mario a Milano un locale insolito, piacevole, rilassante, accogliente.

Don Mario. V. Valpetrosa, 5, 20123 Milano MI. Telefono: 02 617 8502. Instagram

"Esco, vedo gente, mangio cose" Lavora nell'editoria da quasi 50 anni. Legge compulsivamente da sessant'anni. Mangia anche da oltre 60 anni – e da una quindicina degusta e racconta quello che mangia, e il perché e il percome, online e non. Tuttavia, verrà ricordato (forse) per aver fatto la foto della pizza di Cracco.
